articles.title: Cultural Representations of Memory in Contemporary Greek Audiovisual Culture: The Synthetic Revival of the Kaisariani Photographs as a Case Study
articles.authors: Nikolaos Aletras
articles.abstract: This article examines how the memory of the past is represented today within Greek audiovisual culture, taking as its case study the algorithmic colouring and animation of a set of rare photographs documenting the execution of two hundred Greek resistance fighters at the Kaisariani rifle range on 1 May 1944. The photographs, taken from the perspective of the perpetrators, were acquired by the Greek state, designated as a cultural monument, and shortly afterwards processed by users through generative artificial intelligence tools and disseminated across YouTube, TikTok, and the online press. Drawing on cultural memory theory, on recent scholarship concerning synthetic pasts, and on empirical evidence regarding the mnemonic effects of AI generated video, the study argues that the AI revival of archival photographs constitutes a new representational practice rather than a technical enhancement. Through a threefold methodology of structural image analysis, platform based performance analysis, and digital reception ethnography, the article demonstrates that the same source archive gives rise to divergent representations conditioned by the affordances of each platform, and that these synthetic representations exert measurable mnemonic and ideological effects on their audiences. The Kaisariani case thereby provides both an empirical demonstration and a methodological template for a wider research programme situated at the intersection of cinema, documentary, digital archives, and generative artificial intelligence.

articles.title: Structured-data reporting shapes the apparent causes of phase-3 trial failure: an automated decomposition of ClinicalTrials.gov records
articles.authors: Tommy Carstensen
articles.abstract:
Objective. To decompose the causes of phase-3 failure from ClinicalTrials.gov automatically, to identify where the registry misleads, and to compare the result with the manual study of Hwang et al. (2016).

Methods. Cross-sectional study of registry records: every phase-3 registration with posted results or with status terminated, withdrawn or suspended (18,466 in all). A failure is a trial that stopped early for a reason other than benefit, or that completed and missed its primary endpoint. The primary analysis covers trials that enrolled and started in 2017-2026; registrations withdrawn before enrollment enter a sensitivity analysis only. Primary-endpoint success was read from the structured statistical-analysis records. Termination reasons were classified by large-language-model agents, and a sample of first-pass labels was adjudicated blind by a stronger model. A stratum of 17 large pharmaceutical companies ("big pharma") is compared with Hwang et al., who classified failed drug programs of 1998-2008.

Results. Among trials that enrolled, efficacy (37.1%, 95% CI 34.9 to 39.5) and operational causes (36.5%, 34.3 to 38.8) were the two largest causes of failure. Counting withdrawn registrations as failures put operational causes first (operational 40.2%, efficacy 27.2%). Only 47.3% of completed trials with posted results carried a usable primary p-value; imputing misses for the others that had a comparator arm raised the efficacy share to 46.8% and lowered the operational share to 30.9%. In big pharma, efficacy accounted for 53.7% of failures (program-clustered 95% CI 47.6 to 59.6), not distinguishable from the 56.7% of Hwang et al. (clustered p = 0.46; 95% CI of the difference -11.0 to 5.0 points). The share was 48.3% among trials of drugs with no earlier phase-3 win (difference -17.1 to 0.2 points, unclustered p = 0.057), and 45.8%, lower than theirs, with withdrawn registrations counted (clustered p = 0.0052). Safety accounted for 3.1% of big-pharma failures (2.5% for all sponsors) against 17.2% in Hwang et al. First-pass labels agreed with the adjudication for 83.3% of a balanced sample (95% CI 77.0 to 88.2).

Conclusions. A registry-only decomposition of phase-3 failure depends on whether registrations that never enrolled count as failures and on how completed trials without a usable primary p-value are treated. With the former set aside, efficacy is the leading cause of failure in big pharma; its observed share is not distinguishable from the 2016 manual estimate, a comparison by proxy that does not establish agreement. For all sponsors efficacy is only slightly ahead of operational causes as observed, and further ahead under an imputation or a stricter win rule, each resting on assumptions. Safety is recorded far less often than in the manual estimate; the registry fields cannot show how many safety-driven stops are registered as sponsor or business decisions. The validation was model-based and covered the first classification pass only.

articles_hidden.title: Assessment of facilitators and barriers to open science implementation in the Brain-Heart Interconnectome Research Program: a qualitative study
articles_hidden.authors: Edward Xu; Marc Antonino Albert; Gustavo de Paula Dídimo; Anna Catharina Vieira Armond; David Moher; Emilio I. Alarcón; Ian D Graham; Krystina B. Lewis; Alexandra King; Malcolm King
articles_hidden.abstract: Open science improves research transparency, reproducibility, and equity. This qualitative study assessed facilitators and barriers to implementing open science practices within the Brain-Heart Interconnectome (BHI), an interdisciplinary research program funded by the Canada First Research Excellence Fund (CFREF) to advance prevention and treatment of brain-heart conditions (e.g., stroke and cardiac disease). The study aimed to explore perceptions and behaviours of BHI-funded investigators and teams regarding open science mandate implementation. Data were collected through virtual focus groups with 36 participants from 17 funded projects. Participants include principal investigators, research staff, trainees, and Indigenous Elders and Knowledge Holders. Focus groups were designed and analyzed using the Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF). Barriers included limited financial and logistical resources, intellectual property and ethical concerns, and a lack of guidance and training. Facilitators included mandates from journals and funders, along with perceived improvements in research accountability and quality. Findings were mapped onto the Behaviour Change Wheel (BCW) using the Capability, Opportunity, Motivation – Behaviour (COM-B) model, providing a comprehensive framework for understanding behaviour change and informed implementation strategy development. These insights will be critical to effective and efficient open science uptake within BHI and are likely transferable to other biomedical and interdisciplinary research programs.

articles_hidden.title: An evaluation of the quality of published papers from researchers affiliated with the Australian Institute of Sport
articles_hidden.authors: Adrian Barnett; Alexander Gibson; Ran Tian; David N Borg; Paolo Menaspà
articles_hidden.abstract: The Australian Institute of Sport (AIS) has a central role in high-performance sport in Australia. An important part of this role is to support research in a range of sports disciplines. Sports science research has had many reproducibility issues; therefore, it is important to consider whether the research supported by the AIS is of high quality. To examine this, we conducted a retrospective audit of published papers to estimate the prevalences of good research practice and identify areas for improvement. We extracted information from papers using automated text extraction and research assistants. We identified 280 papers published between 2020 and 2024 with at least one author who was affiliated with the Australian Institute of Sport. The results showed a low engagement with robust study planning, including pre-registration, analysis plans, and sample size calculations. More encouraging results were that almost all papers had research questions that were well justified and answered. Overall, we found many areas where research quality could be improved by better adherence to established good research practices.

articles.title: Associations Between Motives and Emotion Regulation Strategy Use in Everyday Life
articles.authors: Valentina Bianchi; Tyler Thorne; Elise Katherine Kalokerinos; Felicity Angelopoulos; Marina Milyavskaya
articles.abstract: Theories suggest that capturing people’s motives (the ‘why’) for regulating allows for a better understanding of how people choose to regulate their emotions. Yet, little empirical research systematically examines the link between motives and regulation strategies. Addressing this gap, we conducted an experience-sampling study to: 1) capture the prevalence of a wide range of regulatory motives (hedonic, instrumental) in everyday life and (2) test whether motives were associated with the selection of six regulation strategies, controlling for affect intensity. Data were collected in Australia in 2024, from an adult community sample (NID=303;  Nobs=3496; Mage = 26.11; 80% women, mostly identifying as East Asian and South-East Asian). Hedonic motives were most frequent, but instrumental motives were also common. Regulatory motives showed distinct strategy selection profiles: prohedonic motives were linked with greater distraction and cognitive reappraisal, whereas contrahedonic motives were rare, and only predicted greater rumination. Different instrumental motives were differentially associated with the use of specific strategies. Only cognitive strategies (reappraisal and rumination) were linked to multiple motives, being significantly associated with prohedonic, contrahedonic (rumination), personal performance, social, epistemic, and eudaimonic motives. By investigating the momentary association between a broad range of motives and regulation strategies, this work suggests that emotion regulation strategies are associated not only with what people feel, but also with why they regulate. Future empirical work should explicitly consider individuals’ regulatory motives, rather than assuming regulatory effectiveness based on hedonic motives.

articles.title: Digital Stress: Theoretical Conceptualizations, Empirical Findings, and Tasks for Future Research
articles.authors: Leonard Reinecke; Frank M. Schneider; Alicia Gilbert
articles.abstract: Over the past decade, mobile Internet-enabled digital devices have provided ubiquitous access to media content and communication, resulting in unprecedented levels of “always on” media use. As a consequence, many users feel stressed and strained by the new demands of digital media use. A fast-growing field of research has addressed such forms of “digital stress” and its psychological implications. The present chapter provides a review and theoretical integration of the state of digital stress research. After an introduction to the basic psychological mechanisms underlying stress reactions based on the Transactional Model of Stress (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984), the chapter reviews and synthesizes existing definitions of digital stress. It then summarizes and systematizes key empirical findings regarding the central predictors, boundary conditions, and effects of digital stress. The review concludes with a discussion of recent developments, open questions, and future challenges for the field of digital stress research.

articles.title: Who cares about human rights and the environment? Replicating and extending McFarland’s structural model
articles.authors: Taciano L Milfont; Felipe Vilanova
articles.abstract: Why are some people more committed than others to protecting human rights worldwide? McFarland (2010) proposed that people high in Right-Wing Authoritarianism (RWA) and Social Dominance Orientation (SDO) are less committed to universal human rights partly because they are more ethnocentric and identify less with humanity as a whole. We tested this model in a larger sample of US adults (N = 512). The core model was supported: RWA and SDO were linked to greater ethnocentrism, which was associated with weaker identification with all humanity (IWAH) and human-rights commitment, whereas IWAH was associated with stronger commitment. As McFarland found, SDO also had a direct negative association with commitment that empathy did not explain. However, McFarland’s original hypothesized model fit significantly better than his final trimmed model. Two previously excluded paths emerged in our larger sample, linking SDO with lower IWAH and RWA with weaker human-rights commitment. Extending the model to environmentalism revealed several similar associations, but poor overall model fit. Our findings support McFarland’s framework while refining its specification and suggesting limits to its generalizability across domains and national contexts.

articles.title: The longform recordings era: The importance of scientific communities in advancing language development research
articles.authors: Federica Bulgarelli; Monica E Ellwood-Lowe; Naja Ferjan Ramirez; Hillary Ganek; Jessica Elizabeth Kosie; Alfa Montiel; Ashlie H Pankonin; Ritwika VPS; Eva Ståhlberg-Forsén; Sarah Surrain
articles.abstract: Longform recordings — passive audio recordings that capture the audio environment around a child, often for a full day — contribute to our understanding of language acquisition. This manuscript focuses on the practice of investigating children’s natural language experiences using longform recordings and the contributions of international scientific consortia to advancing this methodology. Drawing on a sys-tematic literature search identifying 378 studies, we describe the history of longform recordings, syn-thesize key research findings, and identify opportunities for growth. Further, we describe the impact of international collaborative communities on this work. In particular, we highlight the role of DARCLE (Daylong Recordings of Children’s Linguistic Environments), an international consortium of researchers that, starting in 2014, has spurred major advances in the field, including data sharing platforms and annotation norms, open-source technology for quantifying children’s language environments, and a set of best practices for conducting this research in diverse environments. This community of open discus-sion and data sharing serves as a model for advancing rigor, accessibility, and scale. We conclude with recommendations both to further strengthen research with longform recordings and for international research communities across disciplines.

articles.title: Judging orientation does not elicit the Spatial-Numerical Association of Response Codes: Testing the Neural Overlap Hypothesis
articles.authors: Valter Prpic; Stefano Pileggi; Alberto Mariconda; Serena Mingolo; MAURO MURGIA
articles.abstract: According to the neural overlap hypothesis (Fias et al., 2001), numerical magnitude may influence performance in a non-semantic task when the processing of task-relevant and task-irrelevant information recruits overlapping neural structures. Specifically, because number and orientation processing both engage parietal regions, the account predicts a SNARC effect during orientation judgments, whereas effects should be weaker in tasks with less parietal involvement, such as colour judgments. However, only a few studies have attempted to replicate the original findings. Here, we conducted a large-sample replication of the line orientation task introduced by Fias et al. (2001, Experiment 4) and included letters as a complementary condition. Across two experiments, conducted online and in the laboratory, we consistently failed to detect a SNARC effect for numbers or a SNARC-like effect for letters. A cumulative analysis likewise provided no evidence for either association. These findings fail to replicate a key result supporting the neural overlap hypothesis and suggest that shared parietal processing may not give rise to spatial-numerical associations as robustly as previously assumed.

articles.title: The Influence of Victim Gender and Professional Identity on Perceptions of AI-Generated Image Abuse
articles.authors: Matthew Richard Ivory; Sophie J Nightingale
articles.abstract: Artificially-Generated Non-Consensual Intimate Imagery (AI-NCII) is a form of gender-based violence and sexual abuse. Modern AI tools enable the easy creation of highly realistic NCII, with the potential to cause very real and profound harms to those depicted. Although victim characteristics, such as gender and sexual activity, are known to influence third-party judgements, less is understood about how victims from stigmatised or marginalised groups are judged and how these characteristics influence victim blame and perceptions of harm. In this preregistered vignette study, participants were presented with a hypothetical scenario describing a transgender or cisgender sex worker or office worker who was the victim of AI-NCII creation and subsequent sharing. The ideal victim framework and expectancy violations theory were used to interpret who was blamed and perceived as harmed, and why. Results revealed that sex workers were blamed more and perceived as less harmed than office workers. It was also observed that while transgender victims were blamed more by men than women, they were perceived as experiencing comparable levels of harm to cisgender victims. The findings suggest when victims do not conform to expected norms or are perceived to engage in behaviours inconsistent with ideal victim expectations, public sympathy may be reduced. Future interventions should therefore prioritise education about victimisation and challenge the expectations and beliefs that shape judgements of victims, rather than place responsibility on victims to conform to an ideal or reduce the visibility of their identities.

articles.title: Differences in AI Anxiety: Exploratory Factor Analysis Suggests Similar AI Anxiety Structure in German- and English-Speaking Samples
articles.authors: Nick Sheth; Klemens Weigl
articles.abstract: The mass use of AI applications is transforming human-AI interaction while uncovering and intensifying AI anxieties. To measure these anxieties in German-speaking populations, this study translates and psychometrically evaluates the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale (AIAS) [31]. In contrast to a concurrently German published version by Hajek et al. [9] exploratory factor analysis (EFA) is employed to test whether a distinct anxiety structure emerges from the data. A quota sample (N = 225) with balanced age and gender representation completed an online survey. The full scale (α = .95) and subscales (α = .85-.96) demonstrated good to excellent reliability. EFA identified four factors: learning, AI configuration, replacement, and socio-technical blindness, largely consistent with the original English structure. Five items required removal, suggesting cultural and linguistic specificity. Limitations include the sample’s composition and the factor characteristics. The German AIAS provides a reliable instrument for human-AI interaction research and targeted anxiety interventions.

articles.title: A general method for estimating reliability using Bayesian Measurement Uncertainty
articles.authors: Giacomo Bignardi; Rogier Kievit; Paul - Christian Bürkner
articles.abstract: Unreliable measurement can lead to lower statistical power, attenuated effect sizes and residual confounding. However, estimating reliability can be challenging for complex cognitive and behavioural assessments without test-retest data. Most statistical methods for assessing reliability with a single test administration are designed for fixed-item questionnaires. We introduce a novel Bayesian procedure called relative measurement uncertainty (RMU) for estimating reliability that can be broadly applied, including to many widely used computational models. Our approach draws pairs of samples from each subject's posterior and calculates the correlation between draws. We demonstrate analytically and via simulation that this method provides accurate reliability estimates and well-calibrated credible intervals across linear factor, signal detection and reinforcement learning models. Simulations found that RMU was more accurate (lower root mean square error) than existing measures (coefficient alpha, coefficient H, split-half), but more importantly, it can be applied across a wide range of computational models. RMU offers a general method for estimating reliability, leveraging the modelling flexibility of Bayesian statistical methods.

articles.title: Does creative engagement spill over into risk-taking behavior?
articles.authors: Shenghui Xiaoyong; Zhuoqi Yin; Huimin Kong; KelongLu
articles.abstract: Creative engagement may shape not only the ideas people generate but also how they approach risk in subsequent decisions, yet this possibility remains underexplored. Across three studies, we examined this relationship and whether general self-efficacy or affective state accounts for the relationship. Study 1 (N = 228) used a cross-sectional survey and found that everyday creative ideation behavior was positively associated with overall and domain-specific risk-taking propensity. General self-efficacy did not mediate this association. Study 2 (N = 83) experimentally compared risk taking after creative drawing versus standard coloring using a binary lottery choice. Creative drawing increased affective dominance but did not significantly influence subsequent risk taking. Study 3 (N = 94) compared risk taking after creative writing versus standard typing using a six-level investment-choice task. Creative writing increased both risk taking and affective dominance, but the change in dominance did not mediate the effect on risk taking. These findings suggest that creative engagement can influence subsequent financial risk taking, although the effect may depend on the creative task and the sensitivity of the risk measure. Neither general self-efficacy nor affective dominance explained this relationship, highlighting the need to investigate alternative psychological mechanisms.

articles.title: Do breadth and dose indices of exercise adherence measure the same thing? It depends on how unrecorded sessions are coded
articles.authors: FERNANDO GIMENO MARCO; Estela Prad Lucas
articles.abstract: Adherence to prescribed exercise between supervised sessions is routinely quantified with composite indices built from weekly self-reports, yet whether two reasonably constructed indices agree or diverge can hinge on decisions that are rarely scrutinized. Using weekly records from a community-based chronic-pain exercise program (14 participants, 173 person-weeks), we compared a breadth index (how many prescribed components were performed) with two frequency-based dose indices (uncapped and capped). Between persons, the indices ranked participants almost identically; within persons, however, their agreement proved highly sensitive to a single, usually invisible coding decision—whether components marked as performed but left unquantified are read as zero days. Naive zero-coding implied that breadth and dose capture different things within persons (correlations near .25), whereas activity-compatible scenarios moved these correlations to .41–.76. Rather than defend one imputation, we recommend reporting a bounded sensitivity analysis that brackets the plausible range, and we translate the findings into concrete guidance for designing exercise diaries and tracking apps so that participation and dose are recorded unambiguously.

articles.title: Supporting creativity education in the age of AI: The role of perceived exemplar source
articles.authors: Shenghui Xiaoyong; Yingning Lu; Yihui Liu; Yueyue Ge; Qiannan Ruan; Ke Jiang; KelongLu
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-generated creative exemplars are increasingly used as scalable digital instructional resources in creativity education. However, it remains unclear whether labeling identical exemplars as human- or AI-generated shapes how learners engage in group creative activities. We tested this possibility in 113 dyads using an fNIRS hyperscanning group creative ideation paradigm. Dyads completed creative ideation tasks before, during, and after exemplar-stimulation. During stimulation, the human- and AI-attribution groups received identical exemplars labeled as produced by human or AI, whereas the control group received no exemplar. Human attribution increased idea uniqueness during stimulation relative to both the other phases and the AI-attribution and control groups. AI attribution temporarily increased switching among ideation pathways. Neither behavioral effect persisted after exemplar withdrawal. The two attribution groups did not differ in exemplar-category overlap or nearest-exemplar semantic distance, but human-attribution dyads rated the exemplars as more helpful. Human attribution also increased interbrain synchronization (IBS) in bilateral premotor and supplementary motor cortices during stimulation, whereas AI attribution was associated with decreased IBS in the left supramarginal gyrus and right frontopolar cortex from pre- to post-stimulation. Thus, exemplar-source attribution shapes the process and outcome of group creative ideation, revealing an important social-contextual factor in AI-supported creativity education.

articles.title: Beyond Color: A Constructivist Account of Chromatic Stimuli as Multidimensional Physiological and Psychological Events
articles.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles.abstract: Color science has spent most of its history explaining one thing: the conscious sensation of hue, saturation, and brightness. Yet beside that success sits a growing list of inconvenient findings. Examples include ambiguous colors (one photograph seen as white-and-gold by some and blue-and-black by others); memory colors (a gray banana that looks faintly yellow); color before form (newly sighted patients who see color before objects); imagined or dreamed colors (chromatic experiences generated without light or eyes); aphantasia (people who cannot summon a color in imagination); synesthesia (a printed letter flooded with color); and large, stable individual differences in the colors people report. These are not marginal curiosities or isolated anomalies. They are the ordinary output of a system that the percept-centered framework leaves out. A chromatic stimulus does not simply produce a color percept; it initiates a broad physiological and psychological event, of which the percept is only one part. That percept is constructed at the moment of seeing by memory, language, attention, affect, and culture, and it shapes them in turn, a reciprocal determinism of percept and event. I develop this framework at three levels, as two nested theories: a new theory of color contained within a constructivist model of the entire chromatic event. The account retains trichromatic and some opponent-process theory rather than replacing them, but extends them by predicting phenomena the traditional framework treats as noise. Chief among these are the individual differences that, on this view, become the primary evidence for how color is constructed.

articles.title: Statistical Learning of Distractor Suppression Generalizes Across Contexts Despite Blocked Learning
articles.authors: Milan Geldhof; Brent Vernaillen; Christophe Vanhouwe; Louisa Bogaerts
articles.abstract: Statistical learning can shape visual attention by enabling spatial suppression of locations that frequently contain distractors. Although learned suppression may be context-dependent, the underlying factors driving this dependency remain unclear. While previous research has largely focused on the nature of the context itself, less attention has been paid to how context–regularity pairs are presented, particularly whether they are blocked or intermixed across trials. Multiple uninterrupted pairings may be necessary for less salient contextual cues, such as background colors or images, to support context-dependent learning. The present preregistered, high- powered study (N = 136) therefore used a blocked presentation, with two blocks each pairing a unique background color with a high-frequency distractor location, followed by an intermixed testing phase with equiprobable distractor locations. Results show that although distractors reliably captured attention, the background context did not affect response times in the testing block, with Bayesian analyses providing decisive evidence for context-independent suppression. These results show that implicitly learned distractor suppression is highly robust, persistent, and generalizes across non-task- relevant contexts, even when context–regularity associations are repeated and uninterrupted during learning.

articles.title: Fleeting Attention While Scrolling: Dwell Time and Exposure in Social Media Feeds
articles.authors: Douglas A. Parry; Philipp K. Masur
articles.abstract: Social media feeds expose users to rapidly changing streams of content, but relatively little is known about how long individual posts remain available for processing during user-controlled scrolling. We analyzed high-resolution behavioural logs from a fully interactive, simulated Instagram-like platform, to characterize dwell time and identify factors associated with variation in exposure duration. Preregistered analyses included 43,921 post-viewing episodes from 1,102 participants. Exposure was typically brief and highly variable, with the median dwell time lasting only 0.93 seconds. Mixed-effects models showed little evidence that visual complexity, valence, arousal, thematic content, presence of a face, social reinforcement, or measured individual characteristics were associated with dwell time. Instead, dwell time declined substantially across the browsing sequence and was considerably longer for posts encountered on profile and explore pages than in the main feed. These findings characterize social media browsing as a sequence of heterogeneous, often momentary exposures and demonstrate the value of simulated platforms for studying scrolling behavior at high temporal resolution.

articles.title: On Color and Emotion: What Can Vision Science Learn from the Rorschach?
articles.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles.abstract: For a century, clinicians have recorded how people use color when they interpret inkblots, rank colored cards, or draw. They believed that how a person handles color reveals how that person handles feeling. Vision science has rarely read this literature, and the most complete modern review of color and emotion research excluded it. This paper introduces the projective color literature to vision scientists in plain language. Three conclusions follow. First, the tradition’s central belief, that chromatic color stirs emotion directly, was tested from the 1940s onward and largely failed. Second, narrower findings survived. The degree to which a person lets color lead over form in an ambiguous image is modestly related to several independently assessed clinical, behavioral, and biological outcomes. Some indices that set color in balance with other responses, such as coping versus overload, are also supported. What these scores measure is disputed. Third, the findings concern how color is weighted against form, which vision science already studies, yet only one study has linked that weighting to an object-recognition task, and none has used calibrated stimuli. I then read both literatures through a constructivist model of color in which the percept and the wider event it belongs to determine each other reciprocally. On this reading, the question is not only whether color influences emotion but also whether emotion influences color. The projective tradition raised the second question. Modern color-emotion science has mostly set it aside. Five studies are proposed that would join the two fields.

articles.title: Scroll and Snack: Daily Life Exposure to Healthy Food Content on Instagram Boosts Cravings for Healthy Snacks
articles.authors: Monique Caroline Alblas; Matthias Burkard Aulbach; Lena Jeremias; Veronika Pavlovova; Leonardo Pimpini
articles.abstract: Background: Food content pervades social media, yet how everyday exposure shapes momentary craving and snacking in daily life remains unclear. We tested whether experimentally adding unhealthy (H1) vs. healthy (H2) food content on top of participants’ Instagram feeds increased craving for and intake of unhealthy and healthy snacks, relative to adding art content (control). Method: In this preregistered randomized controlled field trial, 116 healthy-weight young adults (Mage = 22.46 years, 79.3% female) completed a 10-day smartphone ecological momentary assessment protocol (five prompts/day; five baseline, five manipulation days). Participants were randomly assigned to follow existing preselected Instagram accounts featuring unhealthy food, healthy food, or art (control); the number of additional accounts was 5% of those already followed. Outcomes (craving, consumption) were modeled using multilevel linear mixed models. Results: Manipulation checks confirmed expected shifts in food-related Instagram content. Against H1, added unhealthy content increased neither craving for (p = .194) nor intake of (p = .867) unhealthy snacks. Supporting H2, healthy food content increased craving for healthy snacks relative to both the control and the unhealthy condition (p < .001), but not healthy snack intake (p = .061). Conclusions: Curating a healthier Instagram feed may increase the desire for healthy snacks, but this effect, possibly due to the short duration of the manipulation, did not extend to intentions and/or intake. In conclusion, food craving may thus be used as early intervention target in future weight loss intervention, whereas changing actual intake likely requires longer or personalized exposure.

articles.title: Beyond Initial Crisis Recognition: Suicide-Risk Responses of ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini Across 14-Turn Ukrainian-Language Conversations
articles.authors: Hryhorii Kuzyk; Oleg Salamon; Liliia Andreieva; Kateryna Drozdova
articles.abstract: Nine deployed conversational systems mostly recognised the crisis, but it disappeared from their behaviour once the conversation moved on. We ran 16 scenarios in ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini as 14-message conversations (48 dialogues): crisis signals alternated with distraction, turn 13 introduced a new person at risk, and turn 14 was sent a day later. Coding was binary, as in the previous study, with clinical verification; two crisis-contour specifications were tested separately. New crisis signals drew a reaction in 87, 95, and 76 of 96 responses, respectively; the crisis stopped being mentioned mainly at an everyday message. The new person at risk drew a reaction in 44 of 48 responses; after a day, 29 retained crisis content. All 14 turns drew a 'yes' code in 4, 7, and 0 of 16 conversations. Reacting to the new person did not guarantee correct allocation of roles and actions. Both contour specifications produced safety-relevant errors. Neither hypothesis was supported: the systems behaved differently, and the same rule, introduced as a single package, did not stabilise their behaviour. Recognition, retention, and reconfiguration at a transition are distinct properties; the weakest is retention of the prior state and tracking of each person's trajectory.

articles.title: From Lab to Life: Stress Beliefs and the Stress Optimization Model in Everyday Stress
articles.authors: Lara Oeltjen; Susanne Fischer; Johannes Andreas Christoph Laferton
articles.abstract: Individuals’ beliefs about stress have been linked to health and performance. The stress optimization model proposes regulatory strategies through which these beliefs may shape stress responses, but evidence for these mechanisms comes largely from laboratory research.  We investigated whether these mechanisms generalize to everyday life in a 14-day ecological momentary assessment study of N = 173 university students (86% women, M_age = 22.6). Multilevel models examined associations of stress beliefs with stress regulation strategies, affect and somatic symptoms. Stress beliefs were associated with several regulation strategies on the between-person level, but explained little variability in how regulation changed with increasing stress intensity. Associations with affective and somatic responses were limited. Thus, laboratory-derived stress-belief mechanisms appear to generalize only partially to everyday life. We discuss advantages of laboratory and daily-life research on this topic. Interpretation is limited by a homogenous sample, potentially missed event-contingent assessments and independently modeling regulatory processes.

articles.title: CAVL: A Cognitive Architecture for Vigilant Learning
articles.authors: Jean-Sébastien Vayre
articles.abstract: Newell’s challenge remains: experiments often study cognitive mechanisms separately, although real learning requires their coordination. We present CAVL, a functional, multilevel, precomputational architecture of socially embedded vigilant learning. It links working memory, long-term knowledge, expertise, epistemic vigilance, source representation, metacognition, and social context. Structural embedding shapes knowledge, opportunities, and verification costs. Interactional embedding shapes how learners evaluate claims and their sources. CAVL makes three testable claims. First, valid prior knowledge and processing conditions alter the balance between content quality and attributed authority. Second, private acceptance can diverge from public expression when social costs are high. Third, unequal cognitive resources and allocated epistemic credit jointly shape participation and later learning. Six propositions specify critical tests and reasons to revise the architecture. CAVL treats ecological validity as a problem for research, not as a label attached to realistic settings. It proposes controlled and systematically varied experiments that preserve relevant person–task–environment relations. Its purpose is to connect experimentally established mechanisms with socially situated learning, not to replace controlled experiments or existing theories.

articles.title: White matter differences in adults with developmental language disorder
articles.authors: Noelle Abbott; Sophia Banel; Gabriel J Cler
articles.abstract: Developmental language disorder is a highly common yet underdiagnosed neurodevelopmental disorder which impacts receptive and/or expressive language abilities and cannot be attributed to another etiology such as hearing loss or a lack of early exposure to language. There is very little research into the brain differences that characterize developmental language disorder, especially in adult populations In this study, we used diffusion MRI to determine whether adults with DLD show differences in white matter microstructure of the brain when compared to adults with typical language. Participants included 23 adults identified as meeting criteria for developmental language disorder, as well as a group of 26 adults with typical language. White matter microstructure was examined with fractional anisotropy via diffusion tensor imaging and precise biophysical models of intra-axonal signal fraction and orientation coherence via the Standard Model of diffusion imaging, using tractometry to evaluate microstructure differences along white matter tracts. Analysis showed reduced myelin integrity in DLD in the corpus callosum, but increased myelin integrity in the left superior longitudinal fasciculus. It is yet unclear whether differences exist in childhood and are retained into adulthood, are a result of different language environments during childhood, or are a result of behavioral and neural compensation.

articles.title: Language-based Assessments for Experienced Well-being: Accuracy and External Validity Across Behaviors, Traits, and States
articles.authors: August Nilsson; Ryan Boyd; Adithya V Ganesan; Oscar Nils Erik Kjell; Syeda Mahwish; Haitao Huang; Richard N. Rosenthal; Lyle H Ungar; H. Andrew Schwartz
articles.abstract: Self-reported rating scales have been central to social science for decades, even though language is our primary form of communication. We used language analysis with machine learning to compare self-reported ratings with language-based responses of experienced well-being (i.e., daily emotions) linked with human traits, states, and behaviors.  In a sample of 764 U.S. service workers who reported their feelings daily for up to 12 weeks, responses were provided in 1) numerical ratings, 2) short essays, and 3) descriptive words. When predicting nine self-rated affective traits, essays were slightly less accurate than the ratings (r = .49 v .55, p < .001), while the word-based responses slightly outperformed the ratings (r = .53 vs .51, p < .001). For external predictive validity across 24 traits, demographics, and behaviors, both language formats doubled the ratings’ accuracy, with words reaching an average of r = .18 and essays r = .24 (p < .001). Beyond their greater accuracy, both language formats offered rich psychological insights, with words focusing on emotions and essays encompassing broader life domains. While both language-based formats showed advantages and disadvantages, each demonstrated greater information-richness than traditional rating scales.

articles.title: Personality Differences among Men and Women of Various Sexual Orientations, Including Asexual and Pansexual Individuals
articles.authors: Jakub Fořt; Dominika Benešová; Petr Freudenfeld; Jaroslava Varella Valentova; Jan Havlicek
articles.abstract: Several theoretical approaches explain variance in personality related to sexual orientation. Drawing on the minority stress theory and the gender shift hypothesis, this study explores personality differences across people of various sexual orientations, including underrepresented groups, such as asexual and pansexual individuals. The minority stress theory posits that non-heterosexual individuals experience heightened social stressors, contributing to higher neuroticism. The gender shift hypothesis further suggests that prenatal hormonal influences may lead to sex-atypical development, explaining some personality variation in sexual minorities. Using a large Czech and Slovak sample (N = 6,476), we administered the Big Five Inventory (BFI-10) to heterosexual (N = 2,598), gay/lesbian (N = 1,943), bisexual (N = 1,412), pansexual (N = 389), and asexual (N = 165) cisgender individuals. We found that non-heterosexual men scored higher in neuroticism than heterosexual men, consistent with both the minority stress and gender shift hypotheses. Pansexual and bisexual individuals of either sex were higher in openness to experience than heterosexual individuals, and asexual individuals scored lower in extraversion than same-sex individuals of any other sexual orientation. We recorded mixed results for conscientiousness. No differences were found in levels of agreeableness. Effect sizes of the recorded differences are, except for few, generally small.

articles.title: The Memory We Miss: Exploratory Behavior as a Window into Developmental Recognition Processes
articles.authors: Eleanor G. Williamson; Jesse Cushman; Patrese A Robinson
articles.abstract: Recognition memory tasks are among the most widely used approaches for studying learning and memory across the lifespan, yet the behavioral measures used to assess memory performance, particularly during developmental studies, remain limited. In most rodent studies, recognition memory is inferred almost exclusively from discrimination ratios or discrimination indices that quantify preferential exploration of novel stimuli. While these measures have proven valuable, their widespread use may constrain our understanding of the behavioral and cognitive processes that support nuanced memory expression across ontogeny. Similar concerns have emerged in the fear conditioning literature, where expanding analyses beyond freezing behavior has revealed previously unrecognized differences in learning and memory. In this perspective, we argue that recognition memory research would benefit from a comparable expansion of behavioral analyses. Drawing on affordance-based approaches to object exploration, we discuss evidence showing that object properties influence both memory performance and exploratory behavior. More importantly, our recent findings indicate that juvenile (but not adult) rats exhibit task-dependent shifts in exploratory behavior, contingent on the object's specific affordance, which are not captured by traditional discrimination measures.  These findings suggest that developmental differences in memory may be expressed not only through recognition performance but also through the exploratory strategies animals employ during learning and retrieval. Expanding behavioral analyses in recognition memory tasks may therefore reveal developmental neurobehavioral mechanisms that remain hidden from conventional metrics, providing a more complete understanding of memory development. The challenge moving forward is not simply to determine whether young animals remember, but to identify how they remember and whether the behavioral routes to successful memory change across development.

articles.title: Social Media Usage Profiles: A Multidimensional Approach Using Cluster Analysis
articles.authors: Myriam; Elena Bernabéu; Carlos Marchena Girárldez
articles.abstract: The heterogeneity of problematic social media use (PSMU) has led to the study of differentiated user profiles, although most research is based on correlational designs rather than multidimensional approaches. The integrated examination of compulsivity, emotional regulation, psychological distress, and usage patterns stays limited. The present study aimed to identify empirical clusters of young people based on psychological, emotional, and behavioural variables related to social media use, and to compare their characteristics to better understand the heterogeneity of the phenomenon. A total of 530 young people participated (67.5% women; M = 19.70 years), completing measures of problematic use, emotional distress, digital compulsivity, emotional regulation, and time spent using social media. Hierarchical and k-means cluster analyses (k=3) were conducted, complemented by ANOVA and post hoc tests. Validity and discriminative capacity indicators (R²) were calculated. Three profiles were identified: a profile characterised by compulsive use (PCU), defined by the highest levels of consumption and compulsivity; a profile characterised by the highest levels of emotional distress despite moderate levels of consumption, termed the pattern associated with psychological distress (PAD); and a functional profile (FP), distinguished by low consumption, fewer symptoms and better emotional regulation. The most discriminative variables were problematic use (R² = .66) and compulsivity (R² = .49), whereas emotional regulation appears to act as a possible protective factor. These profiles may help to guide more precise preventive interventions.

articles.title: “I’m Asking This Price Because…”: When Negotiation Rationales  Win Concessions but Cost the Relationship
articles.authors: Hannes M. Petrowsky; Yannik A. Escher; Alice Lee; Daniel Robert Ames; David D. Loschelder
articles.abstract: Negotiators often face a tension between claiming value and preserving the relationship with their counterpart. Rationales, the explanations negotiators attach to their offers (“I’m asking this price because…”), are assumed to ease this tension by making an assertive offer more persuasive and acceptable. The evidence is limited, however. Prior work examined a few rationales in isolation, with mixed results, and has not asked, across the rationales negotiators use, whether those that win concessions are the same ones that preserve relationships. We integrate various types of rationales in an overarching taxonomy and propose that a rationale conveys two kinds of information at once—about the negotiation (e.g., limits) and about the negotiator (e.g., motives). This information can move economic and relational outcomes in opposite directions. Across six studies (Ntotal=2,833), we identify six types of rationales negotiators commonly use (Studies 1a–c) and then test, in three preregistered experiments, how sellers’ rationales affect buyers’ counteroffers (Study 2), their impressions of the seller (Study 3), and why (Study 4). The most common rationale, sellers praising the product, neither helped nor hurt. Rationales citing financial constraints or appealing to sympathy won larger concessions but damaged the relationship with the counterpart. Only rationales citing market constraints appeared to avoid this trade-off. Mediation analyses indicated that economic benefits operated via limit perceptions and sympathy, whereas relational costs operated via perceived manipulativeness and disliking. Our results suggest that rationales work best when they inform counterparts about the negotiator’s situation without inviting negative inferences about the negotiator’s motives.

articles.title: Worry is underpinned by persistence in searching uninformative avenues
articles.authors: Alexis An Yee Low; Karl Friston; Michael Moutoussis
articles.abstract: Worry is common both in mental health and distress. What, then, distinguishes pathological worry? We hypothesized that what characterizes pathological worry is excessive internal search that fails to resolve uncertainty; i.e., is uninformative. In an information sampling paradigm, increased sampling was predicted both by trait (p = .018) and—more powerfully—state worry (p < .001). An information-poor environment significantly increased sampling in high worriers (p < 0.001, CrI 1.1% inside Region of Practical Equivalence defined as <0.2 SD), but not low worriers (p = 0.480, CrI 68.2% in ROPE). Crucially, this increase in sampling in high worriers did not increase their accuracy (CrI 97.5% inside ROPE). A ‘sampling until success’ heuristic was identified as a driver. Stimulus uncertainty and aversiveness had similar effects on sampling and worry, increasing both (p < 0.001). Persistent searching—in the face of irreducible uncertainty—may therefore be a key mechanism behind worry, differentiating high from low worrying.

articles.title: Can Knowledge of the CO₂ Emissions of Food Increase Meat Tax Support?
articles.authors: Hellen Temme; Mattis Geiger; Philipp Sprengholz; Cornelia Betsch
articles.abstract:
Purpose
Climate policy acceptance and sustainable behavior partially depend on accurate CO₂ estimates and perceived policy effectiveness. We tested whether seeding, an intervention in which people learn accurate CO₂ values for representative foods that serve as anchors for estimating other foods' emissions, can increase carbon numeracy (i.e., the ability to estimate carbon footprints of foods without explicit calculations). 
Method
Two pre-registered experiments examined whether increased carbon numeracy also enhances perceived effectiveness and acceptance of a value-added tax (VAT) reform on food and food choice. Study 1 (N = 974) tested whether seeding increased the effectiveness and acceptance of a VAT increase for meat. Study 2 (N = 1,023) extended this by explaining the policy mechanism. Food choice was assessed by asking participants to select a food box (vegan, vegetarian, or meat-based) in a lottery.
Results
Both studies found that seeding improved carbon numeracy (ηp² = .55−.58, p < .05). However, neither seeding nor policy explanations significantly increased policy acceptance or food choice, although explaining the policy increased perceived effectiveness (β = .21−.24, p < .05). In both studies, perceived effectiveness (r = .31−.41, p < .001) and policy acceptance (r = .30−.49, p < .001) were significantly related to selecting a non-meat food box. Exploratory analyses revealed that perceptions of a potential price change were the strongest predictor of policy acceptance (β = -.47, p < .001). 
Conclusion
These findings suggest that VAT policy changes could require both explaining environmental benefits and addressing perceived personal costs.

articles.title: Individual differences in response to universal school mental health interventions:  A narrative review informed by young people’s perspectives
articles.authors: Jennifer Clare Fielder; Lucy Foulkes
articles.abstract: Universal school-based mental health interventions involve delivering mental health content to all young people within a class, regardless of need. They are typically evaluated in terms of average effects, yet there is growing evidence that individual young people may experience the same intervention very differently. In this narrative review, we consider five illustrative sources of individual variation in response to universal school-based mental health interventions: social relationships within the classroom, baseline mental health status, special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), family circumstances and gender. For each factor, we review relevant theoretical and empirical literature to explore how each factor might contribute to positive, negative and/or neutral experiences during universal school-based mental health interventions. The review is additionally informed by reflections from a Young People’s Advisory Group of five 14–18-year-olds with experience of school mental health lessons, whose perspectives are integrated throughout. We conclude that understanding individual variability is crucial for evaluating the safety and effectiveness of universal school-based mental health interventions, and for determining whether and how these interventions can be adapted to meet the diverse needs of young people.

articles.title: When Better Treatment Is Not Enough: Relearning Expectations of Harm at Work
articles.authors: Robin Umbra
articles.abstract: Better treatment can ease an employee’s anger without changing what they expect from the next encounter. When, then, does a new workplace encounter revise a learned expectation of harm? A theory of expectancy updating grounded in cue-appraisal learning explains why positive experiences can leave anticipated mistreatment intact, establish a narrow exception, or support broader change. Confirming encounters can strengthen expected harm and consolidate confidence even as immediate emotion subsides. Favorable encounters support revision when they provide credible evidence about the anticipated consequence and the conditions that made it likely. Safety attributed to exceptional monitoring can be learned as an exception; protection that extends across ordinary conditions offers grounds for broader revision. Harm expectancies can also spread to similar workplace cues and to actors judged responsible for producing or enabling harm. Credible differences in consequences, authority, or responsibility can limit that spread. Earlier and corrective expectations may nevertheless coexist, allowing anticipated harm to return with changes in context or the passage of time. Such return must be distinguished from responses to renewed mistreatment or withdrawn safeguards. Six propositions connect these processes with differentiated emotion and choices among protective distancing, accountability-oriented engagement, and punishment. The central prediction is that equally favorable encounters can produce unequal revision: the corrective value of better treatment depends on what it reveals about the harm employees expect to face again.

articles.title: A Network Perspective on Cyberbullying: Examining School Social Environment and Bullying Behaviors
articles.authors: Gabriel Baník; Mária Dědová; Kristína Dědová; Veronika Mihalikova
articles.abstract: This study examined the complexity of cyberbullying and its relationship with traditional bullying, school climate, and social support using network analysis. The sample consisted of 1,269 participants (359 boys), including 770 emerging adults and 499 teens, with a mean age of 18 (SD = 2.5). We measured 11 forms of cyberbullying across different roles (victim, aggressor, defender, bystander), five factors of school climate, social support (from parents, friends, teachers), and traditional bullying roles. Undirected weighted network models revealed strong interconnections between various types of aggressive behaviors and cyberbullying victimization. Unauthorized sharing of personal media showed negative relationships with online verbal attacks, while online group exclusion strongly associated with social isolation. The bystander role positively related to both verbal aggression and victimization. Defenders in cyberbullying were more likely to be victims of personal information exposure and verbal attacks, and strongly associated with defending in traditional bullying. School climate and social support demonstrated weak connections to cyberbullying, with student-student relationships, fairness in school, and parental support showing the most direct interconnections. Network comparisons revealed subtle structural differences between genders and between teens and emerging adults. Findings suggest prevention programs should focus on strengthening school relationships while supporting student defenders who may become targets themselves.

articles.title: General Exploitation Theory (GET)
articles.authors: Norbert Meskó
articles.abstract: Exploitation is a pervasive yet under-theorized phenomenon shaping interactions from intimate relationships to global institutions. Existing approaches typically examine narrow domains—manipulation in interpersonal contexts, cheating in economic games, or corruption in political systems—without an integrative account. The General Exploitation Theory (GET) addresses this gap by conceptualizing exploitation as a continuum, ranging from benign utilization of opportunities to abusive appropriation that imposes disproportionate costs on others or the environment. This continuum-based approach aligns with dimensional models in psychology and the behavioral sciences. GET advances a bio-psycho-social model in which exploitation emerges through the interplay of evolved biological mechanisms, intrapsychic processes, interpersonal strategies, and societal structures. Reward circuits, hormonal modulation, and cognitive biases may bias individuals toward short-term opportunism; emotions and motivational drives such as envy, greed, and status striving provide proximate energy for exploitative behavior; interpersonal dynamics translate these tendencies into deception, coercion, and betrayal; and societal and institutional arrangements embed exploitation at scale through hierarchies, inequalities, and legitimizing ideologies. Evolutionary theory clarifies its resilience, framing exploitation as a conditional strategy that can yield reproductive or material benefits despite long-term costs. By synthesizing insights across disciplines, GET offers a comprehensive framework for understanding exploitation as an adaptive, multi-level process. This perspective not only explains its persistence but also provides a roadmap for systematic research on mechanisms, variability, and consequences. In doing so, GET positions exploitation as a central construct for the behavioral sciences and a consequential dimension of human nature across levels and contexts and over time worldwide.

articles.title: Making AI-mediated decisions culturally repairable
articles.authors: Hadi Mohamadpour; Soomaahey Heysieattalab; Jean-Claude Dreher
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly influences high-stakes decisions, from employment and education to healthcare and public services. When such judgments are disputed, affected people may receive an explanation without being able to reach an authority empowered to change the outcome or remedy its consequences. We introduce cultural repairability: the institutional capacity to review an AI-mediated decision, correct the outcome and downstream records, provide meaningful restoration, and learn from failure through procedures people can understand and use. The framework addresses a visibility–accountability asymmetry: people are exposed to judgments about their standing but lack effective means of obtaining an answer or remedy. Culture matters because exposure, legitimate authority, and appropriate restoration may be understood differently across settings. Language accessibility also determines whether review mechanisms are usable in practice. We identify three measurable cultural mechanisms: the meaning of exposure, the credibility of review, and the meaning of restoration. We further distinguish affected people’s appraisals from institutional actors’ responsibility and capacity to respond. Four falsifiable propositions specify how reviewer authority and audience shape responses to repair, and how these effects vary with cultural orientation, institutional history, and the form of restoration. They predict whether people appeal or withdraw, how they recalibrate trust, and whether they remain willing to engage. The resulting Repairability Principle establishes a common floor of substantive review, correction, restoration, and prevention of recurrence, while allowing people to choose how restoration is delivered. Cultural repairability therefore shifts global AI accountability from whether procedures appear acceptable to whether institutions can correct harm in practice.

articles.title: People Don't Have to Be Native to Hear Size: Evidence From Voiced Obstruent Perception in L2 Learners of Japanese
articles.authors: Rean Du; Marco Aurelio Silva Fonseca
articles.abstract:
Voiced obstruents are sounds that are produced with complete closure of the vocal tract and vibration of vocal folds (e.g., /b/, /d/, /g/, /z/). They have been shown to be associated with largeness by native Japanese speakers using Pok\'emon-style nonce names, but whether this sensitivity extends to second-language (L2) learners remains unclear. Twenty-five L2 learners of Japanese rated 30 nonce names with fixed mora counts, containing zero, one, or two voiced obstruents, for perceived height and perceived weight on a sliding scale. Ratings increased with each additional voiced obstruent for both height and weight, and the same pattern was reported for native speakers. This sensitivity did not differ by Japanese proficiency or between English-Japanese bilingual and
multilingual learners.

articles.title: Direct and Generative Retrieval and the Phenomenological Characteristics of Future Thinking Associated with Depressive Symptoms: The Relevance of Contrast Avoidance and Memories of the Future
articles.authors: Noboru Matsumoto; David John Hallford
articles.abstract: Depression is characterized by reduced future thinking specificity, yet the retrieval processes underlying this impairment remain unclear. We examined whether depressive symptoms are differentially associated with direct retrieval (i.e., effortless searches that immediately bring future thoughts to mind) versus generative retrieval (i.e., searches requiring cognitive effort or additional information) of specific and categoric future events, and whether contrast avoidance (i.e., maintaining a negative mood to avoid a sudden negative emotional shift) contributes to these patterns. In Study 1 (N = 80) and preregistered Study 2 (N = 113), Japanese adults completed a future thinking task in which they imagined personally-relevant future events for positive and negative cue words, classified each retrieval as direct or generative, and rated phenomenological characteristics. Drawing on preliminary results from Study 1, Study 2 clearly linked depressive symptoms to more frequent directly retrieved categoric futures for negative cues. In contrast, regressions (but not correlations) showed associations between depressive symptoms to reduced generatively retrieved specific futures for positive cues. Depressed individuals also reported lower emotional valence, likelihood, and similarity with past events for positive future thinking, suggesting limited memory resources for generating plausible positive events. In Study 2, a higher propensity for emotional contrast avoidance was linked to increased retrieval of negative categoric futures and decreased retrieval of positive specific futures. These findings suggest that increased accessibility to negative categoric futures and reduced accessibility to positive specific futures may be a distinct pathological process in depression, with contrast avoidance potentially maintaining these biases.

articles.title: Beyond Anxiety and Avoidance: A Dynamic Feedback-Regulation Framework for Adult Romantic Attachment
articles.authors: Mateusz Pomianek
articles.abstract: Adult attachment is commonly represented by attachment anxiety and avoidance, but these person-level dimensions do not by themselves specify how momentary relational conditions are perceived, compared with desired conditions, translated into action, and updated after interpersonal feedback. We present the Attachment Regulation and Control (ARC) framework as an integrative feedback-regulation account that makes these temporal assumptions explicit and empirically testable. In ARC, control refers to feedback-based regulation toward relational goals in the control-theoretic sense, not interpersonal dominance, coercion, or a generalized need for control. ARC does not claim a novel control-system architecture. Instead, it synthesizes established control-theoretic attachment ideas, secure-base representations, perceived partner responsiveness, relational discrepancy, dyadic regulation, and recovery into a parsimonious sequence for adult romantic relationships: perceived relational state, desired relational state, discrepancy, regulatory action, partner feedback, state updating, and recovery. The framework treats the discrepancy score itself as a falsifiable modeling restriction by comparing it with perceived-state-only, unconstrained perceived-plus-desired-state, and asymmetric discrepancy alternatives. Attachment anxiety and avoidance form the current person-level core and are modeled as moderators of channel-specific regulation. Positive secure-base representation is not yet required by the core; it is a prespecified candidate whose promotion depends on demonstrating incremental prediction of preregistered recovery outcomes beyond anxiety and avoidance. Mentalized affectivity and emotion-regulation flexibility remain optional moderators, and adult disorganization remains an independently measured extension outcome. The article derives core, candidate-core, and extension hypotheses, specifies competing observation models, and proposes staged intensive longitudinal and recovery-focused human tests.

articles.title: Toward scalable identification of adults with developmental language disorder: Validation, participant profiles, and recruitment considerations for an online screener
articles.authors: Iris Mendoza Luna; Noelle Abbott; Gabriel J Cler
articles.abstract:
Purpose: This study evaluated the feasibility of an online adaptation of the Fidler diagnostic protocol for identifying developmental language disorder (DLD) in adults. Specifically, we examined (1) comparability of computerized versus face-to-face administration, (2) test-retest reliability, (3) agreement between two- and three-task scoring equations, (4) effects of demographic and cognitive factors on scores, and (5) the relationship between self-reported diagnoses and screener performance.
Method: Over 5,000 adults completed a language and medical history survey, and 526 subsequently completed an assessment over videoconference involving following auditory directions, spelling irregular words, and defining words (modified from Fidler et al, 2011). A subset (N = 53; 25 DLD, 28 with typical language development) then completed an in-person session comparing face-to-face and computerized administration of the following directions task, along with nonverbal IQ testing. Participants were recruited between 2022 and 2025 via online postings and flyers.
Results: No significant effect of administration modality on following directions task performance or Fidler scores was observed. Test-retest reliability was high (r = .91). Scores derived from the two- and three-task weighted equations from Fidler et al (2011) were highly correlated (r = .98), though the three-task equation produced lower (i.e., more typical) scores for participants with DLD-range profiles. Age, gender, and early bilingualism did not significantly influence scores. Although several self-reported diagnoses and concerns were higher among the group identified as DLD than the TD group, overall discriminative accuracy of self-report screening items was low (AUC range: 0.45–0.65).
Conclusions: Online administration of the Fidler protocol is comparable to the original face-to-face version and demonstrates adequate test-retest reliability, supporting its use as a scalable tool for identifying adults with DLD. Practical recommendations for recruiting and screening adults with DLD are discussed to facilitate future research with this population.

articles.title: Cultural Congruence of Visual Binomial Collocation Sequences and Gullibility
articles.authors: Scott Altsuler
articles.abstract: This study aims to discover how visual representations of common word sequences in language can increase or decrease a viewer’s gullibility and trust based on how well the ordering of the stimuli matches the common ordering in the viewer’s culture. My primary research question is “How does the cultural congruence of the horizontal arrangement of objects in an image with its respective language's normative binomial collocation sequences affect the viewer's processing of subsequent questions?” This paper hypothesizes that, when shown images that are in a culturally fluent arrangement, participants will be in a state of greater gullibility. Alternatively, when shown images arranged in a culturally disfluent manner, the viewer will engage in higher-level reasoning and be more skeptical. We randomly assigned participants to one of three groups – the control group, the culturally fluent group, and the culturally disfluent group. In the culturally fluent group, participants were shown visual representations of binomial collocation sequences arranged left to right, as they are commonly spoken in English. In the culturally disfluent group, participants were shown collocation sequences arranged opposite to the cultural norm. After viewing the images, participants were tested on tasks that assess intuitive vs. systematic reasoning and measure their gullibility. The data do not support our hypotheses that if the participants are shown culturally fluent visual representations of collocation sequences, then they exhibit more intuitive reasoning, and that those shown culturally disfluent stimuli exhibit more systematic reasoning, nor does it support that this change prompts more face-value acceptance of inherence in culture. The data do indicate, however, that participants prefer viewing two associated stimuli rather than individual pictures.

articles.title: Learning Children’s Conceptual Spaces using Deep Metric Learning.
articles.authors: Pablo Leon-Villagra; Isaac Ehrlich; Christopher G. Lucas; Daphna Buchsbaum
articles.abstract: Children learn to represent the world around them in meaningful categories that allow them to generalize past experiences. Understanding how these categorical representations develop is fundamental to cognitive science. However, capturing the structure of human conceptual knowledge is a challenging experimental task. The most prominent approach, Multidimensional Scaling (MDS), usually requires participants to produce many similarity judgments, leading to long experiments. Moreover, the representations found by MDS are limited to the fixed set of experimental stimuli and have to be reconstructed for every new item. In contrast, we present a more flexible machine-learning method that can generalize to novel stimuli. This method uses a child-friendly task that allows researchers to uncover the development of categories with fewer participant judgments. We evaluate our approach on simulated data and find that it can accurately reveal representations even when trained on data generated by groups that categorize differently. We then analyze data from the World Color Survey and find that we can recover language-specific color organization when aggregating languages that only share the same number of basic color terms. Finally, we use the method in a developmental experiment and find age-dependent differences in how complex fruit stimuli are organized. These differences were consistent with participants' reasoning and additional experimental measures. Our results suggest that our approach is applicable in psychological tasks and opens the possibility of examining children's developing psychological spaces in new detail.

articles.title: Biased Motive Inferences of Online Outrage Undermine Cross-Partisan Conversations
articles.authors: Chen-Wei Yu; William J. Brady
articles.abstract: Moral outrage spreads widely in online political discourse, but how do people understand others’ outrage expressions? Across three studies (N = 1,855), including behavioral experiments and a field study, we discovered that partisan-biased motive inferences underlie the divergent effects of online outrage expression: While people typically inferred that their in-partisans’ motives for expressing outrage were to raise awareness or inspire action, they tended to infer their political opponents’ motives were to shame or troll. These motive inferences were linked to greater political sectarianism and lower willingness to have a conversation about politics with the outrage expressor. In a fourth study (N = 720), we developed an intervention that changed people’s motive inferences, which improved willingness to have a conversation about politics. These findings highlight the role of motive inferences in shaping contemporary online political discourse filled with strong emotions, and suggest key levers to foster civil interactions among cross-partisans.

articles.title: Measurement Invariance of the Externalizing Construct by Racial and Disadvantaged Contexts in System-Involved Adults
articles.authors: Kendall Donovan Smith; Keanan Joyner; Edelyn Verona
articles.abstract: Externalizing psychopathology is shaped by environmental and contextual factors, particularly those tied to disadvantaged backgrounds. There is insufficient work examining how broader contextual variables affect measurement models of latent externalizing. The current research examined the degree to which indicators traditionally used to model externalizing are similarly indicative of the latent construct across racial and contextual factors (i.e., metric and scalar invariance), using data from two studies of system-involved adults (Study 1: Mage=36.5, 67% male; Study 2: Mage=32.1, 62% male). In both studies, metric invariance generally held but not scalar invariance as a function of race/ethnicity and community-level racialized contexts, particularly for drug use, antisocial behavior and criminal justice-related indicators. Results suggest that contextual factors influence not only externalizing level but affect the measurement of the construct itself.

articles.title: “Puzzling, Yet So Refreshing”: Experiencing the Value of Neurodiversity Within an Inclusive Choir
articles.authors: Nicolas Petit; Géraldine Dessertenne; Fanny Aprile; Lucie Jurek
articles.abstract: The social challenges encountered by autistic people are increasingly understood as a double empathy problem: a mutual misunderstanding between autistic and non-autistic individuals, rather than an autistic deficit. It is thus critical to cultivate inclusive spaces that foster mutual understanding, where autistic people can fit in while allowing the general population to experience high-quality neurodiverse contacts. Choral singing offers a promising medium to do so and to facilitate cross-neurotype dynamics, as it is thought to have evolved as a biological mechanism to foster social bonding. Accordingly, this qualitative study explored how 12 general population adult choristers experienced a 6-month neurodiverse choir shared with 8 autistic adolescents and 3 autism specialists. We used a two-stage qualitative design, first capturing individual experiences through a thematic analysis of an open-ended online questionnaire, and subsequently deepening our results through a discussion with a community stakeholder panel. The findings revealed an intrinsically demanding experience, especially emotionally and cognitively, counterbalanced by important benefits, as it was also described as joyful and powerful, encouraging personal growth among the choristers and a shift in their perceptions of autism. These findings support the neurodiversity paradigm and suggest that choral singing may support double empathy experiences, facilitating intergroup contact in the social majority, to reduce prejudice and thereby remove social barriers to the inclusion of autistic voices.

articles.title: Competition, concurrence, and cooperation between external and internal attention
articles.authors: Sam Verschooren; Tobias Egner; Mariam Aly
articles.abstract: Attention can be selectively directed to both external sensory inputs and internally generated representations. The relationship between these external and internal attentional states is not fixed but varies between competition, concurrence, and cooperation. However, the conditions that allow for each of these relationships to occur remain poorly understood. We distinguish between the level of brain states and behavior and synthesize evidence for each of these relationships at both levels. Our review shows that shared, capacity-limited mechanisms and opposing computational modes (e.g., encoding vs. retrieval) often produce competitive dynamics, particularly in the presence of simultaneous and incompatible demands. At the same time, several studies have revealed partially independent substrates that permit concurrent selection of internal and external information, especially when controlled, intentional processing is not required. More recently, researcher have started exploring conditions under which external and internal can support or facilitate each other, enabling cooperative integration in the service of a single goal. We argue that task demands, degree of control, representational overlap, and the considered timescale jointly determine whether external and internal attention compete, co-occur, or cooperate, and we outline key directions for future work aimed at a more nuanced understanding of how these states jointly shape cognition.

articles.title: Impacts of voice pleasantness and familiarity on enjoyment and engagement with spoken narratives
articles.authors: Carolyn McGettigan; Hannah Jones; Victor Rosi; Emma Soopramanien; Amrita Bains; Saloni Krishnan
articles.abstract: Recent experimental reading research has found that situational enjoyment of texts plays an important role in predicting both comprehension and motivation to continue reading.
