Here, we used narrative listening to test whether these findings generalise to spoken narratives, and to further investigate how different aspects of the narrator’s voice affect the experience and outcomes of listening. In Experiment 1, participants heard spoken book excerpts produced by a highly-naturalistic synthesised voice. After each excerpt, participants rated their enjoyment of the excerpt, answered a multiple-choice content comprehension question, and finally chose whether to wait to hear more of the narrative (or skip to the next one; a measure of motivation). Replicating the findings from reading research, we found that greater enjoyment was associated with increased probability of both correct comprehension and waiting. In Experiment 2, participants heard the same book excerpts, now narrated by 2 different synthesised voices that significantly differed in perceived pleasantness. Here, we found higher enjoyment for excerpts read by the more pleasant-sounding voice, but no effects of pleasantness on comprehension or waiting. In Experiment 3, we harnessed personalised voice cloning to show that both enjoyment and waiting were increased when listening to personally-familiar narrators (self, friend), compared with unfamiliar narrators. Our findings offer mechanistic evidence for the rewarding role of voice identity perception in spoken language processing, and present interesting implications for how personalised narrators could improve engagement with spoken book language.

articles.title: The role of neuroscience for psychological causal explanation
articles.authors: Beate Krickel; Markus Werkle-Bergner
articles.abstract: Psychology provides causal explanations of behavior but it remains contested whether such explanations are scientifically legitimate without grounding in neuroscience. Two prominent arguments have been put forward to argue for the dependence of psychology on neuroscience: the classical causal exclusion argument argues that higher-level causes are excluded by lower-level causes; According to a more recent line of argument, variables and relations postulated by psychological models must correspond to variables and relations in neuroscientific models – otherwise the psychological model can only provide how-possibly explanation but not how-actually explanation. In this article, we defend the independence of psychological causal explanation. Based on an interventionist account of causation, we argue that a psychological model is causally explanatory when it identifies variables that serve as points of intervention. Still, we show that neuroscience sometimes has a crucial role for validating psychological models: when a psychological model identifies points of interventions that cannot be intervened on at the psychological level.

articles.title: Tools for Helping Identify Behavior Disorders: From Parsimonious Nomograms to Machine Learning Models
articles.authors: Yinuo Liu; Eric Arden Youngstrom; Caroline Bodary; Zhuoyu Shi; Jennifer Youngstrom; Ekaterina Stepanova; Robert L. Findling
articles.abstract:
Objective: Disruptive behavior problems like Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD) and Conduct Disorder (CD) are high burden conditions where accurate diagnosis is crucial for effective treatment. We evaluated probability nomograms and machine learning (ML) algorithms (logistic regression, LASSO, SVM, random forest) on accuracy, calibration, and generalizability for detecting current ODD or CD diagnoses.
Method: Youth aged 5–18 receiving outpatient care were recruited from academic (n=622) and community (n=506) clinics. Predictors included demographics, comorbid diagnoses, mood and behavioral indicators. The criterion was K-SADS diagnoses of ODD/CD. Models were trained in the academic sample, using the community sample for external validation. AUC quantified accuracy, Spiegelhalter's z indexed calibration, and cross-site performance measured generalizability.
Results: For ODD diagnostic prediction, the nomogram selected CBCL Aggression as the strongest predictor and reached AUC≈.70 in both samples. ML models achieved good discrimination (AUC≈.86) with good-to-moderate calibration in the academic sample, deteriorating to fair accuracy with severe miscalibration in the community setting. For CD diagnostic prediction, the nomogram built on CBCL Rule-Breaking showed good accuracy (AUC≈.82) in both samples. ML models showed near-excellent accuracy (AUC≈.88) in the academic sample but underperformed in the community sample (AUC=.73-.76), though LASSO, SVM, and random forest maintained good calibration.
Conclusion: Across both disorders, nomograms demonstrated lower accuracy but strong cross-site stability, while ML using more predictors achieved superior accuracy that did not generalize. The nomogram offers a low-cost and parsimonious tool. Machine learning is best suited for well-resourced clinics where model training data closely resemble the new cases encountered in practice.

articles.title: The effect of unconventional gender role advertisements (femvertising) on female purchase intentions and brand attitude: attitudes towards motherhood and culture: Korea vs. UK
articles.authors: Erin Lim; Adrian Furnham; Alastair McClelland
articles.abstract: This study examined the impact of culture and attitudes towards motherhood (ATM) on the effectiveness of traditional/non-traditional gendered advertisements. Korean and British participants viewed either traditional or non-traditional female portrayals in adverts and rated them for purchase intention and brand attitude. They also completed the Attitudes towards Fertility and Childbearing Scale (AFCS) containing three subscales: Fertility, Hindrance, and Social Identity. The results showed that there was a significant difference between cultures on ATM with more negative attitudes in Korean participants. However, there was no interaction effect between culture and advert type on advertising effectiveness, but main effects of culture and advert type were found. Favourable attitudes towards motherhood significantly positively correlated with the effectiveness of traditional adverts, but not non-traditional adverts except for Hindrance with PI.

articles.title: When Different Relational Experiences with AI Become Visible in Conversation: Linguistic and Dyadic Evidence from Naturalistic ChatGPT Interactions
articles.authors: Nadine Nicole Schmitt; Lennart Seizer; Fanny Alexandra Dietel; Lea Grimm-Keßler; Björn Schuller; Johanna Schuller
articles.abstract: People may experience large language models (LLMs) as therapeutically allied, emotionally close, or socially substitutive, but whether these relationships become visible in conversations is unknown. We distinguished what users discussed, what unfolded relationally, and how they experienced the AI relationship. We linked self-reports from 94 adults to donated, personally meaningful ChatGPT conversations using 21 outcome-blind frozen topics, blinded triple annotation of 500 sequences, and participant-grouped machine learning frozen before outcome access. Digital Therapeutic Alliance (DTA) and AI Attachment were related but showed different conversational correlates. Validation (R²_CV = .423) and uptake (R²_CV = .260) were recoverable out of sample, yet, neither formed a generalizable DTA signature. Conversely, a post-registration multivariate analysis identified a distributed Social Substitution fingerprint beyond conversation length and 21 topics (ΔR²_CV = .070) and improved prediction in 98% of repetitions. Ruptures were rare and consistently repaired; their association with DTA was fragile. Thus, different human–LLM relationships leave different—and sometimes no readily observable—conversational traces.

articles.title: Higher Objective Physical Activity Attenuates the Association Between Daily Stress and Rumination
articles.authors: Alfiannisa Shelma Wikenza; Justin Hachenberger; Sakari Lemola
articles.abstract: Rumination is commonly experienced in response to stressful events and has been linked to adverse psychological outcomes. However, research has predominantly examined rumination as a predictor or consequence of psychological functioning, whereas less is known about factors associated with its day-to-day fluctuations. The current study addressed this gap by examining factors associated with rumination using an intensive longitudinal design. A total of 91 young adults (81,5% female; 14,1% male; 4,3% diverse or preferred not to disclose their gender; aged 18–30 years) participated in a 28-day experience-sampling study. Daily self-reported rumination, stress, and subjective sleep quality (SSQ), as well as accelerometry-derived total sleep time (TST), sleep efficiency (SE), and physical activity, were assessed. Multilevel analyses showed that daily stress was associated with greater rumination. Although physical activity was not directly associated with rumination, it moderated the association between stress and rumination. Higher-than-usual physical activity levels were associated with a smaller difference in rumination between stressful and non-stressful days. Better SSQ was independently associated with lower rumination, whereas TST and SE were not. Higher baseline depressive symptom severity was also associated with greater rumination but did not moderate the stress–rumination association. These findings highlight physical activity as a potential protective factor in stress-related rumination and demonstrate the value of examining rumination as a dynamic outcome in everyday life.

articles.title: Asymmetry in self-comparisons: Focal self bias in comparative judgment
articles.authors: Jareef Martuza; Esra Aslan
articles.abstract: Logical symmetry implies that if X is better than Y, then Y must be worse than X. Does this hold when people compare different versions of themselves? Nine main and three supplemental studies (N = 9,207 US- and UK-based adults) reveal a “focal self” bias—the self that is the subject of comparative judgments is perceived more favorably than the referent or compared self, over and above the content of the selves. When participants compared their present selves to their past or future selves on morality, warmth, and competence, they generally rated whichever self was focal more positively (Studies 1A-C)—contradicting logical symmetry. The focal self bias also extended to role-based self-comparisons between personal versus professional selves (Studies 2A-B), demonstrating it can shape evaluations beyond temporal selves. This pattern persisted even when the same participants made both reciprocal comparisons (Study 3), suggesting that the opportunity to reconcile judgments does not eliminate the bias. Across studies, because focal selves were rated lower on negative attributes, our data favor a selectivity account over a valence-independent extremity account. We also found that self-enhancement is not necessary for the focal self bias, as it emerged also when participants compared other people’s selves (Studies 4-5B). Finally, in direct self-other comparisons, making a peer focal largely eliminated the better-than-average effect (Studies 5A-5B), suggesting focality can partly account for this classic effect. These findings extend comparison asymmetries from distinct entities to comparisons of the same person, suggesting that which self occupies the focal position systematically shapes evaluations.

articles.title: Ulyssean Self-Control: Pre-commitment is effective, but choosing it freely requires good self-control
articles.authors: Hallgeir Sjåstad; Mathias Ekström
articles.abstract: Can pre-commitment strategies be a solution to self-control problems, or do they mainly help those who are already successful at regulating their behavior? In Study 1 (N=1,012), pre-commitment causally improved effort performance in an incentivized matrix-solving task. However, in Study 2 (N=1,010) participants with low (vs. high) self-control as a general trait were 35 percentage points less likely to choose the pre-commitment strategy, which in turn was associated with worse performance and earnings. Information about strategy effectiveness led to a small increase in uptake, whereas a “paternalistic” policy with forced pre-commitment led to superior performance. Study 3 (N=1,037) found that participants with high trait self-control were more likely to choose pre-commitment strategies across work, education, and health domains, mediated by higher future focus, strategy familiarity, and temptation avoidance. Pre-commitment is an effective strategy, but it is most often chosen by those who are already doing well: Individuals with good self-control.

articles.title: The Associations between Social Network Size and Preschool Children’s Visual Perspective-Taking and Non-Verbal Cue Understanding
articles.authors: Esmee Miron Aalders; Stephanie Wermelinger; Moritz M. Daum
articles.abstract:
Exposure to diverse communicative environments fosters a broader, more flexible
repertoire of communicative behaviour. Children’s social networks may constitute a
meaningful, yet underexplored, factor contributing to environmental diversity. In a
cross-sectional study, we examined whether social network size in preschool children
(N = 128, Mage = 4.06, SDage = 0.29) is associated with their communicative behaviour
indicated via three aspects: visual perspective-taking, non-verbal cue understanding,
and theory of mind (ToM). We ran two different types of analysis: first, the
conventional weekly contact threshold to operationalise social network size. This
analysis revealed no significant associations with the outcome variables. Second, we
conducted a data-driven grid search to identify the contact frequency threshold that
best predicted each outcome. The results suggest distinct candidate thresholds across
the three communicative behaviours assessed, indicating that each behaviour is
associated with a different relevant level of contact frequency. Visual perspective-taking
was positively associated with social network size calculated using a threshold of
approximately monthly contact. For non-verbal cue understanding, the best-fitting
threshold was about four interactions per week, at which social network size was
negatively associated with task performance. We found no significant associations
between social network size and children’s ToM. The findings show associations between
children’s social networks and pragmatic communication behaviour, but these
associations are sensitive to how social network size is operationalised.

articles.title: PRELIMINARY FRAMEWORK FOR A DYNAMIC SOCIO-ACOUSTIC MODEL OF SPEECH PERCEPTION
articles.authors: Meghan Sumner
articles.abstract: Listeners store detailed acoustic information and access social information cued by variation fast and early. Yet, how we understand all we understand remains an open question. I propose a Dynamic Socio-Acoustic Model that frames perception as a continuous, multidimensional tracking system where speech variation functions as primary cognitive information. This listener-driven model includes the fluid topological stretching of cognitive space, an acoustic exemplar space that is untethered to linguistic units and allows for multidimensional cross-context categorization. Listeners maintain a sub-lexical, macro-exemplar landscape where incoming acoustic-kinematic trajectories drive real-time resonance. Rather than matching signals to static templates, listeners construct ad-hoc categories on the fly, dynamically scaling an active grid in response to immediate environmental contrasts. By uniting continuous sensory tracking with fluid, experience-dependent spatial restructuring, this framework offers an ecological account of perception and memory that rethinks structural variation from a hurdle into a pathway to social meaning.

articles.title: Beyond Initial Crisis Recognition: Suicide-Risk Responses of ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini Across 14-Turn Ukrainian-Language Conversations
articles.authors: Hryhorii Kuzyk; Oleg Salamon; Liliia Andreieva; Kateryna Drozdova
articles.abstract: Nine deployed conversational systems mostly recognised the crisis, but it disappeared from their behaviour once the conversation moved on. We ran 16 scenarios in ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini as 14-message conversations (48 dialogues): crisis signals alternated with distraction, turn 13 introduced a new person at risk, and turn 14 was sent a day later. Coding was binary, as in the previous study, with clinical verification; two crisis-contour specifications were tested separately. New crisis signals drew a reaction in 87, 95, and 76 of 96 responses, respectively; the crisis stopped being mentioned mainly at an everyday message. The new person at risk drew a reaction in 44 of 48 responses; after a day, 29 retained crisis content. All 14 turns drew a 'yes' code in 4, 7, and 0 of 16 conversations. Reacting to the new person did not guarantee correct allocation of roles and actions. Both contour specifications produced safety-relevant errors. Neither hypothesis was supported: the systems behaved differently, and the same rule, introduced as a single package, did not stabilise their behaviour. Recognition, retention, and reconfiguration at a transition are distinct properties; the weakest is retention of the prior state and tracking of each person's trajectory.

articles.title: A Critical Epistemological Audit of Early Evidence Syntheses in Generative AI Educational Research: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
articles.authors: Tim Fütterer; Nina Peltzer; Peter Gerjets; Detmar Meurers; Tamara Powell Tate; Mark Warschauer; Valentin Emslander; Lisa Bardach; John hattie; Michael Sailer
articles.abstract: The rapid emergence of ChatGPT in education was accompanied by an equally rapid proliferation of meta-analyses synthesizing its effects on educational outcomes. We conducted a systematic epistemological audit of the first wave of these meta-analyses, evaluating both their methodological and reporting quality and the primary evidence they synthesized. We included meta-analyses published after the release of ChatGPT that quantitatively synthesized its effects on educational outcomes. Five meta-analyses comprising 87 unique primary studies met our inclusion criteria. We also reconstructed their quantitative evidence base and conducted exploratory three-level random-effects meta-analyses to examine effect magnitude, heterogeneity, and robustness, and how these varied with theoretically and methodologically relevant characteristics. The five meta-analyses generally searched multiple databases, specified eligibility criteria, and examined heterogeneity and potential publication bias, but showed limitations in independent screening and coding, preregistration, open data and code, and transparent reporting. The underlying primary evidence likewise showed methodological and reporting limitations and substantial conceptual heterogeneity. Among 69 classifiable primary studies, 79.7% assessed performance exclusively, whereas only 11.6% assessed learning exclusively. The reconstructed meta-analysis yielded a positive average effect (g = 0.83, 95% CI [0.68, 0.97]), but heterogeneity was substantial (I² = 94.06%; 95% prediction interval [−0.75, 2.41]), and estimates were markedly attenuated in sensitivity analyses addressing small-study and selection effects. Although positive effects remained among stronger studies assessing learning, increasingly stringent quality criteria rapidly reduced the evidence base, limiting the certainty and generalizability of conclusions about learning effects. Overall, our findings caution against interpreting a single pooled estimate as a stable general effect of ChatGPT on learning and highlight the need for more rigorous, conceptually precise, transparent, and reproducible research.

articles.title: Assessing User-Subjective Experience with Conversational Agents for Behavioral and Mental Health Interventions: Design and Psychometric Evaluation of CUE-Chat
articles.authors: Esther Mertens; Janis Butz; Jean-Louis van Gelder
articles.abstract:
While AI-conversational agents are increasingly integrated into behavioral and mental health interventions, standardized instruments to assess their performance remain scarce. To address this gap, we developed an instrument to measure user-subjective experience with AI-driven agents in the healthcare domain. We focused on user perception due to its direct contribution to intervention effects, and on healthcare given that the rapid adoption of AI-agents in this domain continues to outpace the development of validated evaluation instruments. 
Across four studies, we developed and tested the Chatbot User Evaluation instrument (CUE-Chat). First, we identified relevant assessment domains and items through literature review, existing instruments, input from AI-driven agents, and the research team’s domain expertise. Following this, we requested feedback on draft subscales, definitions, and items from expert and laypeople panels. We then tested the structure of the instrument’s concept version. Finally, we conducted a psychometric evaluation and finalized the instrument.
CUE-Chat consists of four factors: Perceived Efficacy (4 items), Usability (4 items), Intelligence (4 items), and Safety and Risk Management (4 items). Reliability and validity of the total score and each subscale was good to excellent (Cronbach’s α = .73-.92; Ω = .74-.93). Predictive validity was strong with all scales predictive of users’ overall rating of an AI-agent’s performance.
We conclude that CUE-Chat’s strong psychometric properties are promising, and that it is particularly useful for researchers integrating AI-driven agents into behavioral and mental health interventions in both developmental and evaluative stages.

articles.title: Moment-to-Moment Affect During Film-Induced Somatic Anxiety
articles.authors: Micah G. Allen
articles.abstract: A viral video of a dangerous stunt can make a viewer's palms sweat and heart race, even though they know they are safe. Such videos let us study emotion as it naturally unfolds, building, persisting and receding. Here we characterise the response to one such film moment by moment and present the open-source browser platform we built to do so. Viewers rate valence and arousal continuously on an affect grid embedded in the video. Each rating is stored with the frame on screen, the film pauses when viewing is interrupted, and participants are trained and their input checked. The film was a 13.5-min silent first-person recording of unsecured climbing. An exploratory sample (n = 21) informed preregistered tests in an independent confirmatory sample (N = 124). Arousal rose as the climb progressed, held a plateau for several minutes and then declined towards baseline, with valence most unpleasant during the plateau. This time course was highly reproducible across samples. Somatic anxiety increased substantially after the film (dz = 1.03), and participants with larger increases had rated it as more arousing and unpleasant. The film thus carries viewers through a reproducible, interoceptively charged emotional episode, and the platform can characterise other stimuli. Researchers can ask how the shift from a calm to an aroused state changes brain connectivity, interoception and emotion, and whether it is heightened in anxious people. Platform, data and reference time courses are openly available.

articles.title: Psilocybin-Assisted Therapy for Existential Distress in Serious and Life-Limiting Illness: Emerging Trial Evidence, Barriers to Access, and the Case for Individualized Eligibility
articles.authors: Janis Ancans
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Background. Existential distress and treatment-resistant depression are common and difficult to manage in patients with serious and life-limiting illnesses. Psilocybin-assisted therapy has shown early promise for these conditions, but access outside research settings remains narrow, inconsistent, expensive and often shaped by outdated eligibility rules. These include extremely limited lists of diagnosis- or just blanket age-based cut-offs, that are not grounded in evidence specific to palliative populations. Regulators slowly adjust to the state-of-the-art knowledge generated by psilocybin-assisted therapy, and overall, often present poor understanding of palliative populations specific needs.
Objective. To review current and emerging clinical evidence for psilocybin-assisted therapy in serious and life-limiting illness, highlighted with the examples of the EU “Horizon Europe” funded PsyPal project and a Johns Hopkins-led trial in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and to examine the regulatory, informational, and financial barriers that shape access for palliative populations.
Findings. Randomized trials in cancer-related existential distress report sustained reductions in depression and death anxiety. Furthermore, a majority of participants in the founding psilocybin studies rated their session among the most meaningful experiences of their life. Project PsyPal is currently the first randomized trial of psilocybin therapy in non-oncology palliative populations, enrolling patients with COPD, ALS, multiple sclerosis, and atypical parkinsonian disorders across four European sites with no upper age limit; a separate trial at Johns Hopkins is testing psilocybin for mood and hopelessness in ALS specifically. Real-world cohort data from Oregon's regulated program corroborate meaningful symptom improvement and low serious-adverse-event rates. Access, however, remains constrained by diagnostic and research-representation gaps, high out-of-pocket cost, and inconsistent regulatory pathways, illustrated by a Canadian patient refused psilocybin for existential relief who was approved for medical assistance in dying within weeks.
Conclusion. Clinical evidence relevant fort to palliative and serious-illness populations is accumulating rapidly. Eligibility frameworks for psilocybin-assisted therapy in palliative care should be built on individualized clinical assessment rather than systematic exclusions, paired with funding mechanisms that prevent access from becoming a function of wealth alone.

articles.title: Interpretability in the Limit: How Can Understanding Machines Help us Understand Human Language?
articles.authors: Najoung Kim; Ethan Gotlieb Wilcox
articles.abstract: In the coming years, interpretability research will uncover a vast set of machine constructs: causally efficacious representations and processing mechanisms underlying the use of language and other intelligent behavior in AI systems, including LLMs. Assuming that interpretability will be as successful as can be reasonably hoped for (interpretability in the limit), how can the discovery of machine constructs shape linguistics and cognitive science? First, we provide several axes of analysis that can help scientists conceptualize the internal mechanisms discovered in machines. Even under the assumption that interpretability in the limit guarantees that all constructs are causally implicated in a system's behavior, scientists may want to consider several additional properties, including constructs' theoretical status, domain status, ontological status, and complexity. Second, we argue that scientists should prioritize recurrent constructs, meaning those that surface across a diversity of models converging on behaviors of interest while varying on other axes such as architecture, training data, objective function, language, and modality. Finally, we provide three routes for how machine constructs can inform linguistic and cognitive theories, emphasizing that all of these routes treat machine constructs as hypotheses, where additional theorizing and experimentation by domain experts are required. We conclude with several recommendations that can be implemented now for improving the long-term success of this program.

articles.title: What is there to explain about free will? An “easy problem” of consciousness downstream of agency
articles.authors: Nicolas Rouleau
articles.abstract: Free will is one of the most enduring problems in philosophy and cognitive science, yet what, exactly, requires explanation remains unclear. The most tractable target is the experience of free will – the vivid sense of self-authorship, control, and a felt capacity to have done otherwise. As with the scientific study of mystical experiences, this phenomenology can be investigated without resolving the metaphysical claims implied by its content. Here, I argue that free will is an “easy problem” of consciousness: a phenomenon that can be measured, manipulated, predicted, and mechanistically explained. Taking causal determinism as a working postulate, I consider whether prediction and reinforcement could generate the experience of controlling one’s own actions through causal misattribution and superstitious conditioning, without granting consciousness independent causal power. If the experience can be explained under deterministic constraints, the core scientific explanandum of the free will phenomenon has been addressed. Free will can then be distinguished from agency, which remains a causally consequential, graded capacity for goal-directed, adaptive, and self-regulating action across living systems, machines, and hybrids thereof.

articles.title: Breaking Common Ground through Reciprocal Misalignment
articles.authors: Siham Abu Ali; Tatiana Philippova; Isaac Fradkin
articles.abstract: Establishing shared meaning is widely considered the normative, almost ubiquitous trajectory of linguistic interaction, while moments of misalignment are typically viewed as temporary interruptions that individuals attempt to repair. However, it is not uncommon to experience communication breakdowns that actively escalate rather than resolve. This raises a fundamental question: does interaction inherently lead people toward shared meaning, or is semantic alignment a reciprocal, socially contingent process? We conducted four experiments using a novel multiplayer word association task, where participants generated semantic associations while interacting with either human or simulated partners varying in semantic typicality. Our results show that, in general, social interaction motivates individuals to produce more conventional associations to support alignment. However, this tendency depended on partner’s behavior: when interacting with an atypical or difficult-to-align-with partner, individuals actively reduced their own typicality and tendency to match partner’s associations, effectively sacrificing semantic alignment. Such ‘reciprocal misalignment’ persisted even when participants were incentivized to maximize alignment. Our findings suggest that semantic misalignment may reflect a reciprocal, socially-motivated modulation of identity and differentiation, rather than solely a failure of coordination. This work sheds light on the interactional mechanisms underlying interpersonal distancing, communication breakdowns in neurodivergence, and potentially broader patterns of social polarization.

articles.title: Seeing Through the Eyes of Experienced Practitioners: How online training can accelerate expertise development and improve decision quality of novice graduates
articles.authors: Karin S. Moser; Andrew Whittaker; Milou T. Brand; Denise Harvey
articles.abstract: The ability to make high-quality decisions in ambiguous, uncertain, and time-pressured work situations is crucial in many sectors. This can be challenging in fields with high turnover, such as most emergency services, and means that recent graduates and novices in the field are often put on the frontline early on without the chance to acquire in-depth experience-. While previous research has studied how experienced practitioners make decisions in real-life situations, including in the emergency services, we still know little about the processes that allow acceleration of expertise development for novices and how higher education training could contribute to this. This study used the example of child protection and social work education to examine whether decision-making training with video feedback from experienced practitioners could improve novice social workers’ decision quality, using an experimental study design (n=83 novice professionals), with a feedback and no-feedback condition respectively, and realistic child protection scenarios. Results showed an increase of decision-quality for both treatment and control groups, suggesting that the training alone already induced learning, even without expert feedback. However, consistent with our hypotheses, the treatment group with feedback showed significantly greater improvement in qualitative aspects of decision-making compared to the no-feedback control group, namely a better understanding of the risks involved and in assessing the quality of available information. We conclude that online training with expert feedback can be a promising and economically viable educational measure for improving decision quality and accelerating the expertise of recent graduates, namely in high-turnover fields such as child protection.

articles.title: Inconclusive prospective effects between technology acceptance, classroom distraction, and academic engagement among Chinese high school students: A reassessment of Li and Chen (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles.abstract: Li and Chen concluded reciprocal prospective associations between technology acceptance, classroom digital distraction, and academic engagement among high school students. However, significant cross-lagged parameters do not by themselves establish genuine prospective influence because similar estimates may arise through alternative statistical processes. Using simulated data that reproduced the sample size and correlation matrix reported by Li and Chen, I examined whether their conclusions were robust across several defensible analytic specifications. The pattern of results depended strongly on analytic choice: some models suggested positive prospective associations, whereas others indicated negative or null effects. When estimates from all specifications were combined using meta-analytic methods, no overall effect reached statistical significance. Accordingly, the available evidence does not provide a firm basis for concluding that technology acceptance, classroom distraction, and academic engagement exert reciprocal prospective influences on one another. In line with multiverse-analysis recommendations, conclusions should be drawn from the collective pattern across reasonable analytical alternatives rather than from a single model.

articles.title: “Oh No, the Robots Are Here”: AI identity labels, social uptake and sanctioning in mixed human–AI communities
articles.authors: Sara Major; Aleksandar Tomašević; Ana Vranić; Darja Cvetkovic; Dušan Vudragović; Boris Stupovski; Marija Mitrovic Dankulov
articles.abstract: Social media users can now encounter autonomous AI accounts that post, reply and vote alongside other users. In a longitudinal field experiment, we examined how labelling these accounts relates to whom people answer and how they evaluate AI contributions. YSocial is a Reddit-like hybrid platform for social media simulation, where people interact with language-model agents. On it, 36 participants discussed popular culture with 72 AI accounts powered by an uncensored language model over 21 experiment days. The AI accounts kept persistent personas and remembered previous exchanges. They were visibly labelled in one community and unlabelled in the other. Among 2,143 human replies, Bayesian models estimated that the probability of replying to an AI-authored post or comment was 3.5 percentage points higher in the hidden-label community, given the same earlier posts and comments available in the thread (95% credible interval 0.5–6.5). In both communities, participants were more likely to reply to an AI account after it had replied to them and less likely after they had replied to it. The gap in criticism, including polite disagreement, between replies to AI and human accounts was 13.3 percentage points larger in the visible-label community (95% credible interval 5.1–21.4). The toxicity difference was uncertain. Visible labels were associated with less engagement with AI contributions and more criticism of them.

articles.title: Impact of social affiliation and musical agency on movement and interpersonal coordination in adolescence
articles.authors: Martin Hartmann; Alessandro Ansani; Iballa Burunat; Marc Thompson; Pedro Neto; Joshua Silberstein Bamford; Patti Nijhuis; Rita Mustonen; Matias Hämäläinen; Toivo Niemi
articles.abstract: Dancing together to music is a common social activity in which movement coordination emerges from the interplay of interpersonal relationships and a shared musical environment. While previous work on dyadic dance movement has focused on individual differences, third-party judgments of synchrony, and disentangling partner- from music- driven coordination, relational and situational determinants of coordination have received less attention. This motion capture study investigated how social affiliation and agency over the music influence movement characteristics and social coordination in young people. A total of 164 adolescents danced in dyads with both a friend and a stranger, and to self- and researcher-selected music in a counterbalanced design. Extracted kinematic features included head and hand movement magnitude, movement complexity, fluidity, interpersonal distance, mutual orientation, and synchrony. Results showed greater, more complex and less fluid movements when participants danced with friends compared to strangers. Head and hand movement magnitudes were larger for self-selected than researcher-selected music, but only when self-selected music followed researcher-selected music. Friends also exhibited higher interpersonal synchrony, danced closer, and looked more towards each other than strangers. These findings shed light on how social and contextual factors shape dance behaviour in adolescence.

articles.title: Registered Report: Does the valence-dominance model apply to deepfake faces? Validation and its impact on deepfake detection
articles.authors: Gianmarco Convertino; Mara Stockner; Michela Marchetti; Danilo Mitaritonna; Luca Corvitto; Luca Maiano; Lorenzo Papa; Irene Amerini; Giuliana Mazzoni
articles.abstract: Artificial Intelligence has given rise to increasingly more realistic fake contents such as deepfake faces, hardly distinguishable from real faces. However, evidence has shown that social evaluations of real faces are also able to impact the detection of deepfake faces. The present study aimed at applying for the first time the valence-dominance model for face evaluation on deepfake faces. Moreover, the impact of its thirteen attributes on deepfake detection performances was investigated. Specifically, 311 participants categorised 120 faces (50% real, 50% deepfake created ad hoc by Diffusion Model technology) and rated faces in regards to one of the attributes. Principal Component Analysis was applied in order to validate the valence-dominance model on deepfake faces, and a Brunswikian lens model was  applied to understand how each attribute contributes to a face being judged as deepfake. Results replicated the valence-dominance model on real faces as well as on faces categorized by participants as deepfake, but not on actual deepfake faces. Finally, the indirect effects of the Brunswikian model revealed caringness and intelligence to impair detection of deepfake stimuli, whilst weirdness was revealed to be a positive indirect predictor, being positively associated with higher detection accuracy of deepfake faces. Our results shed, for the first time, light into the differential cognitive processing of deepfake faces and their social evaluation whilst also providing novel insight into underlying mechanisms associated with deepfake detection. Interdisciplinary implications regarding the theoretical and applied contribution are discussed.

articles.title: A Three-Domain Framework for Trust in Digitally Mediated Social Life
articles.authors: anonymous; YUAN SHEN; Ke Shen; Jinliang Qin
articles.abstract: Digital technologies increasingly mediate information access, social interaction, and institutional participation, raising the question of how trust in digital systems is organized in relation to trust in people and institutions. Across three independent samples of Chinese young adults, we tested a three-domain framework of trust in digitally mediated social life and developed a concise measure distinguishing interpersonal trust, institutional/rule trust, and digital system trust. Study 1 (N = 1,495) identified a three-factor structure using parallel analysis and exploratory factor analysis. Study 2 (N = 1,333) confirmed this structure: the three-factor model outperformed a unidimensional model and all pairwise-collapsed two-factor alternatives, although the three domains remained strongly correlated. Study 3 (N = 901) provided evidence consistent with measurement invariance across gender and initial nomological differentiation. Learning-oriented digital engagement was more strongly associated with institutional/rule and digital system trust, everyday/relational engagement with interpersonal and digital system trust, and digital information judgment with institutional/rule trust. Sensitivity analyses reproduced the primary patterns. Together, the findings support a three-domain framework in which digital system trust is strongly interconnected with, but not reducible to, trust in people or institutional arrangements.

articles.title: Navigating Autistic College Students’ Career Development: A Capability-Oriented Perspective on Agency and Advocacy
articles.authors: Yilun Jiang; Karly Ball Isaacson; Bradley E. Cox; Brett Ranon Nachman
articles.abstract: Autistic college students navigate career development through their interests and strengths, while encountering deficit-oriented assumptions about autism. Research on autistic students’ career development usually focuses on career support and skill development, while limited studies have examined how they pursue career pathways from a strengths-based perspective. Drawing on a secondary analysis of semi-structured interviews from a national mixed-methods study (n = 36), we examined how autistic college students in four-year U.S. colleges navigate career development. Applied thematic analysis identified three themes: participants developed purpose-driven career goals through long-standing interests, lived experiences, and community exposure; navigated judgments about capability and professional fit across academic and career contexts; and assembled career support across career centers, faculty, and autism support groups. Our findings highlight autistic participants’ capability to explore career pathways that reflect their interests and goals and suggest an agency-beyond-advocacy interpretation, in which agency refers to broader forms of action through which students shape their career development and advocacy represents one important form of agency. Finally, we offer suggestions for universities and employers to develop resources more tailored to autistic students’ career goals and needs.

articles.title: Charting Expectations About Economic Gains and Losses Across Adulthood
articles.authors: Sebastian S. Horn; Alexandra M. Freund
articles.abstract:
Expectations about changes of one’s economic situation impact motivation and decision making. Yet, little is known about how people think about economic changes across adulthood. In this
study, participants (N = 1,045) aged 18–88 years from Germany and Switzerland charted their expectations about (a) normative income and wealth trajectories for average adults of different
ages, (b) their personal past, present, and future trajectories, and (c) anticipated trajectories with and without active investment. Participants also reported their motivational gain, maintenance,
and loss-avoidance orientation for financial goals. Normative economic expectations of all age groups followed an inverted-U pattern of gains into midlife followed by losses in older
adulthood. Bayesian multilevel models showed that participants differentiated income and wealth, with an earlier peak and steeper decline for income than wealth. In contrast to normative
expectations, personal expectations differed markedly by age, with older participants judging their economic development less favorably than younger participants. These judgments covaried
with motivational orientation. All age groups expected future active investment to improve their economic prospects, but older adults anticipated smaller benefits and even losses under active
investment. Participants’ normative judgments corresponded well to representative income and wealth data (German Socio-Economic Panel; Swiss Household Panel), suggesting that adults of
different ages hold shared and relatively realistic expectations about age-graded economic gains and losses. At the same time, the findings highlight substantial age-related differences in
personal expectations.

articles.title: The Emergent Structure of Memory Phenomenology Depends on Whether Memories Are More Episodic or Semantic
articles.authors: Tabatha Blaney-Gale; Jordan Poppenk
articles.abstract: Phenomenological characteristics are central to theoretical distinctions among modern memory constructs. The scene construction framework proposes that episodic remembering involves the construction of coherent scenes, such that the structure of phenomenology may reflect the engagement of the hippocampus and related regions during recall. However, most phenomenology research relies on instruments with content and scoring schemes that embed theoretical assumptions into their measurements. Here, we explored whether phenomenological characteristics emerge from self-reported memory experiences as anticipated by episodic memory theory. We solicited memories from a large online sample, following each response with a novel questionnaire designed to evaluate the phenomenology of individual memories. We used folded bottom-up factor analyses to examine and validate the global latent factor structure of participants’ memory experiences. Consistent with Tulving’s declarative memory framework, our analyses produced five stable dimensions: imagery, autonoetic consciousness, mental time travel, relational memory, and semantic memory. In order, these dimensions reflect multi-modal perceptual reexperiencing, personal meaning, sense of reliving, detailed spatiotemporal context, and conscious use of semantic knowledge during recall. The semantic memory dimension has no clear predecessor, suggesting the strategic use of general knowledge during recall is a distinct and previously uncharacterized aspect of remembering. This factor structure generalized across memories elicited by recent and remote episodic prompts. However, distinct versions of mental time travel and relational memory emerged in response to the semantic prompt, suggesting these dimensions of memory are context-sensitive rather than fixed. While our findings validate the link between episodic memory and its theorized phenomenological elements, they also invite broader investigation of how phenomenology may vary across different classes of memory.

articles.title: Examining the Relations Between Self-Construal, Culture, and Cognitive Dissonance Using the Induced Compliance Paradigm
articles.authors: Tim Figureau; Daniel Priolo; Willem W. A. Sleegers; Kenneth G DeMarree; Omid Ghasemi; Amélie Gourdon-Kanhukamwe; Maxime Mauduy; Asil Ali Özdoğru; Robert M Ross; Bjørn Sætrevik
articles.abstract: Cognitive dissonance, traditionally conceptualized as a fundamental psychological process involving discomfort from inconsistent cognitions, may vary across cultures. These variations could be attributed to self-construal, or how individuals define themselves in relation to others. Although previous cross-cultural research has predominantly used the free-choice paradigm, significant concerns have been raised regarding its procedural validity and the robustness of its findings. To address this issue, this registered report presents secondary analyses of a large-scale international dataset. We investigated the moderating role of cultural variables on dissonance effects within the induced-compliance paradigm across 18 countries (N = 3,804). We hypothesized that dissonance effects would be stronger for participants with higher individuallevel self-construal scores (H1), in more individualistic countries (H2), and in countries with higher country-level self-construal scores (H3). Our results did not support these hypotheses, suggesting that cultural moderation may not generalize to the induced-compliance paradigm. We discuss the necessity of reassessing the procedure’s reliability and clarifying the theoretical role of choice.

articles.title: When Are Less Precise Predictions More Credible?
articles.authors: Eitan David Rude; Amin Shiri; Felipe M. Affonso; Hal Hershfield; Craig R. Fox
articles.abstract: People expressing uncertain values frequently offer point predictions or intervals of varying widths (e.g., “I’d say your investment will be worth $6,000” versus “I’d say your investment will be worth $5,000–$7,000”). Interestingly, prior research has drawn conflicting conclusions concerning the credibility of more versus less precise predictions. We resolve this inconsistency by identifying a key moderator: the perceived nature of uncertainty. Specifically, we find that under epistemic (“knowable”) uncertainty, predictions are seen as conveying experts’ degree of confidence, and more precise predictions are seen as more credible. Under aleatory (“random”) uncertainty, however, predictions are seen as conveying experts’ assessments of the degree of outcome variability, and less precise predictions are seen as more credible (provided they are within reasonable bounds). These results inform literatures on both the communication of uncertainty and the interpretation of confidence intervals.

articles.title: Expertise Diversity Enhances Information Sharing in Wiki settings: Evidence from Sequential Collaboration
articles.authors: Maren Mayer; Joachim Kimmerle
articles.abstract: Online collaborative projects such as Wikipedia and OpenStreetMap rely on sequential collaboration, where contributors iteratively revise a shared product over time. While previous research has examined wikis for computer-supported collaborative learning and sequential collaboration for numerical judgment tasks, little is known about the cognitive mechanisms underlying information sharing in such settings. The present study bridges research on computer-supported collaborative learning, group information sharing, and cognitive models of sequential collaboration. Drawing on a computational model of sequential collaboration, we tested the prediction that higher variation in contributors' expertise facilitates the integration of information into a shared product. In an experimental study with 413 participants we demonstrate that information accumulation increased throughout the sequential chain but at a decreasing rate. Consistent with model predictions, higher expertise variation significantly increased the likelihood that information was incorporated into the shared text. Contrary to expectations, expertise variation did not affect the timing of information inclusion across chain positions, nor did it increase information deletions. These findings demonstrate that predictions derived from a cognitive model of numerical judgment formation generalize to information-sharing contexts. More broadly, the results suggest that diversity in contributors' knowledge can improve collaborative knowledge construction in sequential environments. This research adds to evidence that sequential collaboration is an effective mechanism for integrating distributed knowledge in online collaborative systems.

articles.title: MBB-AVR: a mind-brain-body dataset with dynamic affective states in immersive virtual reality
articles.authors: Antonin Fourcade; Anthony Buck Ciston; Lucy Roellecke; Jeroen de Mooij; Hector Leos; Arno Villringer; Sara Carletto; Francesca Malandrone; Michael Gaebler
articles.abstract: We present MindBrainBody-AffectiveVR (MBB-AVR), a multimodal dataset capturing continuous affective experience and both central and peripheral physiological responses during naturalistic emotional stimulation in immersive virtual reality. Forty-seven healthy adults (24 female, 22 male, 1 non-binary; age = 27.1 ± 5.4) viewed a 23-minute stereoscopic 360° video sequence, composed of computer-generated, language-free content designed to elicit high affective variability over time, presented via a head-mounted display (HTC Vive Pro Eye). While immersed, participants continuously rated their momentary valence and arousal using a previously validated rating tool with real-time visual feedback. Synchronized recordings include 64-channel EEG, ECG, respiration, photoplethysmography, galvanic skin response, and head and eye tracking with pupillometry. Participants additionally completed questionnaires including interoceptive sensibility and alexithymia. The dataset is organized following the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) and includes extracted low-level audio and video features of the stimulus. It may support research on the temporal dynamics of affect, multimodal physiological correlates of emotion, and affective computing. The dataset is available at https://gin.g-node.org/fourcade_a/mbb-avr.

articles.title: Increasing cerebellar beta rhythms shifts cerebral oscillatory signatures of context-driven language processing
articles.authors: Sandra Ambichler; Tessa Portier; Vitória Piai; Jana Klaus
articles.abstract: While there is growing consensus that the cerebellum is part of the cerebrally centred network underlying language processing, the direct nature of its contribution to comprehension and production remains unknown. In particular, while both processes require lexical access, production additionally involves motor processes linked to articulatory planning, which has fuelled the view that the cerebellum is primarily involved in motor control in language production. Cortically, both lexical access and articulatory planning are known to be driven by alpha-beta power decreases. To disentangle cerebellar involvement in language, this study investigated the modulatory effect of transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) over the right cerebellum on context-driven language comprehension and production. In a cross-over, double-blind, sham-controlled within-participants design, 32 healthy volunteers received 20 minutes of 20-Hz tACS (2 mA peak-to-peak) targeting the right posterior cerebellum. Immediately afterwards, they performed a context-driven language task while EEG was recorded from 32 channels. In the task, visually presented lead-in sentences creating a constraining or unconstraining context were followed by a picture depicting the final word of the sentence. Participants were instructed to name the picture (production) or judge its animacy (comprehension). Responses became slower overall following active compared to sham tACS, and this increase was more pronounced in the comprehension task. In line with previous work, reliable context-related oscillatory power decreases were observed in response to the context manipulation, but exhibited a different pattern across tasks and stimulation conditions. For production, beta-centred power decreases following sham shifted to temporally and spatially extended alpha power decreases following active tACS. By contrast, alpha-centred power decreases following sham tACS in the comprehension task increased following active tACS. Increasing beta activity in the right posterior cerebellum thus affected early stages of context-driven language processing linked to lexical access in both language domains. The stimulation-induced spectral, spatial and temporal shifts suggest recruitment of alternative cortical resources as a consequence of cerebellar network modulation. This interpretation is consistent with the cerebellum functioning as a network node coordinating temporal dynamics across distributed language regions.

articles.title: Visual Deprivation Alters Parent-Specific  Autonomic Tuning During Infancy
articles.authors: GIULIA CAPPAGLI; Marta Guarischi; Guido Catalano; FEDERICA MORELLI; gori monica; Sabrina Signorini
articles.abstract: Parents' touch regulates infants' physiology, and vision may be essential for identifying social partners, but whether the absence of visual feedback affects this physiological effect has never been tested. We examined whether visual deprivation alters infants' autonomic responses to affective touch from a parent versus a stranger. Eighteen infants aged 8–13 months (9 with peripheral visual impairment, 9 sighted) received slow stroking (3 cm/s) on the right shin while the parent or an unfamiliar adult sat in front of them as the apparent source of touch. Typically developing infants showed a larger heart-rate deceleration during parent than stranger touch. Infants with visual impairment did not differentiate between adults and showed higher heart-rate responses than typically developing infants in the parent condition (Group × Parent Identity interaction). Visual experience may help link affective touch to its social source. The small, clinical sample limits generalizability, and replication is needed.

articles.title: Techno-Optimism Reduces Willingness to Address Climate Change
articles.authors: Jonas M B Haslbeck; Maien S. M. Sachisthal; Fabian Dablander
articles.abstract: Technological innovation is essential for mitigating climate change, but so are wider socio-economic transformations as well as lifestyle changes. Techno-optimism, the belief that technological innovation alone is sufficient to address climate change, may reduce public willingness to engage in climate action. Here we use a structural causal model to estimate the causal effect of techno-optimism on willingness to contribute 1\% of one's monthly household income to address climate change using a large, population-weighted sample from the Netherlands (N = 23, 395). We find that being a techno-optimist reduces the probability of being willing to contribute by 18.7% (95% CI: 15.6, 20.7). In addition, we find that the causal effect is much smaller for respondents on the political right, where overall willingness is already very low. We close by discussing the importance of adequately framing the role of technology when discussing climate change mitigation.

articles.title: Neural Racing Accumulator Model Estimation With Lightweight Monotonic Flows
articles.authors: Malte Lüken; Stefan T. Radev; Lourens Waldorp; Andrew Heathcote
articles.abstract: Race models describe speeded decision-making as a race between competing runners that accumulate evidence in favor of available choice options. Their parameters can be estimated through the model likelihood that combines the probability and cumulative density functions of each runner. However, estimating parameters of complex race models whose runners have intractable densities with (hierarchical) Bayesian inference has been challenging: Numerical density approximations tend to be slow and amortized neural posterior estimation methods require complex network architectures that can be expensive to train and, in classical settings, tie the trained estimator to a specific prior distribution and generative model. We propose a flexible neural estimation method that decouples training from the choice of prior distribution or model parameterization. We train a small neural network together with a monotonic neural spline flow to simultaneously learn the runners' conditional probability density and cumulative density functions. We then combine both functions to efficiently estimate race model likelihoods that can be used in combination with modern samplers. We demonstrate the utility of our approach on both tractable and intractable versions of the popular racing diffusion model. Based on our results, we argue that, when flexibility in choosing prior distributions or model parameterizations is needed, learning the model likelihood with lightweight neural density estimators is advantageous.

articles.title: The Limits of Identifiability in the Self-Exciting Ornstein–Uhlenbeck Model
articles.authors: Hannah Pongratz; Constantin Gregor Meyer-Grant
articles.abstract:
Evidence-accumulation models play a central role in the field of decision-making research, offering a comprehensive framework for understanding choice behavior and response times, including speed–accuracy tradeoffs (SATs). In this framework, the dominant explanation for SATs has long been that prioritizing speed lowers the boundary separation, meaning less evidence is needed to make a choice. Recently, however, an alternative account has been proposed according to which emphasizing speed induces a confirmation bias toward the currently favored option. Such a behavior can be formally captured by a self-exciting Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process. However, drawing on asymptotic arguments and extensive simulation studies, we demonstrate that under certain conditions, key parameters of the resulting evidence-accumulation model are not jointly identifiable. We explain the underlying cause of this identifiability issue, examine its practical consequences for model-based inference, and
present potential strategies to resolve or mitigate it.

articles.title: Real-time Associations Between Psychological States and Context in University Students with Suicidal Ideation: An Ecological Momentary Assessment Study
articles.authors: Ana Portillo-Van Diest; Gemma Vilagut; Laura Ballester; Johan Bjureberg; Paula Carrasco; Raquel Falcó; Margalida Gili; Mathilde Husky; Glenn Kiekens; Francisco H. Machancoses
articles.abstract: Suicidal ideation (SI) is dynamic and linked to emotion regulation difficulties that may be reflected in associations between momentary psychological states and context. In a 2-week ecological momentary assessment (EMA) study, 476 students reported passive daily SI, momentary psychological states (affect, stress, tiredness, concentration difficulties) and contexts four times per day. Multilevel network analysis compared contemporaneous, temporal, and between-person networks across three groups: one without SI or psychopathology (No-MD/SI), and two with low and high 14-day passive SI (Low- and High-SI). Low- and High-SI groups showed more temporally self-reinforcing negative affect and weaker affect-context connections. No-MD/SI students showed stronger positive affect recovery following negative affect. High-SI students spent less time with loved ones and were more likely to engage in conversation after stress than after positive emotions. Findings suggest that passive SI is associated with greater negative emotion rigidity and a shift in social connectedness from enjoyment to distress-driven coping.

articles.title: fMRI hyperscanning reveals widespread neural coupling during natural conversations
articles.authors: Laetitia Mwilambwe-Tshilobo; Lily Tsoi; Sebastian Speer; Zaid Zada; Shannon M. Burns; Emily B. Falk; Diana Tamir
articles.abstract: Conversation is one of the most powerful tools that people have for building and maintaining social connections. How does conversation bring two minds together? Here we tracked the neural dynamics between dyads during real-time conversation using fMRI hyperscanning, where both people were scanned simultaneously, to explore whether and how conversation aligns brains. Dyads engaged in natural, free-flowing conversation as they co-constructed the content of their dialogue. In a control condition, partners read aloud scripted dialogue from another dyad’s conversation, preserving the turn-taking structure while removing the co-construction. To examine neural alignment, we compared whole-brain intersubject correlation between partners in each condition, assessing both synchronous and predictive neural dynamics. Results showed that naturalistic conversation led to significant widespread neural alignment across brain regions implicated in attention, audition, affect, executive control, and social cognition, compared to scripted conversation. Temporally refined analyses showed that during naturalistic conversation, relative to scripted conversation, both speakers and listeners anticipated each other within a short temporal window, with brain activity preceding their partner’s in the same neural systems. These findings show that live, turn-taking conversations align neural activity well beyond passive or asynchronous communication, providing a foundation for future research examining how spontaneous, co-constructed dialogue allows people to communicate effectively.

articles.title: Developing an adolescent self-report measure of social media experience: Insights from cognitive interviews
articles.authors: Jo Hickman Dunne; Louise Black; Jade Davies; Frederick Jones; Molly Anderton; Pratyasha Nanda; Felicitas Beissel; Lauren Burke; Reihaneh Farzinnia; Margarita Panayiotou
articles.abstract: Despite a rapid increase in research exploring the relationship between adolescent social media use and mental health, the field is hindered by poor quality tools that lack the validity and precision to assess this relationship. The current study presents findings from cognitive interviews that aimed to refine a multidimensional measure of adolescents’ social media experiences relevant to their mental health and wellbeing. We conducted 20 individual, paired or group interviews with 35 adolescents aged 11-16, across three rounds of interviews, testing 83 of a possible 107 items. Through iterative testing, issues relating to comprehension; inapplicability and assumptions within items; and items not addressing their intended experience, were identified and addressed. The interviews also highlighted two wider conceptual issues: (1) the impact of parental restrictions on adolescents’ experiences, and (2) difficulties in responding to items about abstract, identity-based experiences. In addition, the interviews supported an understanding of preferred response options and format. Findings from this study informed specific revisions to measure items to enhance validity, as well as broader considerations for assessing adolescent social media experience. Our study also reinforces the importance of cognitive interviewing in refining adolescent measures more broadly. We identify the need for the development of a set of general recommendations to guide item writing for adolescents, and further work to understand optimal response label options and wording for longer recall periods. Development of such guidance, alongside the greater use of cognitive interviews to pre-test measures, is crucial for improving instrument validity in the field of adolescent mental health.

articles.title: Citation Fabrication and Accuracy in AI-Generated Psychiatric Research: A Comparative Evaluation of Four Contemporary Large Language Models
articles.authors: Jake Linardon; Cleo Anderson; Tayarna Bolger; Claudia Liu; Olivia Marie Soliman; Zoe McClure
articles.abstract:
Objectives. LLMs are increasingly used to support academic writing, but their tendency to hallucinate citations raises concerns about the integrity of AI-assisted scholarly work. This study provides a timely snapshot of citation reliability in LLM-generated academic reviews by testing whether citation fabrication and accuracy differ across four LLMs and review topic specificity.  

Method. ChatGPT-5.4 Plus, ChatGPT-5.3 Free, Gemini-3, and Claude Sonnet-4.6 were tasked with generating 16 literature reviews on mental health, divided into general topics (broad areas with substantial evidence bases) and specialised topics (narrower areas with smaller evidence bases). 

Results. Only 6.1% of the 825 LLM-generated citations were fabricated, with fabrication absent for ChatGPT-5.4 Plus (0%), very low for Claude Sonnet-4.6 (0.5%) and ChatGPT-5.3 Free (5.5%), and highest for Google Gemini-3 (20.2%). A similar model-level pattern emerged for citation accuracy (real citations containing no bibliographic errors). Review topic specificity was not associated with citation fabrication or accuracy. 

Conclusion. Findings suggest possible improvements in citation reliability relative to estimates from prior studies testing older model iterations, while also showing that current performance is strongly model-dependent. These findings highlight the need for rigorous human verification of LLM-generated references and stronger safeguards to protect research integrity as LLMs are integrated into research.

articles.title: Understanding the role of generative artificial intelligence in mental health support: Survey of user experiences, engagement patterns, and perceived risks and benefits
articles.authors: Jake Linardon; Zoe McClure; Cleo Anderson; Claudia Liu; Olivia Marie Soliman; Mariel Messer
articles.abstract: Generative AI – especially ChatGPT – is increasingly used for mental health purposes, but users’ subjective experiences of these tools remain unclear. We characterized how individuals utilize ChatGPT for mental health support through a web-based survey completed by 308 adults (Mage=31.5, SD=5.3; 54% men) who reported prior use of this tool. Around half reported use of ChatGPT for mental health support more than once a week, 80% have used it for more than 3 months, and a third reported increased use over time. Depression (55%), anxiety (74%), stress (66%), and relationship conflict (49%) were the problems most frequently discussed with ChatGPT, with the severity of these problems typically rated as mildly or moderately severe. Endorsed reasons for use were its on-demand availability (71%), free cost (69%), and anonymous nature (54%), while common functions the platform served included obtaining advice (71%), providing a safe space for expression (63%), and to learn coping strategies (61%). Experiences were largely positive, with 8 in 10 agreeing that ChatGPT helped them feel understood, better process their emotions, and improve their mental health literacy. Concerns were also evident, with around half expressing worry about data privacy, and a quarter feeling overly reliant on the platform and reducing their motivation to seek help. Few indicated that ChatGPT had replaced professional help (7%) or discouraged help-seeking (12%). Findings shed light on how users are engaging with generative AI for mental health support and highlight the importance of rigorous research designed to evaluate its safety and long-term efficacy.

articles.title: In AI Do We Trust? Comparing a Transformer-Based Natural Language Processing Model Against a Traditional Content Analysis Approach to Qualitative Research
articles.authors: Matthew Baron; Catherine Stein
articles.abstract:
Central to debates about the use of artificial intelligence (AI) models for qualitative
research are concerns about comparability and trust in AI generated findings. The present
methodological study compared findings from a transformer-based Natural Language Processing
(NLP) model, BERT, against a traditional content analysis approach to qualitative research using
the same text data. We examined claims that AI models generate findings that are identical or
similar to traditional qualitative approaches. The study assessed three aspects of comparability
between the BERT model solution and human-coded findings that included topic labeling,
classification overlap, and AI replicability. Results indicated broad similarity in the semantic
meaning of topic categories generated by the BERT model and themes from content analysis.
There was low overlap in the classification of individual participant responses between BERT
and content analysis categories, even for categories similar in semantic meaning. Running the
BERT model a second time on the same input data resulted in differences in topic categories and
document classification between the two approaches. Study implications and research
recommendations for the use of NLP models are discussed.

articles.title: Do bilinguals avoid ambiguity or minimise processing effort? Insights from an online eye-tracking study in spoken Mandarin
articles.authors: Yajun Liu; Antonella Sorace; Kenny Smith
articles.abstract:
Previous research shows that bilinguals tend to choose more explicit referential forms (e.g., overt pronouns over null pronouns) compared to monolingual speakers, but the mechanisms driving this tendency remain debated. By conducting two experiments examining lexical ambiguity in spoken Mandarin, we tested two hypotheses: 
Hypothesis 1: bilinguals would rather be redundant than ambiguous in general; 
Hypothesis 2: bilinguals avoid ambiguity only when doing so helps reduce cognitive load. 
In Experiment 1, L1 Mandarin L2 English speakers in the UK and more-monolingual speakers in China completed a picture naming task, where we manipulated whether the context in which a picture is named makes the preferred label ambiguous (e.g., do speakers avoid saying “fen3 si1” when describing a picture of glass noodles when it appears alongside a picture of fans which shares the same label?). Experiment 2 extended this task by incorporating online eye-tracking using WebGazer. Our results showed that, contrary to Hypothesis 1, bilinguals were more likely than more-monolinguals to use ambiguous expressions. Eye-tracking analysis revealed that bilinguals tended to direct early attention toward image pairs with more accessible labels, indicating a preference for linguistic choices that are cognitively less demanding; by contrast, more-monolinguals showed proactive monitoring of ambiguity depending on their responses. These findings support Hypothesis 2 and shed light on cognitive constraints in bilingual lexical access and early signs of lexical attrition.

articles.title: Social Support among LGBTQ, Cisgender, and Heterosexual Undergraduate Students:  An Ego-Centric Social Network Study
articles.authors: Allyson Marie Blackburn; Nathan Todd; Nicole Allen
articles.abstract: While the population and acceptance of LGBTQ people are growing, there are persistent mental health disparities for LGBTQ individuals, especially for emerging adults. Social support is critical for the promotion of well-being. Yet, who receives support and the nature of the support provided can vary based on social identity, including sexual orientation and gender identity. In this study, we demonstrate the benefit of using ego-centric social network analysis (ESNA) to advance research about emotional support for sexual minorities. Using a sample of 1,215 undergraduate students (253 sexual minorities) from a large Midwestern university, we show that sexual minorities reported a greater proportion of LGBTQ people yet a lower proportion of family in their social network. We also show that sexual minorities reported that they were less likely to receive support but were more likely to be nominated by both heterosexuals and sexual minorities as network members who provide support. Finally, sexual minority participants relied more on friends than parents for emotional support, whereas the opposite was true for heterosexual students. These (and other) findings show how ESNA allows for testing hypotheses that capture the interconnected context of relationships. We discuss how findings advance the literature along with limitations and implications. Overall, we show that ESNA is a valuable tool to use to understand social networks as a critical context for development and well-being.

articles.title: No evidence that positive outcomes elicit a stronger sense of agency once correcting for publication bias: a commentary on, and re-analysis of, Mariano et al. (2025)
articles.authors: Robrecht van der Wel; Shaheed Azaad; Pernille Hemmer; John Michael
articles.abstract: In a recent meta-analysis, Mariano et al. (2025) conclude that people experience a stronger sense of agency over positive than negative outcomes, indexed by temporal compression. In this commentary, we evaluate that claim and identify several concerns about its validity. First, we argue that temporal compression effects should be standardized before being combined, because values in milliseconds are not necessarily comparable across different paradigms. When we analyzed standardized effects, evidence for a valence effect was absent once adjusting for publication bias. Second, we identified data integrity issues, identifying several studies that were included but either (1) did not manipulate outcome valence at all, or (2) contained only a positive or negative condition compared to a neutral condition. Excluding these studies meant that even unstandardized effects did not support Mariano et al.’s headline finding.

articles.title: Cross-country variation in early childhood family digital media ecology: A ManyBabies 8 registered report
articles.authors: Nevena Dimitrova; Sarah Kucker; Joscelin Rocha-Hidalgo; Koeun Choi; Lucas Gago-Galvagno; Elizabeth Jessica Goldman; Louisa Kulke; Lauren J. Myers; Sarah Pila; Catarina Vales
articles.abstract: Digital media use during early childhood is widespread yet unevenly documented globally, with most evidence drawn from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD; i.e., Minority World) societies. This registered report examines cross-country and context-specific variation in digital media exposure among children 6-36-months-old. Guided by the Dynamic, Relational, Ecological Approach to Media Effects Research (DREAMER) framework, the ManyBabies 8 consortium investigates: (1) age of first direct media use; (2) amount of direct media use and indirect media exposure; (3) social context of media use (joint media engagement, caregiver media disruptions); and (4) caregiver motivations and rule-setting practices. Caregivers from 58 countries will complete standardized surveys in 2027. Countries will be grouped into empirically derived country-clusters based on country-level indicators. Preregistered linear and logistic mixed-effects regression models will examine differences across country-clusters, accounting for participants nested within countries and family structural characteristics included as covariates. It is hypothesized most children will experience direct use and media exposure before 2-years, and that direct media use, indirect exposure, caregiver practices, and motivations will vary across countries and family contexts. By harmonizing measures across countries, this study will provide the first comprehensive characterization of early childhood direct digital media use and indirect exposure.

articles.title: Neural Correlates of Beat Processing in Infancy and Their Association With Later Grammar Development: Evidence for the Atypical Rhythm Risk Hypothesis
articles.authors: Eniko Ladanyi; Srishti Nayak; Catherine T. Bush; Youjia Wang; Tiffany G. Woynaroski; Miriam D Lense; Matthew K. Leonard; Reyna L Gordon
articles.abstract: Infants show evidence of beat processing from birth, but its neural correlates in infancy remain poorly understood. Moreover, although rhythm and grammar abilities are closely linked in older (school-aged) children, it is not known whether individual differences in infant beat processing lay the foundations for those associations.
