This longitudinal EEG study examined neural correlates of beat processing in 6–12-month-old infants (N=37) and their relation to sentence comprehension skills in the same children at 4 years. We analyzed infants’ evoked time–frequency responses to rhythmic tone–tone–rest sequences presented in physically accented conditions and in inferred-beat conditions, in which accents were removed after an initial exposure phase.. Analyses revealed a significant increase in power to physically accented beats (9–24 Hz, p < .001). Individual differences in this response were positively associated with receptive grammar performance at age 4, assessed with the TROG-2 (r = .48, p = .005), and remained significant after controlling for infant age, parent education, and home music environment (β = .45, p = .011). The inferred beat effect was not related to later sentence comprehension performance. These findings indicate that infant neural activity tracks beat structure, with neural correlates broadly similar to those reported in adults, and that early neural sensitivity to beat is associated with later grammar development, supporting the Atypical Rhythm Risk Hypothesis.

articles.title: Infants’ ability to learn novel sound patterns changes with age
articles.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Alejandrina Cristia
articles.abstract: Learning native language phonotactics could render infants somewhat more inflexible with respect to novel pattern learning. Reanalyses of previously published data and a new study aligned to support this hypothesis: performance in phonotactic learning becomes erratic at about 7 months of age.

articles.title: srifm: Role of lexical information for perceptual learning
articles.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Alejandrina Cristia; Annika Hultén; Holger Mitterer
articles.abstract: Linguistic representations continue to be updated, probably implicitly, as a side effect of normal language use. In particular, a large body of work shows that we learn novel pronunciations of well-established phonemic categories rapidly (Norris, McQueen, & Cutler, 2003). This learning is thought to be automatic, such that it operates quickly once there is sufficient information to disambiguate the identity of that novel pronunciation: Effects are seen after encountering 10 instances of the ambiguous sound within unambiguous lexical items. Here, we uses perceptual learning to test predictions from two types of theories of speech perception, lexical feedback models (e.g., TRACE, McClelland & Elman, 1986; Magnuson et al., 2003) and autonomous models (e.g., Shortlist, Norris, 1994; Merge, McQueen & Cutler, 2010). According to TRACE, phonemes, and words are tracked in the input in parallel, and decisions at both of these levels are influenced online by the other levels. In this model, disambiguation is driven by the lexical level. In contrast, Merge postulates that listeners accumulate knowledge of sublexical representations, such as diphone probabilities, in addition to lexical knowledge.

articles.title: Questionable mediated effect of care-resistant behavior in dementia patients on nurses’ occupational burnout: A comment on Ding et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Ding et al., I reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking care-resistant behavior in dementia patients to nurses’ occupational burnout. I demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article. In this alternative account, self-reported care-resistant behavior, psychological detachment, professional calling, and occupational burnout are conceptualized as indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation. The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern. Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives. Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.

articles.title: Do Ocular and Facial Features Reflect Listening-Related Fatigue and Predict Rest Decisions in Adults With and Without Hearing Loss?
articles.authors: Anna Dreneva; Johannes Sebastian Wienen; Alina Schulte; Cora J. Caron; Dorothea Wendt; Tobias May; Hamish Innes-Brown; Lorenz Fiedler
articles.abstract:
Listening-related fatigue is common in individuals with hearing loss and may affect decisions to continue with or disengage from listening, yet its objective assessment remains challenging. We used an effort-based decision-making paradigm to investigate whether subjective fatigue ratings predict objective eye- and face-related measures and whether the combination of subjective and objective measures predicts listen-or-rest decisions during a listening task.
Twenty-seven German-speaking adults with normal hearing (NH; 35.7±13.1 years) and thirty Danish hearing-aid users (HA; 73.7±7.1 years) each completed 126 speech-in-noise trials with varying difficulty and reward, while on each trial they could decide whether to listen or to rest. Subsequently, subjective fatigue ratings were collected after each trial. Eye and facial features were recorded throughout the entire study. Analyses were conducted within groups and proceeded in two stages. First, linear mixed-effects models examined how subjective fatigue, task difficulty, reward, and response correctness predicted each eye and facial metric. Second, these metrics, along with the same predictors, were used to model trial-by-trial rest decisions.
In NH participants, greater subjective fatigue was consistently associated with reduced eye openness and increased gaze velocity (small-to-medium effects), as well as higher blink rates (small effect). In HA users, greater fatigue similarly predicted reduced eye openness and increased gaze velocity (small-to-medium effects), together with a small increase in negative facial expressions. In both groups, rest decisions were more likely when task difficulty was higher, reward was lower, and subjective fatigue was higher. In NH participants, incorrect response and greater eye openness in the preceding trial additionally increased the probability of choosing rest.
This work supports the assumption that ocular and facial indicators may serve as promising markers of preceding subjective fatigue and decisions to rest in people with hearing impairment. Recognizing these markers could play an important role in assessing and managing listening‑related fatigue.

articles.title: External and internal attention: Mind the role of switches for memory functioning
articles.authors: Anaïs Servais; Emmanuel Barbeau
articles.abstract: Attention continuously shifts between information arising from the external environment and internally generated representations such as thoughts and memories. Episodic memory retrieval provides a particularly relevant case in which attention must be redirected from ongoing perceptual processing toward internal memory representations. In this chapter, we examine this transition through the framework of the Attentional Switch to Memory (ASM), a construct proposed to describe the reorientation of attention from the external world toward the internal mental space supporting episodic memory retrieval. We review elements about the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying this switch and discuss how ASM may differ between strategic (i.e., voluntary) and involuntary memory retrieval. In strategic retrieval, the switch is proposed to occur early, following the establishment of the episodic retrieval mode and before controlled memory search. In involuntary retrieval, by contrast, the attentional shift may occur only after a memory representation has already been partially activated. We further discuss candidate behavioral and physiological markers of the ASM, with a particular focus on gaze aversion, eye movements, pupil dynamics, and changes of vergence. Together, these findings highlight attentional switching as a potentially critical but understudied component of episodic memory retrieval and provide directions for future research aimed at characterizing its temporal, cognitive, and neural dynamics.

articles_hidden.title: Clustering of differential conditioned response trajectories using skin conductance: Are fear conditioning studies affected by pre-existing characteristics?
articles_hidden.authors: Luke John Ney; Matthew Greaves; Matthew Paul O'Donohue; Trevor Steward; Yi Wang; Madeline Jarvis; Rachel Patterson; Camilla Luck; Ottmar Lipp
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent research suggests that responses during experimental fear conditioning follow distinct latent trajectory classes. Computational reinforcement learning models can be used to infer latent learning processes during the task (e.g., learning rates and prediction-error sensitivity) that may help explain these classes. The present study re-analysed previously published and unpublished datasets to examine patterns of fear learning using skin conductance responses (SCRs) in a large sample of healthy participants. Data were aggregated from 12 fear conditioning experiments (N = 1,083; Mage = 20.72 years), encompassing acquisition, extinction, and return-of-fear phases. Using k-means clustering, we identified solutions comprising either two or three distinct response profiles. Across clusters, approximately half of participants showed minimal differential SCRs, while the remaining participants exhibited higher conditioned responding during acquisition, with subsets differing in whether fear returned following extinction. Cluster membership was significantly predicted by gender, current anxiety levels, post-acquisition conditioned stimulus pleasantness ratings, and Bayes factors quantifying evidence for model-based learning. Comparison of reinforcement learning models indicated that a latent cause model provided a superior account of SCR data relative to Rescorla–Wagner, Pearce–Hall, and hybrid models, with latent cause parameters differing by cluster and gender. The clustering data provide preliminary evidence that SCR outcomes in fear conditioning studies may be disproportionately influenced by a minority of participants with specific pre-existing characteristics, rather than reflecting uniform learning processes. Moreover, the results provide support for latent cause theories of fear learning and highlight the value of combining clustering and computational approaches to better understand individual differences in fear acquisition, extinction, and relapse.

articles_hidden.title: The Vanderbilt Report’s critique of humanistic scholarship is itself bad scholarship and should be corrected or retracted
articles_hidden.authors: Patrick E. Savage
articles_hidden.abstract: Vanderbilt University’s “Report on the State of Scholarship in the Humanities and the Humanistic Social Sciences” (Boghossian et al., June 25, 2026) argued that humanistic scholarship has experienced “a deterioration in scholarly standards fueled by the substitution of political criteria for properly scholarly criteria”. The initial (August 2026) version of my critique emphasised that these conclusions were primarily based on unpublished, unverifiable data. Now that most of the data underlying the report (largely from unvalidated Large Language Model [LLM] categorisations) have been belatedly published, I show that these data do not support the report’s main claims. I briefly review the main data from each published disciplinary sub-report (music studies, anthropology, sociology, history, literary studies). Overall, there is an utterly indefensible mismatch between the actual empirical data (e.g., decreases in the ratio of Western classical music vs. all other music studied) and Boghossian et al.’s conclusions of an overall “deterioration in scholarly standards”. While I agree with the authors that critical evaluation of the quality of academic scholarship is urgently needed in today’s global political climate, the report’s main conclusions are not remotely justified by their data and are likely to hinder rather than facilitate informed debate. I recommend Boghossian et al.’s report be corrected or retracted to resolve these issues.

articles_hidden.title: A Benchmark for Gaze-Based Target Detection in Immersive Virtual Reality: Effects of Eccentricity, Size, and Speed on Observation and Detection Dynamics
articles_hidden.authors: Arwa Leilah Adib; Margaret E. Sereno; David Schwarz
articles_hidden.abstract: Virtual reality enables studying active visual search and gaze behavior under naturalistic, free-viewing conditions while preserving experimental control. However, free head-eye coordination, extended 3D space, dynamic target trajectories, and headset-specific field of view and eye-tracking constraints mean that findings from traditional 2D paradigms cannot be assumed to generalize to immersive environments. Interpreting gaze-based outcomes in VR requires bench-marks that establish how basic target properties influence detection. We used target eccentricity, size, and speed as benchmark predictors of visual detection in an immersive VR coin-foraging task. Using in-headset eye-tracking, participants guided a gaze-controlled avatar to collect coins that varied in gaze-relative eccentricity, size, and speed. We modeled gaze-based observation probability, observation latency, dwell time, gaze-coin angular distance, and saccade dynamics. Observation probability was analyzed using mixed-effects logistic regression, whereas latency was analyzed with a censoring-aware Cox framework that retained never-detected coins. Eccen-tricity and size showed the clearest benchmark effects. Peripheral and small coins were less like-ly to be detected. Speed’s role was more nuanced. Although slow coins were detected more of-ten in a binary model, this advantage did not persist in a censoring-aware survival analysis, suggesting that speed influenced the opportunity for observation more than momentary salience. Consistent with this interpretation, slow coins produced longer dwell times, and gaze-coin an-gular distance and saccade measures indicated that target properties shaped both the geometry and effort for acquisition. These findings establish a feature-based benchmark for gaze-based de-tection in immersive visual search and demonstrate the importance of modeling missed targets as censored detection opportunities.

articles_hidden.title: Navigating Autistic College Students’ Career Development: A Capability-Oriented Perspective on Agency and Advocacy
articles_hidden.authors: Yilun Jiang; Karly Ball Isaacson; Bradley E. Cox; Brett Ranon Nachman
articles_hidden.abstract: Autistic college students navigate career development through their interests and strengths, while encountering deficit-oriented assumptions about autism. Research on autistic students’ career development usually focuses on career support and skill development, while limited studies have examined how they pursue career pathways from a strengths-based perspective. Drawing on a secondary analysis of semi-structured interviews from a national mixed-methods study (n = 36), we examined how autistic college students in four-year U.S. colleges navigate career development. Applied thematic analysis identified three themes: participants developed purpose-driven career goals through long-standing interests, lived experiences, and community exposure; navigated judgments about capability and professional fit across academic and career contexts; and assembled career support across career centers, faculty, and autism support groups. Our findings highlight autistic participants’ capability to explore career pathways that reflect their interests and goals and suggest an agency-beyond-advocacy interpretation, in which agency refers to broader forms of action through which students shape their career development and advocacy represents one important form of agency. Finally, we offer suggestions for universities and employers to develop resources more tailored to autistic students’ career goals and needs.

articles_hidden.title: Predicting and explaining public support for environmental policies: A comparative analysis of two theories
articles_hidden.authors: Violetta Vysevkova; Claire Farrow; Jason Thomas; James Reynolds
articles_hidden.abstract: Environmental policies are crucial for mitigating climate change and protecting people’s health. Public opposition, however, often undermines their adoption and success. Theories that seek to explain and predict policy support and opposition are insufficiently tested or have not received empirical support. This study tested how well one influential theory, and one new theory explain and predict support for environmental taxes on frequent flying, fast fashion, and red meat. These two theories are the Value-Belief-Norm (VBN) theory and the Integrative Public-Policy-Acceptance (IPAC) framework. A cross-sectional online survey was conducted with a nationally representative sample of adults in the United Kingdom (N = 1,270). Data were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling. The IPAC model explained a substantially greater proportion of variance in support for all three policies (R2 = .81–.85) than the VBN model (R2 = .20–.26). The IPAC model also produced practically meaningful predictions of policy support (RMSE/MAE = 0.63–0.91), whereas the VBN model did not (RMSE/MAE = 1.40–1.78). The direct comparison confirmed the IPAC is the superior model of policy support (BICIPAC < BICVBN). Several propositions of the IPAC framework were not supported, highlighting the need for further tests and perhaps refinements to its structure. To enhance the precision of explanations and predictions, we recommend that theories of policy attitude include policy-specific beliefs, such as perceived policy fairness and effectiveness—the strongest determinants of policy support. Other relevant factors can be considered in assumptions that supplement theories for application in specific contexts.

articles_hidden.title: A Person-Centered Analysis of Change in Supports for Child Welfare-Involved Families and Caregiver and Child Outcomes
articles_hidden.authors: Qiong Wu; Lenore M McWey; Melissa Radey; Ming Cui
articles_hidden.abstract: Families involved with the U.S. child welfare system are overwhelmingly lower-resourced and often experience multiple hardships, which can adversely affect mental health. Research indicates that public, private, and child welfare system supports may individually shape caregiver and child well-being. Conversely, loss or insufficiency of support is linked to more family hardship and worse parent and child mental health. With data from the National Survey of Child and Adolescent Well-being II, we used a person-centered approach to examine longitudinal configurations of public, private, and child welfare system supports over three years and caregiver and child outcomes. Results revealed distinct patterns of family supports over time, and that public and private supports tended to be stable, but child welfare system supports were likely to change over time. Mean difference comparisons across classes generally revealed that parents with strong private safety nets reported better mental health outcomes for themselves and lower behavioral problems for their children compared to those with high public and low private supports. Findings from this study have practical implications for supporting families involved with the child welfare system.

articles_hidden.title: The Structure and Content of Meaning in Speech Reflects Mental Health
articles_hidden.authors: Luke Leckie; Alicia Meuret; Thomas Ritz; Olivia Losiewicz; Michelle G. Craske; Jacob G. Foster
articles_hidden.abstract: Mental health shapes the progression and content of thought. Studies have linked depression, anxiety, and stress with repetitive negative thoughts, but it remains unclear whether these disturbances are reflected in the structure of an individual's speech. We introduce an approach to quantify the structure of thought as expressed in language, applying it to memory recountings from 82 individuals across six psychotherapy sessions. We model each recounting’s semantic progression with contextual embeddings, and use persistent homology to identify loops of meaning, as recountings circle back upon themselves. More loops are associated with depression, anxiety, stress, and negative affect, and with negative self-referential language, implicating them as geometric markers of negative fixation and rumination. Semantic content also relates to mental health. However, neither semantic structure nor content mediate therapeutic improvement. These findings reveal that the semantic structure of speech offers a quantitative window into thought disturbances in depressive and anxiety disorders.

articles_hidden.title: Everyday Encounters with Economic Inequality
articles_hidden.authors: Carla Moccia; Matthew John Easterbrook; Matthias S Gobel
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on economic inequality has traditionally relied on macro-level indices, though a growing body of work examines how economic inequality is perceived in everyday life. Whether different forms of everyday encounters carry different political and psychological consequences remains unclear. Across four studies with London-based samples (N = 1,554), we used a situation-sampling approach to identify forms of real-world inequality encounters and test how they relate to appraisal, redistribution support, and psychological distress. Study 1 identified two forms of inequality: Structural Inequality, describing disparities in essential goods and institutions, and Lifestyle Inequality, involving differences in consumption, leisure, and social participation. Study 2 showed that Structural situations were perceived as more unequal and unfair and elicited stronger redistribution support than Lifestyle Inequality situations. Study 3a, reported in Supplementary Materials, showed that greater redistribution support for Structural Inequality situations was largely carried through greater perceived unfairness. Study 3b modelled Structural and Lifestyle Inequality content continuously: Structural Inequality was linked to redistribution support and distress through unfairness, whereas Lifestyle Inequality was linked to distress through upward social comparison. The political and psychological consequences of inequality therefore depend on the form of encounter, not only on its perceived magnitude.

articles_hidden.title: Attentional network processing in children and adults shows comparable behavioural effects but distinct ERP and time–frequency activity
articles_hidden.authors: Praghajieeth Raajhen Santhana Gopalan; Otto Loberg; Jarmo Hamalainen; Paavo H. T. Leppänen
articles_hidden.abstract: Visual attention comprises alerting, orienting, and executive-control networks. Although these networks are behaviourally evident in childhood, age differences in the neural processes supporting them remain unclear. Typically developing 12–13-year-old children (n = 77) and 19–33-year-old adults (n = 21) performed the Attention Network Test while electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded. Behavioural performance was assessed using reaction time and accuracy. Neural processing was examined using event-related potentials (N1 and P3 amplitudes and latencies) and induced time–frequency analyses of theta (4–7 Hz), alpha (8–12 Hz), and beta (13–25 Hz) band activity. Significant alerting, orienting, and executive-control effects were observed in reaction time, with children responding more slowly overall than adults. Children showed longer N1 latencies than adults during the orienting comparison, indicating slower early target-related processing. Alerting cues increased target-related N1 amplitudes similarly in both groups. Adults, but not children, showed smaller P3 amplitudes for incongruent than congruent trials, whereas children showed larger P3 amplitudes overall, suggesting age-related differences in conflict-related processing. Time–frequency analyses showed that alerting modulated theta-, alpha-, and beta-band activity similarly in both groups. Orienting-related theta activity differed between age groups, with children showing higher theta power for spatial- than centre-cue trials. Alpha-band activity also differed between orienting conditions similarly in both groups. These findings indicate that children and adults can show comparable behavioural attentional network effects despite differences in neural processing. The results further suggest that electrophysiological measures of attentional processing show age-related differences beyond late childhood.

articles_hidden.title: EEG in Parkinson’s Disease: Mechanisms, Biomarkers and Translational Opportunities
articles_hidden.authors: Sümeyye Özdemir; Sahar Allouch; Manon Auffret; Mahmoud Hassan; Marc Vérin
articles_hidden.abstract: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is characterized by nigrostriatal dopaminergic degeneration and basal ganglia dysfunction, yet these pathophysiological abnormalities alone do not fully explain its heterogeneous motor and non-motor manifestations. Over recent decades, electroencephalography (EEG) has evolved from a primarily descriptive technique into a quantitative approach for investigating cortical electrophysiological dynamics associated with PD. Accumulating electrophysiological evidence implicates altered oscillatory synchronization and interactions across cortical and subcortical circuits in PD-related dysfunction, suggesting disturbances in the temporal coordination of neural activity. Emerging approaches, including large-scale datasets, multimodal integration, individualized modeling and wearable EEG technologies, offer opportunities for physiological phenotyping and real-world monitoring. However, methodological heterogeneity, limited reproducibility, insufficient external validation and uncertainty regarding clinical utility continue to constrain translation. This Review critically synthesizes EEG-derived measures spanning spectral activity, oscillatory coupling, functional connectivity and dynamic brain states, examining their relationships with motor, cognitive and neuropsychiatric manifestations of PD. By distinguishing mechanistic interpretations, clinical associations and current levels of biomarker validation, it identifies opportunities and requirements for translating EEG-derived measures into reliable tools for individualized assessment and clinical decision-making.

articles_hidden.title: Enduring or Adaptable? A formal model and meta-analytic test of the stability of personality disorders
articles_hidden.authors: Orestis Zavlis; Michael Moutoussis; Peter Fonagy; Patrick Luyten
articles_hidden.abstract: Personality disorders have been traditionally framed as enduring dispositional conditions. Yet accumulating evidence suggests that they also reflect dynamic patterns of contextual adaptation. In this paper, we develop a formal framework that partitions personality stability into two components: an enduring portion (which is retained perfectly over time) and an adaptable portion (which dissipates over time, at either a fast or slow rate). After validating the model in computer simulations, we conduct a meta-analysis of 12 longitudinal investigations (N=17,785), yielding 145 test-retest correlations that quantify the stability of all personality conditions over 18 years. We then apply our formal model on these meta-analytic stability estimates to quantify the extent to which personality disorders are enduring vs. adaptable over time. Results indicate that most of personality pathology (60-70%) is adaptable over 18 years’ time, though it dissipates at a moderate rate (R≈55%). We conclude by suggesting that there is no formal distinction between personality pathology and psychopathology and outline a program aimed at studying all mental disorders as personality disorders.

articles_hidden.title: Checkmating Cognitive Aging?  A Pilot Study Examining the Relationship between Chess Play and Cognitive Functioning in Older Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Caton Tsao; Aman Sreshta; Kaileigh A. Byrne
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives: Engagement in cognitively stimulating activities may support cognitive functioning in older adulthood, yet the potential benefits of chess participation remain understudied. This pilot study explored differences in working memory and global cognitive functioning between older adult chess players and non-chess players, while accounting for demographic characteristics and social engagement.
Methods: Eighty-three older adults (46 chess players; 37 non-chess players) completed computerized assessments of working memory capacity using a shortened Operation Span task and global cognitive functioning using a battery assessing memory, language, orientation, and executive functioning. Participants also reported their chess experience and social engagement. Analyses of covariance examined differences in cognitive performance between chess players and non-chess players, adjusting for age, gender, education, and social engagement.
Results: Older adult chess players (M = 14.62, SD = 6.35) exhibited better working memory capacity than non-chess players (M = 13.08, SD = 6.04, p=.032) independent of demographics and social engagement, while social engagement was associated with broader cognitive functioning (r = .267, p = .030).
Conclusions: These preliminary findings suggest that chess participation is selectively associated with working memory capacity, whereas broader social engagement is associated with global cognitive functioning. This distinction highlights the importance of examining specific forms of cognitive and social enrichment when investigating healthy cognitive aging. Larger longitudinal and experimental studies are needed to determine whether chess participation contributes to maintaining working memory in later life.

articles_hidden.title: Development and Validation of Team Functional Degrees of Freedom (TfDoF): An Eco-Physical Variable for Functional Collective Off-ball Movements in Football
articles_hidden.authors: Li Xiao; Daniel Carrilho; enrico serra; Nelson Caldeira; Rui J. Lopes; Duarte Araújo
articles_hidden.abstract: In football, limited research has considered both the processes underlying collective behavior and its functional outcomes, constraining its practical applicability. In this study, we developed and validated an eco-physical variable, Team Functional Degrees of Freedom (TfDoF), to quantify how off-ball players dynamically coordinate their movements with teammates, opponents, and the ball to afford functional passing opportunities for a team in football. TfDoF was developed through a “glocal” spatial framework integrating centroid dynamics, Voronoi diagrams, dynamic pitch zoning, and a rule-based degrees-of-freedom approach. Validation comprised two complementary stages. First, expert-based validation involved seven football experts who evaluated the computational framework and identified passing opportunities in 30 match clips at the instant of passing. TfDoF showed a very strong correlation with expert-perceived passing opportunities (r = .98, p < .001), while all content validity indices exceeded .86, providing preliminary evidence of its content and convergent validity. Second, performance-based validation examined the relationship between TfDoF and pass outcomes using synchronized tracking and event data from 35 Italian Serie A matches (20,531 passes). Among six machine learning algorithms, XGBoost achieved the best classification performance (AUC = 0.909). SHAP analysis identified TfDoF as the most influential predictor of pass success (FI = 1.453), providing evidence of its predictive validity. Notably, TfDoF’s contribution to pass success was non-linear, with the greatest marginal effect occurring between TfDoF values of 5 and 7. Finally, we proposed a multi-timescale analytical framework demonstrating how TfDoF can support tactical analysis and coaching practice.

articles_hidden.title: Group psilocybin in an integrative retreat setting enhances social connection: an observational case report
articles_hidden.authors: Dayne Rayford; Shivani Dayal; Kosu Boudreau; Dingle Spence; Marik Hazan; AZA Stephen Allsop
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background and aims
Psilocybin can induce profound alterations in perception, emotion and self-referential processing. These changes are often accompanied by increased feelings of interpersonal connection, found via both psychometric survey data and anecdotally collected qualitative data. Despite recent increases in psychedelic research and treatment, most clinical trials have been performed in individualized patient treatment paradigms. Few studies have examined the outcomes of psilocybin in group contexts, even though ceremonial and group-based usage is historically ecological and may uniquely enhance group dynamics and social bonding.
Methods
This case study investigated psychological and social outcomes among participants (n=14) of a group psilocybin ceremony conducted in an integrative retreat setting. Participants completed a series of psychometric surveys and performed a social behavioral task designed to measure social perceptions at baseline and again at two timepoints following the psilocybin ceremonies.
Results and conclusions
Our results indicate significant increases in perceived social connectedness on the Social Perception Assessment (SPA) and the Watts Connectedness Scale (WCS) as well as significant decreases in distress on the Subjective Units of Distress Scale (SUDS). These findings highlight the importance of studying group-based psychedelic administration and suggest that collective settings may generate synergistic social benefits not captured in individual therapeutic models.

articles_hidden.title: Relationship between physical activity and resilience to stressors in non-clinical samples of adolescents and young adults: A systematic review
articles_hidden.authors: Bertalan Polner; Nina van den Broek; Anna Tyborowska; Linda Visser; Jacqueline Vink; Jonas Wachner; Margarita Karakara; Imke Adams
articles_hidden.abstract: While the benefits of physical activity for physical and mental health are well-established, it is less clear whether it also boosts resilience, defined as preserved mental health after exposure to stressors. Resilience in adolescents and young adults is critical given the high prevalence and lasting impact of mental health problems that emerge during development. Despite increasing recognition of the importance of physical activity for resilience, a structured overview is missing. Therefore, a systematic review of the literature was conducted including records published until December 2025 in PsycInfo, PubMed, Embase and Web of Science. We included 90 intervention and longitudinal studies on physical activity, and resilience in adolescents and young adults (10- 25 years) without a diagnosed mental health problem. In general, controlled intervention studies (n=39) showed various physiological and psychological benefits of physical activity in youth exposed to adversity and stressors. Intervention studies without a control group (n=26) and longitudinal observational studies (n=25) yielded comparable results. These findings imply that physical activity may causally impact resilience in youth exposed to adversity and stressors. It should be noted, however, that more preregistered, well-powered studies are required to corroborate these conclusions before formulating clinical or policy recommendations.

articles_hidden.title: Using Language Models to Predict Values, Personality, Well-Being, and Meaning in Life From Ideal-Life Descriptions
articles_hidden.authors: Joffrey Fuhrer; Théo Desbordes
articles_hidden.abstract: Does the way we picture our ideal life reveal what we value, who we are, and how we thrive? In a preregistered study (N = 273), we tested whether free-form descriptions (median 109 words) and seven-keyword lists of one's ideal life predict a broad battery of psychological constructs: the Big Five, the ten Schwartz values, social dominance, political orientation, meaning in life, and subjective well-being. Using regularized linear probes on embeddings from transformer large language models (LLMs), inspired by model-interpretability research, we find that ideal-life narratives predict most constructs above chance in both conditions (mean r = 0.24 for free-form, mean r = 0.12 for keywords). This free-form advantage was concentrated on constructs people rarely name outright, such as achievement, benevolence, conformity, and emotional stability, implying that part of the signal lies in the manner of the telling rather than in the referents alone. Nineteen of the 24 constructs were recovered from roughly 120 words of text, a far broader battery than earlier language-based work, which has relied on much longer samples and focused on personality and well-being. Our approach offers an open, privacy-preserving alternative to zero-shot commercial LLMs, with comparable accuracy, no API cost, and freely released data and code.

articles_hidden.title: A Two-Stage Scaffolding Model of Color and Luminance Development: Retinal Waves, Global Impoverishment, and Luminance-Grounded Object Representations
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: How does the visual system construct object representations that are robust to the removal of color? I propose a two-stage scaffolding model. In Stage 1 (prenatal), retinal waves establish spectrally non-selective spatiotemporal contrast sensitivity, the necessary structural foundation of the visual system, before any visual experience occurs. Because the wave-generating circuitry encodes only contrasts in firing rate with no access to spectral information, this foundation is necessarily achromatic: whatever circuits retinal waves entrain, they are trained on a signal that carries no chromatic content. In Stage 2 (postnatal), the globally degraded neonatal visual signal, low spatial resolution, low contrast sensitivity, and immature chromatic processing, all coupled through shared photoreceptor immaturity, forces the first object representations to be built on luminance structure, the only dimension with sufficient fidelity under maximal front-end degradation. Together, these two stages explain why normal observers recognize objects in grayscale as readily as in color: luminance structure was the foundation of object representations from the beginning. The model also explains why late-sighted individuals who gain sight after dense congenital cataracts show disproportionate reliance on color: they retain the prenatal structural scaffold (intact retinas generating normal retinal waves) but lack the postnatal experiential scaffold (years of globally impoverished visual experience that normally grounds object representations in luminance). The model generates testable predictions that distinguish it from color-specific developmental accounts, and several can be evaluated on existing computational architectures without new patient data.

articles_hidden.title: General and domain-specific genetic signals shape educational outcomes in children and adults
articles_hidden.authors: Alexandra Starr; René Pool; Hailey Adelene Davis; Iorana Fosca Alice Fey; Ana Luisa Henriques Fürst; Eugenia Kis; Yola Sol; Lannie Ligthart; Bruno Sauce; Elsje van Bergen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Purpose: Individual differences in literacy and numeracy – that is, how well one can read, write, and work with numbers – emerge early in childhood and are crucial indicators of later educational success. Twin and family studies revealed substantial heritability of literacy and numeracy, and genetic overlap between these domains. Yet, it is unclear whether measured genomic variation shows a similarly overlapping or domain-specific pattern, and whether such molecular signals also predict adults’ educational attainment.
Method: In N=15,669 participants (52.7% female; Netherlands Twin Register), we predicted children’s literacy, numeracy, and academic achievement, and adults’ educational attainment from genetic predispositions. Children’s learning outcomes were assessed via teacher and parent reports and a nationwide test (age M=12.25 years). Adults reported their highest educational qualification (age M= 42.47 years). We derived polygenic scores (PGSs) for years of education, dyslexia, and reading skills to predict these outcomes. 
Results: All three PGSs significantly predicted educational outcomes, but the broad years-of-education PGS exceeded the domain-specific dyslexia and reading-skills PGSs. The years-of-education PGS explained up to 10.7% in children’s academic achievement and 13.2% in adults’ attainment, suggesting that broader, large-scale PGS of general education capture much of the genetic signal shared across learning domains.
Conclusion: Findings indicate both shared and specific genetic influences on learning. Broad, high-power PGSs maximise prediction, whereas literacy-focused PGSs highlight domain-specific signal. While current PGSs are not suitable for individual prediction, they are valuable for accounting for genetic propensities and improving causal inference in developmental and education research.

articles_hidden.title: Color cues, developmental coupling, and the limits of the late-sighted model: A commentary on Vogelsang et al. (2024)
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract:
Vogelsang et al. (2024) report in Science that congenitally blind individuals who gain sight late in life rely disproportionately on color cues for object recognition, unlike normally sighted controls. They propose that this pattern reflects the adaptive value of neonatal color immaturity: because typical infants experience a period of degraded chromatic input, they develop object representations grounded in luminance rather than color.
The theoretical account, however, rests on an incomplete engagement with the developmental literature. Decades of research indicate that color and luminance sensitivity are developmentally coupled through shared photoreceptor immaturity: the same front-end bottleneck that degrades chromatic input in neonates simultaneously degrades luminance and spatial processing. If this coupling is real, there is no luminance-first window, because the bottleneck lifts for both dimensions together. The account's central premise is therefore undermined not by arguing independence, but by showing that color and luminance do not develop in the sequence the account requires.
I further identify methodological concerns: a small and unusual sample, a fixed order confound in the primary behavioral task, a computational model implementing a binary switch rather than the gradual chromatic cascade of normal development, and a color sensitivity test using non-equiluminant stimuli, leaving open the possibility that luminance rather than chromatic contrast sensitivity drove performance.
Together, these issues require qualification of the conclusions of Vogelsang et al. and reconciliation of the proposed account with classical findings in infant visual development. This broader question remains important, but the answer is unlikely to hinge on color alone.

articles_hidden.title: Registered Reports as the default pathway for confirmatory publication
articles_hidden.authors: Marta Topor; Joshua Silberstein Bamford; Marina Bazhydai; Zhang Chen; Hu Chuan-Peng; Clare Conry-Murray; Thiago Leiros Costa; Antica Culina; Mario Dalmaso; Zoltan Dienes
articles_hidden.abstract: By rewarding speed, volume, and coherent positive narratives, traditional publishing incentivizes questionable scientific practices and analytic flexibility. The latter especially contributes to blurring the distinction between exploration and confirmation, which inflates the apparent strength of confirmatory claims. This systemic issue has gone unchecked for decades, leaving the scientific community with a body of scholarly literature that is unreliable and lacking validity. Registered Reports (RRs) address problematic publishing practices by requiring a priori registration of confirmatory tests, which is peer-reviewed before the research begins (stage 1). The editorial acceptance of a stage 1 plan establishes a commitment to publication regardless of research outcomes. Publication remains, nonetheless, contingent on a second peer review and editorial scrutiny (stage 2) to verify that the approved plan was followed, all deviations were transparently disclosed and justified, confirmatory and exploratory claims are clearly delineated, and the integrity of the design was maintained. Meta-scientific comparisons indicate that RRs reduce outcome-based publication bias and improve methodological rigor without compromising perceived novelty. By making accepted RR protocols and their review history citable research outputs, RRs also strengthen recognition for peer-review work. In this perspective, we argue that RRs should become the primary mode of confirmatory publication moving forward.

articles_hidden.title: Artificial observers and real individual differences: A roadmap for a computational psychometrics of vision
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly used as models of vision, yet they are evaluated against the average observer: average performance, average neural response, average representational geometry. This discards one of the richest constraints on theory: stable individual differences. Fitting the average is necessary but not sufficient. I argue that future models should be judged not only by their fit to mean human performance, but by whether populations of artificial observers reproduce the covariance structure and latent factors found across human observers. Two mature but disconnected literatures motivate this. Decades of factor-analytic psychophysics and electrophysiology show that interindividual variation is signal, not noise: the pattern of correlations among observers reveals the number and tuning of underlying mechanisms, and fractionates vision into many narrow factors rather than one general ability. Meanwhile, neural networks differing only in random initialization develop measurably different internal representations, so any single trained network is one sample from a distribution of possible observers. Joining these yields a computational psychometrics of vision: construct a designed population of artificial observers (varying in architecture, initialization, training diet, and front-end sampling), submit them to the same latent-variable analyses used on humans, and test whether the recovered factor structure matches. Recent work showing that seed-varied networks align with specific individuals is an existence proof. This article generalizes it into a framework, a staged roadmap, and a benchmark, together with the safeguards that keep such a benchmark from becoming an optimization target, for testing hypotheses about human visual variation with artificial observer populations.

articles_hidden.title: Latent visual mechanisms as computational phenotypes: Toward a precision science of vision
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: Vision science has traditionally sought mechanisms shared across observers, treating individual differences as noise. Yet factor-analytic and latent-variable studies show that variation among observers is highly structured, recovering reproducible dimensions in contrast sensitivity, color, stereopsis, motion, and face recognition, among others. What are these latent dimensions? I propose they be treated as candidate computational phenotypes: a term borrowed from computational psychiatry and re-operationalized for vision as a stable, measurable pattern of visual information processing recovered from the covariance structure of individual differences. A computational phenotype is not a latent factor, mechanism, endophenotype, or biomarker; it occupies Marr's algorithmic level, between behavior and biology, and earns the name only by meeting stringent criteria of reliability, replication, convergent validity, and mechanistic relevance. I review candidate phenotypes drawn from many laboratories, recast development, aging, and disease as perturbations of phenotypic structure, and turn the strongest objection (that vision has no common factor) into support, since the relevant phenotypes are narrow and mechanism-specific. The payoff spans audiences: diagnostic profiles for clinicians, a non-invasive way to count and test visual mechanisms for basic scientists, and performance-predicting traits for human-factors work. The framework moves vision science from the average observer toward a precision science of visual computation.

articles_hidden.title: A Brief Intervention Highlighting Counter-stereotypical Role Models Changes Children’s  Gender Stereotypes about Values and Careers
articles_hidden.authors: Katharina Block; Sophie Arnold; Heather MacRae; Andrei Cimpian
articles_hidden.abstract:
Care-oriented values and careers are vital, yet men remain less engaged with them. We tested a
brief, preregistered role-model intervention to reduce children’s gender stereotypes about
communion (caring for others) and agency (achievement and independence). We also examined
whether this intervention would narrow gender differences in children’s own values and career
interests. Seven- to 10-year-olds from the US and Canada (N = 244; 121 boys, 123 girls) viewed
six animated vignettes about fictional children who grew up to choose careers aligned with their
values. In the “stereotypical” condition, girls were communal and entered communal careers,
while boys were agentic and entered agentic careers. In the “counter-stereotypical” condition,
these pairings were reversed. A third, “counter-stereotypical + status” condition added wealth
cues to both careers. Compared with the stereotypical condition, both counter-stereotypical
conditions weakened children’s gender stereotypes about communal and agentic values and
careers. They also reduced gender differences in children’s own communal values and career
interests, although these effects were smaller and less consistent. Wealth cues did not strengthen
the intervention. These findings suggest that counter-stereotypical role models are a promising,
scalable method for combating stereotypes that steer boys away from communion—though
likely one component of broader efforts.

articles_hidden.title: Choosing Stimuli Wisely by Using Individual Differences: A Step-by-Step Tutorial for the One-Stimulus-Per-Factor Principle in Vision Science and Optometric Assessment
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: Given that data collection time in vision research and clinical assessment is limited, investigators and clinicians must select stimuli that maximize diagnostic information with minimum redundancy. This article proposes that analyzing individual differences—through factor analysis (FA), principal component analysis (PCA), and multidimensional scaling (MDS)—offers a principled approach. The covariance structure of individual variation reveals the minimum number of independent factors underlying a visual function, and therefore the minimum number of stimuli needed for efficient, non-redundant characterization. I term this the One-Stimulus-Per-Factor Principle: one well-chosen stimulus per factor is both necessary and sufficient. A complementary rule governs discovery: at least two to three stimuli per expected factor are needed to establish the factor structure. Converging evidence from luminance and chromatic contrast sensitivity, stereoscopic disparity, motion, hue scaling, face recognition, perceptual organization, and other domains shows that the dimensionality of individual variation is often lower than dense sampling suggests—and sometimes higher than sparse clinical testing captures. The approach also tests construct validity, revealing whether behavioral measures index the mechanisms investigators assume. These findings carry implications for clinical instruments across contrast sensitivity, color vision, stereopsis, and visual field assessment, many of which either oversample a single factor or undersample the full factor space. The same framework clarifies psychiatric applications—including contrast-sensitivity changes in depression, schizophrenia, and ADHD—by separating retinal-neural deficits from optical contributions such as higher-order aberrations and from attentional lapses, and it extends to oculomotor biomarkers. The article develops the Principle as a step-by-step tutorial, with a worked example.

articles_hidden.title: Comparative Optimism for Getting Infected With COVID-19: An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis and Critical Reflection on Research Practices
articles_hidden.authors: Lars König; Frank Renkewitz
articles_hidden.abstract: Comparative optimism (believing one’s own risk is lower than others’) has been widely studied. Nonetheless, important methodological features have largely remained unrecognized. Focusing on a single event (contracting COVID-19), we estimated the average effect, tested moderators with attention to measurement artifacts, and appraised methodological quality. We synthesized 135 effect sizes from 50 studies (38 articles; sample sizes summing to 88,935, not necessarily unique participants) using a multilevel model with random effects for study, article, and nationality. We then examined moderators at both aggregated and individual-participant levels. Although, on average, comparative optimism was observed (d = 0.334, 95% CI [0.225, 0.444]), true effects varied substantially, and the meta-analytic prediction interval ranged from −0.371 to 1.040. Strikingly, this substantial heterogeneity was observed despite our efforts to control for various potential sources of heterogeneity during data collection. Measurement format was the most consistent moderator, with indirect assessments yielding larger adjusted effects than direct assessments, whereas longer response scales were not consistently associated with smaller effects. Effects were larger in samples collected in 2021 than in 2020, but this exploratory finding was sensitive to one article. The association with national collectivism was unclear in the primary model. Individual-participant analyses showed no clear overall associations for age, gender, or education. Response distributions indicated that nearly half of participants reported lower personal risk than others, more than one third reported equal risk, and about one sixth reported higher risk. Small-study and selection-model analyses suggested possible selective reporting. In sum, although we observed an average comparative optimism effect for contracting COVID-19, the generalizability of the effect and its measured correlates is limited by substantial heterogeneity and the influence of measurement choices and study context.

articles_hidden.title: Investigating the Factors Motivating the Adoption of Optimal Attentional Strategies
articles_hidden.authors: Tianyu Zhang; Molly R McKinney; Isaac Savelson; Jessica Irons; Andrew B. Leber
articles_hidden.abstract: Our goal-directed attentional control abilities enable us to flexibly maximize how efficiently we search the visual environment.  However, a growing body of research reveals that we often fail to use these abilities.  Here, we question how motivational incentives might be used to improve attentional control strategies.  Using the Adaptive Choice Visual Search (Irons & Leber, 2018), a task designed to measure attentional strategy use, we manipulated motivation in two ways.  In Experiment 1, we limited the exposure of the visual search items, and in Experiment 2, we provided a greater monetary reward for faster search performance.  In both experiments, we reasoned that participants would choose the search strategies that enabled faster target identification times; faster search would reduce errors in Experiment 1 and increase earnings in Experiment 2.  Results showed that the time-pressure manipulation failed to induce more optimal strategy choices, while the performance-contingent reward manipulation did induce a modest improvement in strategy.  Overall, we find some evidence of a link between motivation and strategy optimization, although methods to elicit a more robust boost in optimization remain elusive.  Further work is needed in this understudied but vital domain of research.

articles_hidden.title: The Psychology of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists: Evidence for Distinct Effects on Reward, Interoception and Cognition
articles_hidden.authors: Poppy Watson; Simone Rehn; Mike Kendig; Dominic M. D. Tran; Justin Mahlberg; Kristi Griffiths
articles_hidden.abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are widely used for obesity and type 2 diabetes, supporting weight loss and glycaemic control through effects on appetite and ingestive behaviour. The psychobiological mechanisms underlying these effects remain unclear. We reviewed evidence for candidate mechanisms and analysed quantitative and qualitative self-reported changes in appetite-related experiences from 704 people using GLP-1 RAs. Participants reported multiple changes that appeared distinct for food versus alcohol, with reductions in food urges and cravings largely independent of changes in alcohol use. Enhanced awareness and utilisation of hunger and satiety signals were frequently described, suggesting potential changes in interoceptive processes. Changes in enjoyment of eating were largely independent of reductions in food cravings, urges to eat, and gastrointestinal side effects. Improved ability to eat in a goal-directed manner was also frequently reported. Results support the presence of multiple cognitive and behavioural processes contributing to reduced food intake and provide testable hypotheses to explore in experimental work designed to isolate effects of GLP-1 RAs on goal-directed control, interoceptive awareness, attention, memory, and executive function.

articles_hidden.title: Group psilocybin in an integrative retreat setting enhances social connection: an observational case report
articles_hidden.authors: Dayne Rayford; Shivani Dayal; Kosu Boudreau; Dingle Spence; Marik Hazan; AZA Stephen Allsop
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background and aims
Psilocybin can induce profound alterations in perception, emotion and self-referential processing. These changes are often accompanied by increased feelings of interpersonal connection, found via both psychometric survey data and anecdotally collected qualitative data. Despite recent increases in psychedelic research and treatment, most clinical trials have been performed in individualized patient treatment paradigms. Few studies have examined the outcomes of psilocybin in group contexts, even though ceremonial and group-based usage is historically ecological and may uniquely enhance group dynamics and social bonding.
Methods
This case study investigated psychological and social outcomes among participants (n=14) of a group psilocybin ceremony conducted in an integrative retreat setting. Participants completed a series of psychometric surveys and performed a social behavioral task designed to measure social perceptions at baseline and again at two timepoints following the psilocybin ceremonies.
Results and conclusions
Our results indicate significant increases in perceived social connectedness on the Social Perception Assessment (SPA) and the Watts Connectedness Scale (WCS) as well as significant decreases in distress on the Subjective Units of Distress Scale (SUDS). These findings highlight the importance of studying group-based psychedelic administration and suggest that collective settings may generate synergistic social benefits not captured in individual therapeutic models.

articles_hidden.title: LOVE AND CHANGE
articles_hidden.authors: Elzė Sigutė Mikalonytė; Julian Savulescu; Brian D. Earp
articles_hidden.abstract: Philosophers and laypeople often have two seemingly conflicting intuitions: that love must be caused by who the beloved is and that it should persist despite personal change. Little attention has been paid to which changes are, and which are not, compatible with the requirement that real love should persist – and associated obligations. Across three online studies with UK-based participants (total N = 2482), we used vignettes in which a person’s moral character, memory, or physical appearance changed. We found that judgments on whether love that ended after the change was real and whether people should remain bound by their marital obligations depend on the same properties as judgments about the continuity of personal identity. For both the continuity of personal identity and love, together with the obligations that love brings, moral properties were the most important, followed by memory, while physical properties were considered considerably less important. Negative changes in moral character or autobiographical memory, compared to positive changes, were seen as more disruptive both to identity and marital obligations, and more compatible with past love being real.

articles_hidden.title: Feasibility and engagement of smartphone delivered yoga imagery with or without personalized avatars in residential substance use treatment: The AT-REACH nonrandomized pilot
articles_hidden.authors: Dennis McChargue; Byrav Ramamurthy; Wenyue Wang; Ashlin Ondrusek; Srikar Chanamolu; anna henson
articles_hidden.abstract: Background. Brief guided imagery may provide a practical way to rehearse a yoga experience between live sessions. We evaluated smartphone delivery and repeated use of yoga imagery and explored whether adding a personalized animated avatar was associated with different outcomes. Methods. This nonrandomized pilot enrolled 35 adults in four cohorts at residential substance use recovery facilities in Nebraska. Participants received an introductory yoga session and brief app delivered imagery practices, with three daily prompts. Thirteen participants received imagery with an animated avatar and 22 received imagery without the avatar. Allocation was by seat choice rather than a randomized sequence; the fourth cohort received the comparison condition only. We summarized app use over the first 28 days of logs, rated emotion changes around practice, and baseline to exit questionnaire outcomes. Results. All 35 initiated the app and 27 (77%) completed the exit assessment. Participants logged 2901 sessions, a median of 86 per person (interquartile range 62 to 104). At least three sessions were logged on 59% of days and at least one on 68%. The between group engagement effect was close to zero but imprecise (Hedges g = 0.03, 95% CI -0.66 to 0.71). Mean negative emotion intensity changed by -8.9 points on a 0 to 100 scale (95% CI -15.9 to -1.9). The baseline adjusted DERS total difference was 9.2 points (95% CI -6.7 to 25.2). The exploratory DERS Awareness change effect favored animated visual support (g = 0.89, 95% CI 0.06 to 1.73), but the cohort adjusted exit difference was smaller and imprecise (-1.30 points, 95% CI -5.05 to 2.46). Other questionnaire findings were mixed. Conclusions. The pilot documents repeated use of brief guided yoga imagery in residential recovery settings. It does not establish imagery efficacy, equivalence between formats, or an added benefit of animated visual support. Randomized evaluation with consistent assessment and complete delivery logs is warranted.

articles_hidden.title: Preliminary Effects of PRECISE, a Personalized and Idiographically-Tailored Adjunctive Intervention for Treating Suicidal Ideation and Psychiatric Symptoms in Young Adults: Open Trial
articles_hidden.authors: Kevin Scott Kuehn; Raeanne C. Moore; Katherine T. Foster; Colin A. Depp
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Individuals at high risk for suicide are phenomenologically heterogeneous, yet most evidence-based interventions deliver the same content to everyone. Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) is effective but lengthy, in part because every patient receives the full skills curriculum regardless of which skills address their own drivers of risk. PeRsonalizEd Clinical Intervention for Suicidal Events (PRECISE) uses idiographic models derived from each participant’s ecological momentary assessment (EMA) data to identify and teach only the DBT skills most relevant to that individual, allowing treatment to be delivered in six weeks.

Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary impact of PRECISE on suicidal thoughts and behaviors (STBs), depressive and anxiety symptoms, and related secondary outcomes.

Methods: Thirty young adults (ages 18–26) with active STBs, recruited from a university and the surrounding community, enrolled in a six-week course of PRECISE alongside five times per day EMA in a single-arm open trial. STBs were assessed at baseline, 6 weeks, and 12 weeks using the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (CSSRS) and the Modified Scale for Suicidal Ideation (MSSI); depressive and anxiety symptoms (PROMIS), coping self-efficacy (CSES), and emotion regulation strategy use (CERQ) were also assessed. Bayesian multilevel models with participant-level random intercepts estimated change over time.

Results: Retention was 93% (28/30) at 6 weeks and 87% (26/30) at 12 weeks. Participants attended a mean of 5.4 of 6 coaching sessions and rated the intervention as highly acceptable (AIM: M = 17.2), appropriate (IAM: M = 16.9), and feasible (FIM: M = 17.2; each out of 20). From baseline to 12 weeks, suicidal ideation declined on both measures (CSSRS: −2.28 points, 95% CrI [−2.75, −1.81]; MSSI: −5.38 points, 95% CrI [−8.21, −2.53]; probability of direction [pd] ≥ 99.99%). Depressive symptoms (−6.51 T-score points, 95% CrI [−8.60, −4.38]) and anxiety symptoms (−3.60, 95% CrI [−5.70, −1.50]) also declined, and coping self-efficacy increased (+29.30 points, 95% CrI [18.21, 40.50]; all pd ≥ 99.95%). Maladaptive emotion regulation strategy use showed a smaller, less certain decline (−3.20 points, 95% CrI [−6.42, 0.03]; pd = 97.36%), and adaptive strategy use showed no credible change (0.97 points, 95% CrI [−3.75, 5.63]). No serious adverse events or suicide attempts occurred; 11 mild episodes of non-suicidal self-injury were reported by 5 participants.

Conclusions: In this open trial, a brief intervention that personalizes DBT skills using participants' own idiographic EMA data was feasible, acceptable, and associated with clinically meaningful and sustained reductions in STBs, psychiatric symptoms, and maladaptive coping skills as well as improvements in coping self-efficacy. Pending further confirmatory testing, PRECISE may be a useful suicide prevention approach.

articles_hidden.title: Rumination under the microscope: causal discovery and inference of the effect of rumination on depressive symptoms in an N-of-1 time series
articles_hidden.authors: Pedro Henrique Ribeiro Santiago; Alyssa Sawyer; Mark Kohler; Lisa Jamieson; Carly Sutherland
articles_hidden.abstract: Depression is one of the most prevalent and disabling mental health conditions worldwide, with an estimated 5.7% of adults currently experiencing depression, around 332 million people globally. Rumination, a repetitive pattern of thinking that involves comparing one’s circumstances with how one would ideally like them to be without engaging in problem-solving, is the cognitive vulnerability most strongly associated with depression. Despite the evidence, there are no studies that have employed causal discovery and inference to investigate whether rumination has a causal effect on depressive mood using N-of-1 psychological time series data. To address this gap, this study conducted a secondary analysis of publicly available data on an American Latino Female diagnosed with Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) who reported on her feelings 4 times per day over 39 days. To conduct causal discovery, the Vector Autoregressive Linear Non-Gaussian Acyclic Model (VAR-LiNGAM) algorithm was used. To conduct causal inference, the g-formula, implemented via a Monte Carlo simulation, was used to estimate the Contemporaneous Effect, the 1-lag Structural Direct Effect and the 1-lag Total Effect of rumination on depressed mood. The findings indicated that high rumination was associated with a 15.6-point increase in depressed mood contemporaneously and a 1.7-point increase in depressed mood approximately 4 hours later. This evidence further substantiates the importance of interventions designed to reduce ruminative thinking and, consequently, improve depressive symptoms.

articles_hidden.title: Poor reliability in measuring habituation: Implications for clinical and translational research on exposure and extinction
articles_hidden.authors: Emma Dear; Gabrielle Rose Messner; Julia Levitan; Richie Ward Gray; Cheri A Levinson; Eric Lenze; Jaclyn Weisman; Thomas Rodebaugh
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: The purpose of this study was to investigate the reliability of change indices in exposure therapy. 
Method: We analyzed data from 119 adults with elevated social anxiety who participated in studies of public speaking exposures. Participants reported their distress using the Subjective Units of Distress Scale (SUDS) at regular intervals. The reliability of within-session habituation, between-session habituation, and expectancy change measures were estimated. 
Results: Commonly used measures of between-session habituation (BSH) typically demonstrated only moderate reliability, and commonly used measures of within-session habituation (WSH) typically demonstrated poor reliability. Exploratory tests in expectancy change indices suggests these findings apply to other measures of change during exposure.  
Conclusions: Our results indicate that measures underlying the study of habituation may be inadequate because of low reliability. This threatens the foundation of clinical and translational research, such that no substantive conclusions can be drawn from them.

articles_hidden.title: Reward Contingency Shapes Incidental Reward Effects on Cognitive Flexibility
articles_hidden.authors: Joseph M Orr; Beatrice Lomeo; Juan Balcazar; Daniela Porro
articles_hidden.abstract: Voluntary task switching (VTS) provides a useful paradigm for examining how recent reward outcomes are associated with the balance between cognitive stability and flexibility. We investigated whether reward-history effects on task choice varied as a function of cue–outcome contingency. Participants (N = 616) completed a VTS task with performance-contingent rewards. Reward contingency was manipulated between-subjects at probabilities of100\%, 80\%, 70\%, and 60\%. Switch probability was modeled using logistic mixed-effects regression. The relationship between prior reward outcomes and the current reward prospect in predicting switch behavior differed across probability conditions. Reward transition effects were larger at 100\% and 80\% than at 70\% and 60\%. Secondary analyses further indicated that outcomes that were unexpected given the cue–reward mapping were associated with subsequent switching in some comparisons, although evidence that these associations systematically varied with probability was mixed. Because task choices did not influence reward outcomes, the observed effects are more consistent with carry-over associations between reward history and task selection than with reward-guided exploration or reward maximization. Exploratory individual-differences analyses suggested that reward transition effects were more pronounced in males than in females; additionally, trait-level reward sensitivity moderated the magnitude of reward transition effects on switch behavior. Overall, the findings are consistent with the hypothesis that cue-outcome contingency modulates the extent to which recent rewards are followed by particular task-choice patterns, although further research is required to clarify the mechanisms through which reward uncertainty may contribute to these effects.

articles_hidden.title: Feeling the heat: How climate emotions shape trust in government and policy support across 68 countries
articles_hidden.authors: Jlenia Avellino; Fabienne Stucki; Omid Ghasemi; Viktoria Cologna; Theofilos Gkinopoulos; Niels G. Mede; Stylianos Syropoulos; Sebastian Berger
articles_hidden.abstract: Negative emotions related to climate change can adversely impact people’s mental health and wellbeing. However, they could also accelerate action on climate change by driving support for environmental policies. Using the TISP Many Labs data, we present results from a cross-sectional secondary analysis of survey responses from 69,534 participants across 68 countries worldwide. The survey included items on people’s emotional response to climate change, perceptions of government responses to climate change, and support for environmental policies. Participants experienced relatively low levels of negative emotions toward climate change (M = 2.79, SD = 1.01; 1 = not at all, 5 = very strongly), with relatively little variation across countries (SD = 0.27). Individuals reporting stronger negative emotions were less satisfied with their government’s climate action and expressed greater support for environmental policies. Our results thereby contribute to a global assessment of climate emotions and its correlates, crucially augmenting past research that has been more limited in global scope.

articles_hidden.title: Multilevel meta-analyses of emotional processing deficits associated with callous-unemotional (CU) traits: Do they differ by age and sex?
articles_hidden.authors: Emily C. Kemp; Paul Frick; Taylor Miller; Julianne Speck; David Gertz; Zeying Du
articles_hidden.abstract: Callous-unemotional (CU) traits, defined by deficient empathy and remorse, characterize a distinct subgroup of antisocial individuals with more severe behavioral problems and unique affective profiles. Two processes implicated in the development of CU traits are hyporeactivity to and inaccurate recognition of others’ emotions. Although many studies link CU traits to emotional processing deficits, findings have been inconsistent across age and sex. We conducted multilevel meta-analyses of emotional reactivity and recognition, accounting for age and sex as moderators, to clarify these discrepancies. A four-level meta-analysis indicated CU traits were negatively associated with emotional reactivity to both broad emotional stimuli (r = -.23, p < .0001; k = 106, n = 402) and distress-specific stimuli (r = -.22, p < .0001; k = 83, n = 234), with no moderation by age or sex. Similarly, a three-level meta-analysis showed CU traits were negatively associated with recognition accuracy for both broad facial emotions (r = -.09, p < .0001; k = 97, n = 437) and distress (e.g., fear, sadness; r = -.10, p < .0001; k = 60, n = 140). Sample age moderated broad (r = .003, p = .01) and distress (r = .004, p = .04) recognition deficits, such that effects diminished with sample age. These results have important implications for causal theories of CU traits and support emotional hyporreactivity as a core deficit that may cause delays in the development of emotion recognition abilities. Such developmental changes have implications for improving treatments for individuals with elevated CU traits.

articles_hidden.title: A clinician-informed framework for precision psychotherapy in psychosis
articles_hidden.authors: Shenaya Maria Lisboa; Maria Chiara Del Piccolo; Anna Georgiades; Sandra Vieira
articles_hidden.abstract: Background. Despite evidence supporting cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis (CBTp), engagement and treatment response remain highly variable, and robust predictors are lacking. Existing research may overlook clinically relevant factors. We aimed to identify candidate predictors of CBTp engagement and outcomes by integrating clinicians’ perspectives with the existing literature. Methods. Twenty clinical psychologists experienced in delivering CBTp participated in semi-structured interviews. Using a mixed-methods design, we first identified candidate predictors through inductive framework analysis of unprompted accounts. Clinicians subsequently rated the perceived importance of these and 32 literature-derived factors on a 10-point scale. Mean ratings and variability were examined to characterise clinician agreement. Findings were integrated into a candidate predictor framework linked to available measurement instruments. Results. Clinicians spontaneously identified 38 factors, of which 16 were absent from the literature-derived list. Frequently identified factors included readiness and motivation (90%), cognitive flexibility (85%), social support (80%), previous experiences of care and therapy (70%), and socioeconomic and environmental stability (70%). Clinicians emphasised therapy-related, contextual, and clinical management factors, including expectations of therapy, substance misuse, and medication, which remain underrepresented in prediction research. Literature-derived factors receiving relatively high importance ratings and agreement included insight, cognitive flexibility, hopelessness, and social functioning. Demographic characteristics were generally considered less important. Conclusion. Clinicians identified factors extending beyond those conventionally investigated as predictors of CBTp engagement and outcomes. The resulting clinician-informed measurement framework provides a broader, clinically grounded candidate predictor set to guide prospective studies and the development of personalised prediction models in psychosis. Keywords: Precision psychotherapy, psychological intervention, CBT, psychosis, schizophrenia

articles_hidden.title: Comparing Time- and Event-Contingent Ecological Momentary Assessments of Daily Stressors
articles_hidden.authors: Lara Oeltjen; Johannes Andreas Christoph Laferton
articles_hidden.abstract: Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) studies offer a unique access to within-person variability processes. Despite their widespread use in psychological research, we know very little about the factors that determine their successful application. This study combines time- and event-contingent assessments to examine the reliability of event-contingent reporting, person-level predictors of compliance, and qualitative differences between assessment methods in a 14-day EMA study of daily stressors. Our results indicate that stress beliefs, personality and mental health are associated with compliance and event-contingent reporting. There was no evidence that event-contingent reports might have been omitted in high-stress situations. On the contrary, event-contingent assessments were generally more extreme in terms of stress-intensity, affect and somatic symptoms. Event-contingent assessments may thus capture a more extreme subset of events and certain types of participants may be particularly likely to self-initiate these assessments. We discuss implications of these findings for the design of future EMA studies.
