Extending the autonomy argument already accepted for terminally ill patients, competent adults who understand the potential benefits and risks of a psilocybin experience should be able to choose it for reasons of psychological wellness or existential anxiety relief, not only because a clinician has certified a qualifying illness, a right the legal literature calls “cognitive liberty”. Just as important, the cost of access is not fixed; it reflects the regulatory framework under which psilocybin is provided. No jurisdiction has yet completed medicines authorisation pathway; the furthest-advanced clinical programme, Compass Pathways' COMP360, met its Phase 3 primary endpoint and reported six-month durability data for TRD by July 2026, and its developer has since signalled an annual cost close to that of esketamine nasal spray, USD 50,000–65,000, or roughly USD 17,000–22,000 per dose. Meanwhile, Australia's narrower authorised-prescriber legal route for TRD, using GMP-manufactured but unregistered psilocybin, already costs AUD $20,000 per course. Three distinct non-medical routes cost far less. Truffles in the Netherlands, sold under food law with no diagnosis and no supervision required, and Colorado and Oregon's state-licensed psilocybin services, which require no diagnosis but do involve a supervising facilitator, cost up to $3,000 per session. Removing the diagnosis requirement while leaving this cost structure untouched risks replacing the regulatory barrier with the wealth-based one, unless expanded access is paired with public subsidy. Article also briefly reviews the safety evidence, the political origins of psilocybin's scheduling, and the double standard in how its risks are treated. A Canadian case illustrates the institutional and regulatory framework dysfunction, a dying man denied psilocybin for existential relief while approved for medical assistance in dying within weeks, before the article closes with policy recommendations addressing both access and funding.

articles_hidden.title: Teacher Help and the Development of Socioeconomic Ability Stereotypes: Longitudinal Evidence From Real Classrooms
articles_hidden.authors: Jonne Bloem; Iris Boer; Jellie Sierksma
articles_hidden.abstract: Teacher help is crucial for learning and boosts children’s development. Receiving help may also have unintended negative consequences as it may signal that recipients are not competent enough to solve tasks independently. Teachers often provide more help to children from lower-socioeconomic status (SES) backgrounds, and lab-based studies show that when help is distributed unequally it can reinforce negative ability stereotypes. In this preregistered study, we examined whether children (7-13 years) perceive differences in who receives help in their own classrooms and whether perceived SES-based differences in help lead to stronger SES stereotypes over time. At three time points across one school year Dutch children (N= 565, 65 classrooms, 49.5% boys, 49.5% girls, 1.1% other/prefer not to say; 65.2% native Dutch; mixed SES backgrounds) identified which classmates most often received help from their teacher and how much they endorsed ability stereotypes about SES groups. Across all time points, children perceived that teachers helped lower-SES classmates more than higher-SES classmates. This pattern emerged for two types of help, and was more pronounced among children from lower-SES backgrounds and older children. Moreover, perceived SES-based differences in teacher help at the start of the school year predicted stronger SES-based ability stereotypes halfway through the year, although this association was limited to one type of help. These findings suggest that everyday classroom practices intended to support children who need additional help may inadvertently shape which children and societal groups are seen as less capable. This has important implications for how SES-based stereotypes take root.

articles_hidden.title: Mapping the Dynamics of Depressive and Anxiety symptoms in Coronary Artery Disease  over two years: A Network Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Stefana Vida; Heidi Hermans; Joris Mulder; Mihai Alexandru Constantin; Nina Kupper
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Coronary artery disease (CAD), a leading cause of morbidity and mortality 
worldwide, negatively impacts psychological well-being. Depressive and anxiety symptoms are 
commonly reported by patients with CAD, but little is known about symptom 
interconnectedness in this population. Insight into this interconnectedness may improve our 
understanding of how comorbidity arises and persists. Therefore, our aim was to gain new 
insights into the comorbidity of anxiety and depression symptoms in patients with CAD by 
estimating psychological networks at multiple time points. 
Methods: 2241 patients who had undergone percutaneous coronary intervention (22.2% 
women; mean age = 65.0, SD= 10.3) were included. With five cross-sectional psychological 
networks measured at five timepoints over two years, the symptom-level dynamics of 
depressive and anxiety symptoms were studied. Besides the overall network structure, network 
communities, centrality measures and sub-group differences were explored.  
Results: The estimated Bayesian Gaussian graphical models showed predominantly positive 
associations, and symptoms were mostly connected within their own domain of depression or 
anxiety. Two symptom clusters remained relatively stable: Depressed mood, feelings of 
worthlessness, and suicidal ideation consistently clustered together, while in the first month 
post PCI, fatigue, sleep disturbance, and appetite disturbance tended to co-occur. Fatigue, 
depressed mood, difficulty relaxing, and restlessness showed high connectivity and acted as 
bridging symptoms between different symptom groups.  
Conclusion: These findings suggest that both symptoms related to depression and to anxiety 
should be targeted within cardiac rehabilitation programs to reduce patients' psychological 
burden.

articles_hidden.title: LGBTQIA+ Family-Making Through Assisted Reproduction (ART): A Narrative Review
articles_hidden.authors: António de Pádua Jesué Oliveira; Henrique Pereira
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: LGBTQIA+ people and couples increasingly pursue parenthood through assisted reproductive technologies (ART), yet the psychological, relational, and institutional processes
involved remain dispersed across reproductive health, family studies, psychology, sociology, and LGBTQIA+ scholarship.
Objective: This structured narrative review synthesizes recent literature on how LGBTQIA+ individuals and couples construct parental projects through ART, with attention to reproductive
aspirations, route selection, relational negotiation, minority stress, institutional encounters, and family narrative construction.
Methods: PubMed and Scopus were searched for publications from 2016 to 2026. After deduplication, 260 unique records were screened, 126 underwent refined relevance appraisal,
and 49 articles were retained as the mapped corpus. From these, 17 index studies were purposively selected for in-depth discussion as they offered particularly rich evidence on
psychosocial, relational, and institutional processes. The review followed a structured narrative synthesis approach guided by the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles
(SANRA).
Results: Three family-making domains structured the synthesis: lesbian couples’ donor conception, IVF, and reciprocal IVF pathways; gay fatherhood through surrogacy and thirdparty reproduction; and transgender, gender-diverse reproductive planning, including fertility preservation and institutional barriers. Across domains, LGBTQIA+ ART family-making
involved six recurring psychosocial tasks: aspiration, feasibility appraisal, route selection, relational negotiation, institutional navigation, and narrative integration.
Conclusion: ART is not only a set of reproductive techniques but a psychosocial and institutional context in which LGBTQIA+ parental aspirations are translated into reproductive
pathways, negotiated through relationships, shaped by clinical and legal conditions, and incorporated into family narratives. These findings support cautious, pathway-sensitive, LGBTQIA+-affirmative fertility counselling.

articles_hidden.title: The Same Memory Retrieved Differently: Competition Enables Flexible Generalization in Hippocampus-like Networks
articles_hidden.authors: Robby Ralston; Brandon Turner; Vladimir Sloutsky
articles_hidden.abstract: Hippocampus supports the retrieval of richly detailed episodic memories from sparse cues. However, an event can be detailed and also lead to generalization. To explain both phenomena, researchers have proposed multiple memory systems or distinct memory traces for specific and general content. In contrast, we argue that a single system can support both specificity and generalization. To do this, we present ATHENA, a formal framework that reinterprets cognitive memory models as recurrent neural networks. We show that many episodic memory models are single-step approximations of dynamic networks with competitive retrieval mechanisms, similar to Modern Hopfield Networks. Notably, under a cognitive interpretation, the intensity of the competitive process is a psychologically-meaningful parameter that shapes generalization in the network. Through simulations, we demonstrate that modulating this parameter during retrieval leads the same traces to produce qualitatively different forms of generalization over the same memory traces. We then extend our analysis to sequential memory, and show how the same competitive retrieval process can be combined with known hippocampal circuits to achieve more sophisticated forms of generalization. These results demonstrate the flexibility of single-system memory retrieval and highlight the interplay of specific and general mnemonic content.

articles_hidden.title: The Entangled Loop: Emotion, quantum-like interference and hierarchy in the architecture of consciousness
articles_hidden.authors: Morten L. Kringelbach; Fernando Rosas; Ruben Eero Laukkonen; Shamil Chandaria; Yonatan Sanz Perl; Gustavo Deco
articles_hidden.abstract: Why does consciousness feel like something, and why is experience unified rather than fragmented? We propose that these properties arise from an entangled trefoil of emotion, interference-based inference and hierarchical orchestration, shaped by the thermodynamic constraint that living systems must remain far from equilibrium using limited energy. Emotion compresses actions into valenced signals of what matters, while a pleasure cycle schedules competing biological needs through predictive wanting and satiety organised around the true hedonic outcome of liking. Hierarchical orchestrating regions integrate and broadcast information through interference between classical coupled oscillators, shaped by the spectral gaps of the connectome driven by long-range exceptions to local cortical wiring. The architecture of the Entangled Loop consists of three inseparable strands, each continually constraining the other two, with the one operator linking computational possibilities to the arrow of time and energetic cost of running them. Evidence suggests that the same three signatures emerge independently in large language models trained on human language, but as shadows of the generating architecture rather than evidence of consciousness. The trefoil predicts a distinctive human vulnerability because our abundance of rare long-range connections promotes more computation for less energy while making the architecture more fragile. Neuropsychiatric disorders could therefore arise from perturbations entering through any strand and propagating through the others, while the more robust architecture of other species may help explain why animal models reproduce human psychiatric disorders poorly. Sustaining and restoring flexible entanglement in the Entangled Loop may provide mechanistic routes towards flourishing.

articles_hidden.title: Questionable necessity effects on patient safety competency among nursing students: Re-examining Yang et al. (2027)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles_hidden.abstract: Using Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA), Yang et al. concluded that adequate levels of organizational support, patient safety culture, adverse event risk perception, professional identity, and self-efficacy constitute necessary prerequisites for achieving high patient safety competency among master's-level nursing students. However, NCA-derived necessity effects may arise solely from associations between variables rather than reflecting genuine necessity relationships. In the present reanalysis, we evaluated whether the necessity effects reported by Yang et al. exceeded expected levels attributable to correlation alone. All reported effects were found to fall within or below estimated ranges of spuriousness, indicating that they were not stronger than would be anticipated in the absence of true necessity. Accordingly, the evidence presented by Yang et al. does not provide robust support for the claimed necessity relationships. We recommend that researchers employing NCA routinely assess ranges of spuriousness and only interpret necessity effects as substantive when they exceed these benchmarks.

articles_hidden.title: What Do People Dream About? Themes and Emotions in 400,000+ Dream Reports Shared on Weibo (2018–2023)
articles_hidden.authors: Yanqi Lyu; Wuwei Tang; Huanyu Liu
articles_hidden.abstract: Dream research has traditionally relied on small samples and retrospective self-reports, which are vulnerable to memory decay. The present study combines big data with natural language processing to investigate dreams that users spontaneously shared on Weibo, a major Chinese social media platform. Using the keywords “dream of,” “dream about,” and “in a dream,” we collected posts from April of each year between 2018 and 2023 and, after five rounds of screening, obtained 418,961 dream reports. We analyzed the demographic characteristics of the posters, the thematic content of the dreams (via word-frequency analysis and a co-occurrence semantic network), and the emotional tone of the reports (via lexicon-based sentiment scoring). Women shared dreams more often than men; users aged 20–35 predominated; posting peaked in the early morning. Six broad themes emerged—family, school, romantic relationships, work, danger, and body—covering a broader range but occurring at lower frequencies than typical-dream themes assessed by questionnaire. Themes related to danger and death moved in the opposite direction to the national urban unemployment rate after 2019, suggesting that dreams may buffer waking emotional states. Negative emotion scores consistently exceeded positive scores, indicating that negative content dominates dream sharing. We discuss the implications of these findings for understanding the emotion-regulation function of dreams and outline directions for future research.

articles_hidden.title: Does machine learning generalize across political change? Predicting approval of political violence four years later
articles_hidden.authors: Oskari Lahtinen
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examined whether approval of political violence could be predicted from individual characteristics and whether models developed in one political context would still work four years later. Logistic regression and XGBoost models using 18 demographic, political, and psychological predictors were developed in a Finnish adult sample collected in 2022 and applied without refitting to an independent 2026 sample. Cross-validated ROC-AUC was .676–.677 in 2022. Despite a decline in violence approval from 12.6% to 7.9%, discrimination remained similar or better in 2026 (ROC-AUC = .751 for logistic regression and .707 for XGBoost). The political distribution of violence approval, however, changed markedly. Midpoint-or-higher responses remained nearly unchanged in the left-party bloc (17.4% to 16.8%) but fell from 18.0% to 3.8% in the right-party bloc. Thus, models trained in 2022 continued to predict violence approval in 2026 even though its relationship with political orientation had changed substantially.

articles_hidden.title: Individual differences in the computational processes that support face recognition
articles_hidden.authors: Fournier Raphaël; Paul Downing; Richard Ramsey
articles_hidden.abstract: Face recognition ability varies substantially across the population, yet the cognitive and computational processes that give rise to this variation remain poorly understood. Here, we combined approaches from experimental, differential and mathematical psychology to test how individual differences in face recognition ability relate to latent parameters of the decision-making processes involved in face recognition. Participants (N = 300) completed a face memory task with learned and novel faces, together with independent measures of face recognition ability (Cambridge Face Memory Test) and general object recognition ability (car recognition). We modelled task performance with an evidence-accumulation model that translates accuracy and response times into latent parameters, including drift rate (the signal-to-noise ratio of the evidence) and threshold (response caution). Higher face recognition ability was associated with greater drift rate discrimination between correct and incorrect response accumulators in the face memory task, for both learned and novel faces and to a similar degree, consistent with expertise effects in other domains. This association remained largely unchanged when accounting for car recognition ability, suggesting that it is at least partly tied to face processing itself. Higher face recognition ability was also associated with greater response caution, which may reflect better calibration to task demands. Although the associations were modest in size, these findings suggest that individual differences in face recognition ability are reflected in distinct computational mechanisms, namely more efficient extraction of information from faces and a more cautious decision policy. This approach enables a more explicit and computational basis for cognitive theories of face recognition to be developed, as well as for testing whether these mechanisms operate similarly across the full spectrum of face recognition abilities.

articles_hidden.title: Adolescents’ Economic Circumstances and their Mental Health: Identifying Candidate Causal Mechanisms through Review and Expert Consultation
articles_hidden.authors: Thomas Steare; Kelly Rose-Clarke; Sara Evans-Lacko; Gemma Lewis; Praveetha Patalay
articles_hidden.abstract: Living in poorer economic circumstances is routinely associated with poorer mental health throughout the life course. In adolescents, explanatory theories have almost exclusively focused on the role that economic circumstances have on parenting behaviors, and the resources families can provide for their children, which in turn influence adolescents’ mental health outcomes. Through a systematic search of mediation studies and expert consultation we propose candidate causal mechanisms through which economic circumstances might impact adolescents’ internalizing mental health outcomes such as anxiety and depression. Most of the candidate causal mechanisms we identified have not been considered in adolescent-specific theories of health inequalities to date and many have not been empirically investigated within mediation studies, indicating clear limits in current awareness of the processes through which economic circumstances affect adolescents’ mental health. We propose a conceptual model that highlights how economic circumstances may shape environmental and material factors, which we theorize in turn influences an interconnected set of behavioral, biological, psychological and social mechanisms linked to mental health outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation for Schizophrenia: From Circuit Dysfunction to Insight and Functional Recovery
articles_hidden.authors: Medhat Elsabbahy; Yasaman Mohammadi; Arash Khojasteh Zonoozi; danish Anwar; Muhammad Nasar Sayeed Khan; Kamonnet Wannasewok; Johannes Wancata
articles_hidden.abstract:
Schizophrenia remains a major challenge in psychiatric practice, characterized by a heterogenous constellation of symptoms, including positive symptoms (e.g., hallucinations and delusions), negative symptoms (e.g., social withdrawal and diminished motivation), cognitive impairments, and frequently, lack of insight. Standard psychoeducation has served as a vital partner to psychological medicine for decades, trying to reduce the relapse rates by emphasizing medication adherence. However, many conventional models often rely on descriptive clinical phenomenology that fails to resonate with the patient’s subjective experience and rarely explain the neurological causes behind the hallucinations or illogical thinking. This disconnection can inadvertently reinforce stigma and fail to support the patient's remaining cognitive capacities to reinforce recovery. Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation (NIPE) emerges as a transformative paradigm, integrating cutting-edge insights from brain science into the educational dialogue. By establishing the explanation of symptoms in neurobiology and shifting the narrative from "mental illness" to "circuit dysfunction", NIPE aims to bypass psychological defenses, objectify the disorder, and foster a collaborative therapeutic alliance. This chapter presents the neurocognitive aspects of the psychoeducational content, the neurocognitive considerations that must be addressed when providing psychoeducation, and examples of NIPE for Schizophrenia, aiming to advance brain health literacy for practitioners who will support patients as active partners in recovery alongside daily functional restoration.
Keywords: Schizophrenia; Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation; Psychoeducation; Neurocognition; Brain Health Literacy; Therapeutic Alliance; Patient Education

articles_hidden.title: Examining the Relations Between Self-Construal, Culture, and Cognitive Dissonance Using the Induced Compliance Paradigm
articles_hidden.authors: Tim Figureau; Daniel Priolo; Willem W. A. Sleegers; Kenneth G DeMarree; Omid Ghasemi; Amélie Gourdon-Kanhukamwe; Maxime Mauduy; Asil Ali Özdoğru; Robert M Ross; Bjørn Sætrevik
articles_hidden.abstract: Cognitive dissonance, traditionally conceptualized as a fundamental psychological process involving discomfort from inconsistent cognitions, may vary across cultures. These variations could be attributed to self-construal, or how individuals define themselves in relation to others. Although previous cross-cultural research has predominantly used the free-choice paradigm, significant concerns have been raised regarding its procedural validity and the robustness of its findings. To address this issue, this registered report presents secondary analyses of a large-scale international dataset. We investigated the moderating role of cultural variables on dissonance effects within the induced-compliance paradigm across 18 countries (N = 3,804). We hypothesized that dissonance effects would be stronger for participants with higher individual-level self-construal scores (H1), in more individualistic countries (H2), and in countries with higher country-level self-construal scores (H3). Our results did not support these hypotheses, suggesting that cultural moderation may not generalize to the induced-compliance paradigm. We discuss the necessity of reassessing the procedure’s reliability and clarifying the theoretical role of choice.

articles_hidden.title: Early intervention for young children with motor learning impairments: the approach and processes of Dame Vera Lynn Children’s Charity
articles_hidden.authors: George Horne; Antonina Pereira; Glenys Creese; Benjamin T Sharpe
articles_hidden.abstract: Early intervention is widely viewed as important to improve functional outcomes in children with motor learning impairments. According to existing recommendations, early intervention should be holistic and target different areas of development such as sensorimotor, attention, and communication skills. Currently though, no guidelines or examples describe how to do this. This study presents Dame Vera Lynn Children’s Charity’s early intervention services as an example. Produced as part of a critical realist ethnography, this article outlines how the charity integrates allied health and educational approaches to support children and their families. Our reflexive thematic analysis then identifies processes of family-led, collaborative, and flexible support that underly DVLCC service provision, and principles of care and pragmatism that underly these processes. This ethnography adds context to the charity’s preliminary positive research results and provides an example model of UK-based early intervention for future development and critical engagement.

articles_hidden.title: Associations Between Global Emotion Beliefs and Three Stages of Emotion Regulation in Everyday Life
articles_hidden.authors: Valentina Bianchi; Imogen Smith; Felicia Semple; Amy S G Lee; Eeske van Roekel; Peter Koval
articles_hidden.abstract: Everyone experiences emotions, but people vary in their orientations to and beliefs about emotions. Research has linked global beliefs about the controllability and usefulness of emotions with psychological functioning and well-being, but the mechanisms through which those beliefs shape people’s well-being remain unclear. Ford and Gross (2019) proposed emotion regulation as a candidate mechanism, such that emotion beliefs influence whether people initiate emotion regulation (identification), which strategies people use to regulate their emotions (selection), and how successfully people are able to implement their selected emotion-regulation strategies (implementation). We tested predictions based on Ford and Gross’s (2019) framework in everyday life in a seven-day experience sampling study (Australian community sample recruited in 2024; N = 326; 80% female; MAge=26.11, SDAge=8.52). At the identification stage, neither controllability nor usefulness beliefs were associated with initiating emotion regulation. In terms of strategy selection, stronger beliefs about the usefulness of negative emotions were associated with greater use of situation selection and lesser use of expressive suppression, as predicted. Finally, at the implementation stage, controllability beliefs did not moderate the hedonic effects of any regulation strategy, whereas usefulness beliefs about negative emotions predicted a weaker positive association between cognitive reappraisal and negative affect, and believing positive emotions to be more useful predicted a stronger inverse association between rumination and positive affect. Our findings suggest that individual differences in global emotion beliefs may play a smaller role than theorised in daily emotion regulation processes.

articles_hidden.title: Aging and Hearing Loss in Emotional Prosody Processing: Divergent Neural Adaptation and Behavioral Performance
articles_hidden.authors: Yi Lin; Yangfan Lu; Hongwei Ding; Yang Zhang
articles_hidden.abstract: Emotional prosody perception is vulnerable in later adulthood, yet the contributions of central aging and peripheral hearing loss remain unclear. Across two experiments, we combined event-related potentials (ERPs) , time-frequency analyses and behavioral measures to examine how aging and hearing sensitvity shape emotional prosody processing. Experiment 1 used acoustically matched speech and nonspeech stimuli in a passive oddball paradigm to assess preattentive processing. Experiment 2 examined explicit emotion identification and implicit stimulus judgment to evaluate goal-directed performance and its associations with neural responses. Aging was associated with reduced neural differentiation between emotions and lower behavioral efficiency, alongside enhanced P3a amplitude. Older adults also responded more slowly than younger adults during emotion identification. Hearing sensitivity showed no significant main effect on accuracy or reaction time, despite associations with delayed early neural processing and stronger theta- and alpha-band activity. Hearing-related neural effects were most evident in older adults and varied across emotions and stimulus types. Brain–behavior associations were selective: reduced mismatch negativity (MMN) was associated with slower responses during stimulus identification, whereas longer MMN latencies were associated with lower accuracy and slower responses during emotion identification. These findings indicate that aging and hearing loss have distinct yet interacting associations with emotional prosody processing, with neural responses not necessarily corresponding to behavioral performance. We propose an “asymmetric adaptation” account in which neural responses to degraded auditory input reorganize selectively across processing stages and contexts, potentially explaining this neural-behavioral divergence and informing more sensitive assessment of socioemotional communication in later adulthood.

articles_hidden.title: Now I See Me, Now I Don’t: A Replication and Psychometric Exploration of the Invisible Face Illusion
articles_hidden.authors: Lucy Stafford; Catherine Preston; Paul Mark Jenkinson
articles_hidden.abstract: Current theories of multisensory integration explain how conscious feelings of body ownership arise, at least in part, from the integration of simultaneously felt and observed touch. The same principles apply to illusory ownership of another face and even to the experience of having an invisible body or body parts. D’Angelo et al., (2021) demonstrated how a sense of invisibility can extend to the face. However, no attempts have been made to independently replicate the so-called Invisible Face Illusion (IFI), and the underlying phenomenological components of the illusion experience remain unknown. The aim of this preregistered study was to replicate the IFI and explore its underlying psychometric components. Participants (n=152) viewed a video of an invisible face being stroked in- or  out-of-synchrony with touches applied to their own face, and completed an IFI questionnaire after each condition. Separate exploratory factor analyses on the synchronous and asynchronous conditions found the same 14-item, two-factor model to be the best fit to the data, with the factors capturing 1) facial disembodiment and 2) feelings of touch referral. As expected, overall factor scores were significantly higher in the synchronous versus asynchronous condition, and significant increases were evident for eleven of the fourteen individual questionnaire items. This is the first study to replicate the IFI, suggesting that the illusion involves experiencing referral of touch on one's own face as arising from the invisible face, and a sense of disconnection or disembodiment from one's own face. We suggest possible therapeutic benefits of the IFI which require further exploration.

articles_hidden.title: Effects of a Web-Based Debiasing Intervention on Brazilian Psychologists’ Accuracy on Major Depressive Disorder Diagnostic Tasks: A Randomized Training Intervention
articles_hidden.authors: Kalil Maihub Manara; Eric A. Youngstrom; Joshua A Langfus; Clarissa Marceli Trentini
articles_hidden.abstract: This randomized experimental study evaluated a web-based debiasing intervention designed to improve clinical judgment in the assessment of adult major depressive disorder (MDD) in Brazil. The intervention, adapted from prior work on pediatric bipolar disorder, taught Bayesian probability estimates and other debiasing strategies. Brazilian psychologists (N = 535) were assigned to either the intervention or an active control condition featuring a brief educational video, and were assessed post-intervention (n = 299). Outcomes were decision-making errors and diagnostic accuracy in response to vignettes, which depicted diagnostic challenges that could elicit cognitive biases. Assignment to intervention was associated with significantly fewer decision-making errors and greater diagnostic accuracy. Intervention effects were stronger for the vignette involving diagnostic risk estimation, as supported by intervention-by-vignette interaction effects. Intervention effects across vignettes were not statistically significant when only categorical diagnostic tasks were considered. Years of clinical practice and postgraduate training were largely unrelated to outcomes, and decision-making errors were not associated with treatment decisions. Overall, findings provide preliminary evidence of the transferability of this brief, web-based debiasing intervention to a distinct clinical and cultural context, although effect sizes were substantially attenuated compared with those observed in the original intervention.

articles_hidden.title: Identifying the Critical Period of Academic Burnout: A Computational Simulation Approach Based on Large-Scale Assessment Data
articles_hidden.authors: Xin Tang; Xiaofeng Wen; Jianxiao Jiang; Danhua Lin; Yiqun Gan; Yu Zhang
articles_hidden.abstract: Understanding student engagement and burnout has long been a central concern in educational research. While prior studies have extensively examined levels and correlates of them, far less is known about the timing at which students transition into amotivation (i.e., burnout) state from motivated state. In present study, based on Cox proportional hazards modeling and using large-scale data from the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), we develop a computational simulation model to infer individual- and group-level distributions of academic burnout onset across study weeks. Results demonstrate systematic variation in the timing of academic burnout onset as a function of weekly study time, with longer study hours associated with an earlier increase in burnout risk. To facilitate practical application, we further implement an interactive ShinyApp that allows users to estimate academic burnout onset periods at the individual, classroom, and school levels. This study contributes a novel methodological framework for temporally locating motivational breakdown and offers a scalable tool for translating large-scale assessment data into actionable educational insights.

articles_hidden.title: Polarity and the speed of scalar implicature processing
articles_hidden.authors: Michael Vrazitulis; J E Loy; Vera Demberg
articles_hidden.abstract: Scalar implicatures (SIs) such as the inference from 'some' to 'some but not all' are known to vary in processing cost. According to the Polarity Hypothesis (van Tiel et al., 2019; van Tiel & Pankratz, 2021), this cost depends on the polarity of the scalar term: SIs from positively polar expressions (e.g., 'some' implicating 'some but not all') are expected to be slower to compute than literal interpretations, while the reverse should hold for SIs from negatively polar expressions, sometimes referred to as indirect SIs (e.g., 'not all' implicating 'not all but some'). We tested this prediction in a sentence–picture verification experiment with 538 English-speaking participants. Each participant judged whether sentences containing weak or strong scalar terms matched a corresponding picture, allowing us to measure response times as an index of processing effort. Our results showed no clear evidence for the Polarity Hypothesis effect. Specifically, we found that the effect strongly varies across the different scales included in our experiment. We additionally conducted a meta-analysis pooling our estimate with all existing evidence so far: the pooled effect is small and in the predicted direction, but the study-specific estimates behind it vary widely in magnitude. Surprisingly, our results do also not clearly validate the traditional assumption of a B&N effect (Bott & Noveck, 2004), i.e., a general polarity-independent processing slowdown under SIs: a subsequent analysis including trial order revealed that the B&N effect was present in early trials of our study, whereas later trials do not show the effect. Overall, we conclude that polarity may influence the speed of scalar implicature processing, but that this effect is not robust across all types of scales.

articles_hidden.title: Continuative Development of Traditional Psychology: Rethinking Inheritance and Innovation through Traditional Chinese Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Xianglong ZENG
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychological research increasingly draws on resources inherited from historical traditions, with the potential both to advance contemporary psychological knowledge and to sustain and further develop those traditions. Existing methodological discussions have often emphasized fidelity to inherited meanings in reconstructing and transforming traditional resources. Yet when contemporary research substantially revises inherited responses, can such work still count as inheritance, and if so, where does the boundary between continuation and departure lie? Focusing on traditional Chinese psychology, this conceptual article identifies a shared developmental logic across theoretical, practical, and methodological cases that go beyond the reconstruction of inherited responses. On this basis, it conceptualizes continuative development as a mode of inheritance distinct from reconstructive transformation. Its central argument is that continuity lies at the level of inquiry rather than in the preservation of particular inherited responses. The inquiry itself may even develop to address new questions under changing conditions. What distinguishes continuation from mere influence or use of traditional resources is an intelligible developmental relation to an inherited inquiry. The article further argues that, compared with reconstructive transformation, continuative development opens a broader space for ongoing knowledge generation by allowing new answers, practices, methodological approaches, and questions to emerge beyond the historical repertoire. This also means that contemporary psychology need not treat inherited traditions only as repositories of existing intellectual resources, but can also feed back into and further develop those inquiries. In turn, such development may contribute to cultural continuity while enabling inherited traditions to generate new psychological knowledge that may extend beyond their original cultural contexts. In sum, the article articulates the principles and potential contributions of continuative development as a distinct, methodologically defensible research orientation and clarifies the relationship between inheritance and innovation in traditional psychology.

articles_hidden.title: The emergence of language-specific biases in visual attention in pre-reading toddlers from two cultures
articles_hidden.authors: Christine Potter; Nadeen Kherbawy; Christopher Sepulveda; Sagi Jaffe-Dax
articles_hidden.abstract: Skilled adult readers show biases in their visual attention that reflect the direction of their native writing systems (e.g., English readers scan left-to-right while Hebrew readers scan right-to-left), but it not yet clear when these biases develop. We tested the hypothesis that language-specific patterns of behavior precede the ability to read by testing how toddlers (2.5-4 years) exposed to different writing systems allocated their attention in a picture naming task. Across two communities, children tended to name objects in the direction that matched their native language. Hebrew-learning toddlers labeled objects from right-to-left, while English- and Spanish-learning toddlers showed the reverse pattern, and language-specific tendencies strengthened with age. These results demonstrate that children have begun to discover directional regularities associated with their language even before they receive literacy instruction and illustrate how cultural conventions exert a direct influence on children’s attention from a very young age.

articles_hidden.title: The Impact of Multilingualism on Self-esteem and Linguistic Identity
articles_hidden.authors: Subhangi Roy
articles_hidden.abstract: This study explores the effects of multilingualism on self-esteem and linguistic identity among individuals living in the UK. Although the cognitive advantages of multilingualism are extensively proven for children and adolescents, its impact on socio-emotional aspects, especially self-esteem and identity in adults, is inadequately investigated. The current study aims to fill this gap using a quantitative methodology, utilising data gathered from 50 participants representing diverse age, gender, ethnic, educational, and linguistic backgrounds, implementing the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (RSES) and a Linguistic Identity Questionnaire (LQ). The primary argument put forward was that, multilingualism would improve self-esteem and foster a richer distinctive language identity. Descriptive statistics, correlation analyses, ANOVA, and independent sample t-tests were employed to investigate the relation among multilingualism, self-esteem, and linguistic identity, including differences among different language groups and sub-constructs of the assessments. The findings suggested no significant direct correlation between multilingualism and self-esteem; however, a noteworthy inverse relationship was identified between the ‘Language and Social Status’ sub-domain of linguistic identity and self-esteem, inferring that, individuals who associated higher social status to a language other than their native language experienced reduced self-esteem. These results indicate that societal perceptions of a language’s prestige can negatively impact self-esteem, especially for native speakers of languages deemed less socially valuable. The hypothesis that multilingualism improves self-esteem was not entirely proven; nonetheless, the study elucidates the impact of linguistic identification on self-esteem, especially for the subcategories that constitute Linguistic identity. The limitations encompass the restricted sample size and reliance on self-reported data. Future study may investigate these processes longitudinally with bigger, more varied samples to further understand the socio-emotional implications of multilingualism.

articles_hidden.title: Likert Versus Visual Analogue Scales in Ecological Momentary Assessment: Initial Evidence That Likert Scales Come With Reduced Capacity to Sustain Attentiveness
articles_hidden.authors: Esther Ulitzsch; Dominik Vollbracht; Lijin Zhang; Alberto Jover Martínez; Benjamin Domingue; Jonas M B Haslbeck; Tanja Lischetzke; Leonie V. D. E. Vogelsmeier
articles_hidden.abstract: Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) prompts participants to report on their current emotions, cognitions, or behaviors multiple times per day across several days, yielding rich, high-frequency data. However, the high frequency of measurement can burden participants, leading to disengagement in the form of non-compliance or careless/insufficient effort responding (C/IER), which compromises the validity of conclusions drawn from EMA data. To minimize these effects, it is crucial to understand how EMA design factors influence respondent disengagement. This study investigates how response format, a comparatively subtle design choice, affects C/IER as an important but hard-to-detect aspect of disengagement. We re-analyzed data from two experimental EMA studies, in which surveys were administered either in a Likert or a visual analogue scale (VAS) format in between-subjects designs. Each dataset was analyzed with one of two state-of-the-art confirmatory mixture modeling approaches to examine whether response format affects (a) the overall level of C/IER and (b) its associations with two fatigue- and attention-related contextual factors: the cumulative number of EMA study days and time of day. Across datasets and analytical approaches, we found indications that Likert scales yield up to 3 percentage points higher rates of C/IER than VASs, though the temporal patterns varied across studies. In Study I, differences were observed in overall C/IER levels, with parallel increases across EMA days. In Study II, initial C/IER was comparable between formats, but the Likert format showed a steeper increase over time. Implications for EMA design are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Revealing the latent geometry of dream content with language models
articles_hidden.authors: Daniele Gatti; Tomaso Vecchi; Pietro Pietrini; Emiliano Ricciardi; Giulio Bernardi; Luca Rinaldi
articles_hidden.abstract: Dreams provide a unique window into human cognition, as their content may reflect individual and collective experiences. Here, we use language models to analyze 21,607 dream narratives, representing each report as a vector in a high-dimensional semantic space that enables continuous comparison without predefined categories. We ask whether different sources of information are organized within the same representational space and across multiple levels of semantic representation; we also tested how dream representational geometries evolve over time. We find that dreams produced by different individuals, as well as by individuals of different genders, occupy distinct regions of this space, particularly in abstract semantic representations. Similarity among descriptions of dreamers also predicts similarity in their dream content. Finally, we show how the semantic geometry of dream content evolves over time, with its trajectory shaped by the cumulative history of past reports. Together, this study provides evidence for the semantic structure of dream content and its evolution over time.

articles_hidden.title: Trait or Bias? Why item keying is indispensable when comparing language model responses across languages
articles_hidden.authors: Qing Li
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychological scales designed for humans are increasingly administered to language models, and differences between their responses in two languages are read as evidence of cultural tendency. Such comparisons presuppose that the two language versions measure the same thing. This study tests that premise. Three established social orientation scales were administered to four models built by United States and Chinese developers in Chinese and English under two temperature settings. Responses were then decomposed, using a psychometric model that separates a latent trait from a directional response bias, into the component that tracks what the instrument is meant to measure and the component that does not. The cross-linguistic difference is not one quantity. On scales with balanced keying, every estimate showed a higher trait and a lower bias under Chinese prompting, the bias moving further than the trait in most conditions. Because the two components run in opposite directions, they offset one another on scales containing no reverse-keyed items, where they also cannot be separated. A difference reported on such a scale therefore does not establish that models differ in the construct, only that they answered differently. Two further manipulations show that the difference is produced by item wording, though not by negation, and that the stability of a model identifier over four weeks varies by an order of magnitude between vendors. We set out three checks that would make cross-linguistic comparison interpretable: balanced keying, decomposition to the item level, and a contemporaneous control whenever collections are compared across time.

articles_hidden.title: Statistics Anxiety and Data Literacy for Sustainable Development: Preliminary Psychometric Evaluation of the Indonesian Statistics Anxiety Rating Scale
articles_hidden.authors: Dina Nazriani; Anang Dwi Santoso; Vena Jaladara; Suri Mutia Siregar; Rahma Fauzia
articles_hidden.abstract:
Education for sustainable development (ESD) emphasizes critical and systems thinking, and both depend on students' ability to read and interpret data such as Sustainable Development Goal indicators. Statistics anxiety is a documented barrier to this kind of data literacy, yet few multidimensional measures of it are available for Indonesian higher education. This study reports a preliminary psychometric evaluation of an Indonesian version of the 51-item Statistics Anxiety Rating Scale (STARS), in which items referring to outdated technology were updated. Data came from 100 undergraduate psychology students at Universitas Sumatera Utara. Each of the six subscales was analyzed with the Rasch rating scale model to examine item fit, rating scale functioning, dimensionality, reliability and separation, and differential item functioning (DIF) by high school track and entry cohort. Correlations with statistics course grades (n = 69) provided criterion-related evidence. Forty-five of the 51 items fit the model. Person reliability ranged from .71 to .86, and thresholds were ordered in every subscale, although respondents barely distinguished between the two highest categories of Worth of Statistics. Four items showed DIF by entry cohort, which appears to reflect whether students had already taken a statistics course. Anxiety subscales correlated negatively with course grades (ρ = -.28 to -.40). The Indonesian STARS shows promising measurement properties, but several items need review, and the results remain preliminary until back translation and expert review are completed.

Keywords: statistics anxiety, Rasch model, data literacy, education for sustainable development, Indonesia

articles_hidden.title: Quality of Life and the Case for Consent-Based Psilocybin Access – Questions on the Regulatory Framework and Cost
articles_hidden.authors: Janis Ancans
articles_hidden.abstract: Legal access to psilocybin almost always requires a medical diagnosis first, usually treatment-resistant depression (TRD) or severe PTSD, as though informed consent alone was not sufficient. This article makes two connected arguments. Extending the autonomy argument already accepted for terminally ill patients, competent adults who understand the risks of a psilocybin experience should be able to choose it for reasons of psychological wellness or existential anxiety relief, not only because a clinician has certified a qualifying illness, a right the legal literature calls “cognitive liberty”. Just as important, the cost of access is not fixed; it reflects the regulatory framework under which psilocybin is provided. No jurisdiction has yet completed medicines authorisation pathway; the furthest-advanced clinical programme, Compass Pathways' COMP360, met its Phase 3 primary endpoint and reported six-month durability data for TRD by July 2026, and its developer has since signalled an annual cost close to that of esketamine nasal spray, USD 50,000–65,000, or roughly USD 17,000–22,000 per dose. Meanwhile, Australia's narrower authorised-prescriber legal route for TRD, using GMP-manufactured but unregistered psilocybin, already costs AUD $20,000 per course. Three distinct non-medical routes cost far less. Truffles in the Netherlands, sold under food law with no diagnosis and no supervision required, and Colorado and Oregon's state-licensed psilocybin services, which require no diagnosis but do involve a supervising facilitator, cost up to $3,000 per session. Removing the diagnosis requirement while leaving this cost structure untouched risks replacing the regulatory barrier with the wealth-based one, unless expanded access is paired with public subsidy. Article also briefly reviews the safety evidence, the political origins of psilocybin's scheduling, and the double standard in how its risks are treated. A Canadian case illustrates the institutional and regulatory framework dysfunction, a dying man denied psilocybin for existential relief while approved for medical assistance in dying within weeks, before the article closes with policy recommendations addressing both access and funding.

articles_hidden.title: My Personality—Wrapped: Protocol for a Measurement-Burst Design Study to Investigate the Development and Dynamics of Individual Differences Across Time
articles_hidden.authors: Amanda Jo Wright; Peter Haehner; Michael Dominik Krämer; Nicholas Poh-Jie Tan; Christopher James Hopwood; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles_hidden.abstract: People and their environments continuously shape one another across time. Understanding person-environment transactions is essential for describing, predicting, and explaining the dynamics and development of individual differences. Yet, progress on this has been constrained by two common limitations: study designs driven by practical rather than theoretical considerations and neglecting how person-environment processes unfold across multiple timescales. Here, we present the rationale and design of the My Personality––Wrapped (MPW) Study, a measurement-burst study designed to investigate how individual differences in personality, well-being, attitudes, social and interpersonal behaviors, and health develop and dynamically fluctuate alongside environmental influences across multiple timescales. Across 1 year, participants (Nmax = 1,230) completed baseline (T0) and post-study (T6) assessment batteries, five bimonthly surveys (T1–T5), and 15 pseudorandomly scheduled 1-week bursts comprising mobile sensing, experience sampling, daily, and weekly surveys. This intensive, multi-method study provides comprehensive cross-timescale data on psychological constructs and contextual experiences. The MPW Study is designed to advance the field’s understanding of temporal dynamics underlying individual differences by disentangling within-person processes from between-person differences, facilitating theory development and testing of multi-timescale person-environment transactions, and informing future theory-driven research on the dynamics of personality and well-being, social and health processes, and life disruptions.

articles_hidden.title: The Same Memory Retrieved Differently: Competition Enables Flexible Generalization in Hippocampus-like Networks
articles_hidden.authors: Robby Ralston; Brandon Turner; Vladimir Sloutsky
articles_hidden.abstract: Hippocampus supports the retrieval of richly detailed episodic memories from sparse cues. However, an event can be detailed and also lead to generalization. To explain both phenomena, researchers have proposed multiple memory systems or distinct memory traces for specific and general content. In contrast, we argue that a single system can support both specificity and generalization. To do this, we present ATHENA, a formal framework that reinterprets cognitive memory models as recurrent neural networks. We show that many episodic memory models are single-step approximations of dynamic networks with competitive retrieval mechanisms, similar to Modern Hopfield Networks. Notably, under a cognitive interpretation, the intensity of the competitive process is a psychologically-meaningful parameter that shapes generalization in the network. Through simulations, we demonstrate that modulating this parameter during retrieval leads the same traces to produce qualitatively different forms of generalization over the same memory traces. We then extend our analysis to sequential memory, and show how the same competitive retrieval process can be combined with known hippocampal circuits to achieve more sophisticated forms of generalization. These results demonstrate the flexibility of single-system memory retrieval and highlight the interplay of specific and general mnemonic content.

articles_hidden.title: Concordance of Parents’ Anger Responses are Linked with Parents’ and Adolescents’ Psychopathology Symptoms
articles_hidden.authors: Emma Ilyaz; Prakash Thambipillai; Amy Byrd; Salome Vanwoerden; J. Richard Jennings; Stephanie Stepp; Vera Vine
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective: Parents’ emotions shape children’s understanding of emotions and their management. Children of parents with borderline personality disorder (BPD), in which anger dysregulation is a cardinal symptom, are at elevated risk of psychopathology, which tends to onset in adolescence. The nature of anger dysregulation associated with parental BPD symptom severity and how it relates to adolescents’ psychopathology is not well understood. We characterized parents’ anger dysregulation multimodally and examined how concordance across emotion channels (e.g., subjective, and physiological) predicted both parent BPD symptoms and child psychopathology symptoms. Method: Participants were 162 parents (Mage =40.37 years; 93% women; 47% racial/ethnic minority) of young adolescents oversampled for emotion dysregulation (Mage=12.59 years; 47% women; 60% racial/ethnic minority). Parents’ BPD symptom severity was clinician-rated using semi-structured interview, and adolescents’ psychopathology symptoms were assessed by parent- and adolescent-report on a well-known, validated questionnaire. During a dyadic, parent-child conflict interaction, parents’ anger responses were measured in two ways, using respiratory sinus arrythmia (RSA; low values indicating stress-like responding) and self-reported anger. Results: Using polynomial response surface modeling, we found that parental BPD feature severity (Model 1) and child psychopathology severity (Model 2) were each related to greater numerical misalignment between parental anger responses, primarily manifesting in this sample as a combination of low RSA and high subjective anger, or anger concordance. Conclusions: Findings help show which forms of parental anger dysregulation are related to psychopathology in parents and adolescents, which could have implications for understanding the intergenerational transmission of psychopathology.

articles_hidden.title: From the Inside Out: School Stressors Identified by Autistic and ADHD (AuDHD) Students Experiencing School Non-Attendance
articles_hidden.authors: Jia Ying Sarah Lee; Dawn Adams; Chris Paradisis; Raechel Smart; Tiffany Westphal; Leah Heale; Kate Simpson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Research into school non-attendance is expanding, yet the perspectives of young people, particularly neurodivergent students, remain underrepresented. Card-sorting tasks offer a promising, accessible method for capturing these perspectives. The Student Stress Investigation (SSI) uses a structured card-sort approach to facilitate young people’s self-report of school-related stressors.

This study used the SSI to explore school-based stressors among 31 children and adolescents (mean age = 12.16 years) diagnosed with both autism and ADHD (AuDHD). On average, they missed 3.46 days of school per month. Participants first categorised stressors as relevant or irrelevant, then ranked relevant items from smallest to largest stressors.

The most frequently identified major stressors were classroom environments that were too loud or quiet (35.5%), uninteresting tasks (32.2%), unpredictability (29.0%), school days being too long (29.0%), and being rushed (29.0%). Qualitative responses highlighted variability in how stressors were experienced. For example, some students reported that the classroom being too loud or quiet was a sensory-related stressor, while others reported it as having an impact on attention or executive functioning.

These findings provide direct insight into the everyday school experiences contributing to stress and non-attendance among AuDHD students. The results underscore the value of self-report tools and highlight the need for targeted, individualised, and proactive adjustments to reduce stress that may in turn support an increased capacity to consider a return to school.

articles_hidden.title: Consensus Embedding Geometry for Taxonomy Discovery in Psychological Domains
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel Steven Stutts; Jeffrey Humpherys; Ting Shen
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychological domains contain many constructs whose meanings are specified through natural-language definitions and examples. Organizing these vocabularies requires methods that connect semantic representations to interpretable categories and expose the effects of analytical choices. We present a researcher-guided framework combining construct prototypes, consensus similarity across embedding models, classical multidimensional scaling, and clustering in theory-guided feature spaces. Averaging model-specific cosine matrices produces a positive-semidefinite consensus kernel that accommodates different embedding dimensions. Global geometry supports broad organization, domain features support intermediate grouping, and local geometry supports finer subdivision. We demonstrate the framework on 224 abuse constructs represented by working definitions supplied by generative artificial intelligence and seven synthetic examples per construct. The resulting hierarchy distinguishes psychological domination from environmental violation and provides finer categories within each branch. Comparisons with single-model, definition-only, example-only, and direct-clustering alternatives identify the roles of representation and subdivision choices. The contribution is a reproducible workflow and stage-specific evaluation for exploratory taxonomy discovery. The case study establishes the dependence of its output on identifiable modeling choices, with category validity and cross-domain transfer remaining questions for further study.

articles_hidden.title: Familiar Content Changes Performance and Processing in Matrix Reasoning in Early Adolescence
articles_hidden.authors: Paulo Guirro Laurence; Marcela M. Weiss; Elizeu Macedo
articles_hidden.abstract: Matrix-reasoning assessments commonly use abstract geometric figures, although familiar content may change both performance and processing. This within-participants study compared accuracy and gaze-defined patterns of visual exploration for abstract and contextual items requiring corresponding relational rules. Participants were 56 children and adolescents recruited from a public school in São Paulo, Brazil, aged 11 to 15 years. Each participant completed six abstract and six contextual 3 × 3 matrices while gaze was recorded. Trial-level transition matrices were constructed from fixation sequences across nine matrix cells and the response alternatives, and k-means clustering identified two recurring patterns. Contextual items were answered more accurately than abstract items, with 2.44 times higher odds of a correct response. Completion time, fixation count, and fixation duration were similar between conditions. Cluster 1 was characterized by localized transitions involving the final row and response alternatives, whereas Cluster 2 involved broader, more sequential exploration across the matrix. Contextual items had lower odds of Cluster 1 classification, indicating that representational format modestly altered the distribution of gaze patterns. A significant condition-by-cluster interaction further showed that Cluster 2 was associated with higher accuracy for abstract items, but no cluster difference was detected for contextual items. These exploratory findings suggest that familiar content changes how matrices are explored, indicating that abstract and familiar matrix items should not be treated as interchangeable.

articles_hidden.title: Experiencing the Queer Collective Through Time:  Exploring Perceptions of Cultural and Historical Continuity Among LGBTQ+ Emerging Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Kit Demetrius Greyson; Nic M. Weststrate; Kate C. McLean
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective. Using a pre-registered explanatory sequential mixed method design, we examined collective continuity, which until now has been studied in populations where its transmission is assumed to occur naturally via familial and cultural engagement. We examined collective continuity among LGBTQ+ emerging adults for whom access to the culture and history of the collective is not always available. Method. In Study 1, we examined associations across three measures of collective continuity, and their associations with LGBTQ+ identity and well-being in college and community samples of emerging adults (N = 246). Results. We found little association between the measures of collective continuity, modest associations between collective continuity and LGBTQ+ identity, and no relations between collective continuity and well-being. Method. Given the lack of empirical overlap in measures of collective continuity, in Study 2 we employed a qualitative interview approach (N = 8) to provide greater descriptive data on the phenomenon. Results. These analyses revealed a lack of collective continuity and highlighted unique factors that facilitate or forestall the development of collective continuity among LGBTQ+ people, distinguishing this process from other groups (e.g., ethnic, national) in important ways. Conclusion. Together, these findings provide the opportunity for theoretical refinement and expansion of collective continuity.

articles_hidden.title: Making good decisions with counterfactuals
articles_hidden.authors: Ma Ricky; Scott Mueller; Thomas Icard; Tobias Gerstenberg
articles_hidden.abstract: Making a good decision often requires knowing something counterfactual: whether a person would be better off if we acted than if we didn't. Formal work shows how both experimental and observational data ought to be combined to inform good decisions. Here, we ask whether people's intuitions follow this normative standard. In three experiments (N = 354), participants decided whether or not to act based on observational and experimental data. Participants performed better than chance but far from optimally. Trial-by-trial feedback about the consequences of their choices, including what would have happened had they chosen otherwise, didn't improve performance. The breakdown was at the inference step: participants' estimates of whether a person would benefit from the treatment, be harmed by it, or be left unaffected were almost unrelated to normative predictions. Yet, participants' decisions followed coherently from those (incorrect) estimates. Experts in statistics, economics, and data science made better decisions than novices, but their counterfactual inferences were no more accurate. Counterfactual reasoning is critical for making good decisions from experimental and observational data, but its logic doesn't come naturally to people.

articles_hidden.title: Health and Personality Contributions to Cybersickness in Virtual Reality
articles_hidden.authors: Jonathan Kelly; Taylor Doty; Sydney Hicks; Stephen B. Gilbert; Michael Dorneich
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Cybersickness reflects interactions between system (hardware and software) properties and user characteristics. Although motion sickness susceptibility is a known predictor, individual differences including transient and enduring health, psychological, and personality factors have rarely been examined and never simultaneously.

Method
Participants (N = 252) were exposed to one of five VR games. Cybersickness was assessed using self-reported symptoms (Simulator Sickness Questionnaire; SSQ) and tolerance (time in VR). Hierarchical regression models evaluated whether health, psychological functioning (affective state, psychological distress), and personality predicted outcomes after accounting for game, sex, and motion sickness susceptibility.

Results
Fatigue, pain sensitivity, and sex were key predictors of symptom severity: higher fatigue, greater pain sensitivity, and female sex were associated with higher SSQ scores. Motion sickness susceptibility and agreeableness predicted reduced tolerance. Final models explained 29.3% of variance in SSQ and 23.8% in tolerance.

Conclusion
Cybersickness reflected established stimulus and susceptibility factors as well as outcome-specific user characteristics: health-related factors and sex were associated with symptom severity; susceptibility and agreeableness were associated with tolerance.

Application
User state (e.g., fatigue), sex, motion sickness susceptibility, and tolerance-related individual differences should be considered in the design and deployment of immersive systems to improve comfort and support sustained VR use.

articles_hidden.title: Selective maintenance of aversive memories as a mechanism of spontaneous recovery of fear
articles_hidden.authors: Isabel Berwian; Yongjing Ren; Sashank Pisupti; Jialing Ding; Seohyun Moon; Jamie C. Chiu; Deepta Chandrasekhar; Yael Niv
articles_hidden.abstract:
Return of fear after exposure poses a significant challenge for treatment of anxiety dis-
orders. In this study, we used computational modeling to test competing mechanisms
underlying spontaneous recovery of fear over time. We fit computational models of a
novel theory of spontaneous recovery—selective maintenance of aversive memories—
to behavior from a fear conditioning and extinction task (N=316), and showed that they
uniquely captured spontaneous recovery and quantitatively outperformed alternative
models embodying theories from the literature. The results were supported across mul-
tiple datasets, including a preregistered replication (N=355) and a sample with mental
health symptoms (N=520). The selective maintenance modeling framework addition-
ally offers mechanistic insights into overgeneralization and the development of anxi-
ety. Indeed, in the symptomatic sample we found that symptoms of generalized anxiety
disorder correlated with estimates of overgeneralization in the model. Through simu-
lations, we further demonstrated that insights from our model can explain how targeted
interventions such as retrieval cues and cognitive interventions can prevent the return
of fear. These results highlight selective maintenance of aversive events in memory as
a critical and testable target for improving anxiety treatments and preventing relapse.

articles_hidden.title: Persecutory and Grandiose Thinking in Mental Disorder, Religion, and Politics: Common Causes, Processes, and (Dys)Functions
articles_hidden.authors: Ari Brouwer; Charles L Raison
articles_hidden.abstract: Persecutory and grandiose thinking (PGT) is evident in mental disorder, religion, and politics. This paper offers an interdisciplinary explanation of PGT with a focus on common causes, mechanisms, and functions. First, psychopathological and ideological variants of PGT are introduced and compared. Theories of stress-induced psychological and social change are invoked next to explain shifts towards PGT in individuals and groups. These include a Status Threat/Reward Model of psychopathological PGT and a relative deprivation theory of political violence. Potential functions and dysfunctions of PGT are considered next, with a focus on how persecutory and grandiose thinking may orient individuals towards mitigating social threats and gaining social rewards, respectively. Conditions for collective PGT are then explored, including systemic stress and exposure to redemptive ideological narratives. Finally, we consider how religious and political institutions regulate PGT.

articles_hidden.title: Inconclusive prospective effects between fear of failure, academic buoyancy, and academic procrastination among Chinese primary school students: A reassessment of Fang et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles_hidden.abstract: Fang et al. concluded reciprocal prospective associations between fear of failure, academic buoyancy, and academic procrastination among primary school students. However, significant cross-lagged parameters do not by themselves establish genuine prospective influence because similar estimates may arise through alternative statistical processes. Using simulated data that reproduced the sample size and correlation matrix reported by Fang et al., I examined whether their conclusions were robust across several defensible analytic specifications. The pattern of results depended strongly on analytic choice: some models suggested positive prospective associations, whereas others indicated negative or null effects. When estimates from all specifications were combined using meta-analytic methods, no overall effect reached statistical significance. Accordingly, the available evidence does not provide a firm basis for concluding that fear of failure, academic buoyancy, and academic procrastination exert reciprocal prospective influences on one another. In line with multiverse-analysis recommendations, conclusions should be drawn from the collective pattern across reasonable analytical alternatives rather than from a single model.

articles_hidden.title: Maturational constraints on tracking of temporal attention in infant language acquisition.
articles_hidden.authors: Tineke M. Snijders; Katharina Menn
articles_hidden.abstract: Children are active learners: they selectively attend to important information. Rhythmic neural tracking of speech is central to active language learning. This chapter evaluates recent research showing that neural oscillations in the infant brain synchronise with the rhythm of speech, tracking it at different frequencies. This process predicts word segmentation and later language abilities. We argue that rhythmic neural speech tracking reflects infants’ attention to specific parts of the speech signal (e.g., stressed syllables), and simultaneously acts as a core mechanism for maximising temporal attention onto those parts. Rhythmic neural tracking of speech puts a constraint on neural processing, which maximises the uptake of relevant information from the noisy multimodal environment. We hypothesise this to be influenced by neural maturation. We end by evaluating the implications of this proposal for language acquisition research, and discuss how differences in neural maturation relate to variance in language development in autism.

articles_hidden.title: Ongoing thought varies around individualised defaults in an experiential state space across contexts and depressive symptoms
articles_hidden.authors: Clara Wakonigg Alonso; Sian Panton; Dominique Makowski; Giulia Poerio; Theodoros Karapanagiotidis
articles_hidden.abstract: Ongoing thought varies continuously, yet previous research has shown that people engage in a small set of recurring thought patterns that are consistent across contexts and individuals. However, it remains unclear whether individuals show idiosyncratic, stable configurations, akin to a default experiential state from which momentary experiences deviate. We combined an emotional-induction task with Multidimensional Experience Sampling of ongoing thought in the lab and daily life. Dimensionality reduction revealed five dominant population-level patterns of thought, forming orthogonal axes of a shared experiential space. Within this space, thought patterns were more similar within individuals than between, supporting person-specific signatures. Position within this space carried psychological meaning: depressive symptom severity predicted both the intensity and frequency of negative intrusive thought in daily life. Default thought patterns were then estimated as each participant's geometric median across daily-life experiences and we assessed how affective contexts displaced thought from these defaults. Positive and negative stimuli shifted thought away from default thought patterns in systematic context-dependent ways, and these shifts varied with depressive symptom severity. Together, the findings suggest that default thought patterns define stable regions within an experiential space, while emotional states and individual differences relate to how momentary experience is displaced from these defaults.

articles_hidden.title: From Impulse to Goal-Consistent Action: Testing an Intervention Targeting Predictions About One’s Own Behavior
articles_hidden.authors: Tilia Linthout; Pieter Van Dessel; Marie Vandenbogaerde; Yannick Boddez
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Impulsive behaviors, such as unplanned snacking, doomscrolling, or angry reactions, often persist despite people’s intentions to act differently. Across two preregistered studies, we tested a novel intervention designed to strengthen people’s predictions that they will act in line with their goals in tempting situations. In Study 1, adults with self-reported impulse control difficulties recruited online (N = 68) completed either this prediction-based intervention or a comparison intervention that included go/no-go training. The prediction-based intervention produced stronger expectations of impulse control improvement. Study 2 used daily smartphone assessments over three weeks (N = 30; 21 repeated measurements per participant). Participants receiving the prediction-based intervention reported larger reductions in impulsive behaviors during and after the intervention period than participants receiving go/no-go training or waitlist control. Limitations include reliance on self-report and short-term follow-up. These findings provide preliminary evidence that interventions targeting predictions about one’s future action may support impulse control behavior change in daily life.
Keywords: impulse control, impulsive behavior, goal-directed predictive processing, inferential theory, self-regulation, behavior change

articles_hidden.title: Predict to Resist: A Mixed-Method Evaluation of a Prediction-Based Impulse Control Intervention
articles_hidden.authors: Tilia Linthout; Lieke Reintjes; Pieter Van Dessel
articles_hidden.abstract:
Impulsive behaviors often persist despite people’s intentions to act in line with personally valued goals. A recently developed intervention based on the Goal-Directed Predictive Processing (GDPP) framework aims to change such behaviors by helping people construct and practice inference chains in which personally relevant risk situations lead to predictions of goal-consistent behavior. The present study was designed as a replication and qualitative extension of a previous study testing this intervention. Ten Dutch-speaking adults with self-reported impulse control difficulties were allocated to a GDPP-based intervention condition or a waitlist control condition. Participants reported the frequency of their personally selected target behavior daily across baseline, training, and post-training phases. Participants in the GDPP condition also completed semi-structured interviews after the intervention. Single-case analyses showed heterogeneous response patterns. Two participants in the GDPP condition showed reliable reductions in impulsive behavior, but other participants did not, and reliable change was also observed in the waitlist control condition. The quantitative results therefore did not provide strong evidence for a uniform intervention effect. The qualitative results identified three main themes: intervention experience, perceived factors contributing to intervention effects, and perceived barriers to intervention effects. Participants described the rationale as recognizable and reported that the intervention increased awareness of impulsive and alternative behaviors, but also identified barriers such as mismatch between the rationale and the target behavior, persistent risk situations, insufficient repetition, motivational barriers, and strong craving. These findings suggest that GDPP-based impulse control interventions require further refinement and careful personalization before larger-scale efficacy testing.
Keywords: impulse control; behavior change; goal-directed predictive processing; single-case design; qualitative methods
