Language-distance analyses further revealed that valence-related orthographic and phoneme-bigram transfer was stronger between more closely related languages, particularly genealogically and the modest correspondence between fitted form coefficients indicated that transferable prediction coexisted with differences in feature weighting across languages. These findings characterize affective iconicity as graded and representation-dependent: valence generalizes most strongly through distributional meaning, whereas arousal leaves a more consistent cross-linguistic trace in word form. This pattern motivates an account in which culturally and historically shaped evaluative mappings coexist with activation-related mappings that may draw more broadly on shared embodied constraints, connecting linguistic form with the conceptual organization of affective experience.

articles_hidden.title: Using conversational artificial intelligence to dissect the psychoneuroimmunology of social safety and threat
articles_hidden.authors: Julian Packheiser; Sigrid Elsenbruch; Harald Engler; Dirk Scheele
articles_hidden.abstract: Human health is profoundly shaped by the quality of our social environments, yet the mechanisms through which social experiences become biologically embedded remain poorly understood. Social Safety Theory (SST) proposes that perceived social safety and threat influence health through neuroendocrine and immune pathways, but it remains unclear which features of social interaction engage these pathways. Here, we argue that conversational artificial intelligence (AI) provides a powerful experimental tool to address this mechanistic gap. Synthetic agents allow researchers to systematically vary core social signals, including responsiveness, reciprocity, empathic cues, agency, and multimodal information, while holding other features of the interaction relatively constant. This controllability creates a unique opportunity to identify which social signals are necessary or sufficient to generate perceived safety or threat and to engage downstream biological responses. Building on SST, we propose a psychoneuroimmunological framework linking experimentally controlled features of synthetic social interaction to neuroendocrine and immune processes and derive testable hypotheses concerning perceived humanness, social-signal strength, and multimodal embodiment. By enabling the causal decomposition of social interaction, conversational AI could help reveal what makes an interaction biologically social and clarify the mechanisms linking social disconnection to health.

articles_hidden.title: Sleep Helps You Make Good Social Decisions, Even If You’re Not Sure Why
articles_hidden.authors: Lewis Vincent Ball; Yicheng Qiu; Heather Jane Ferguson; M. Gareth Gaskell
articles_hidden.abstract: Memory supports trust decision-making in social encounters. We investigated whether this support is influenced by sleep, given the beneficial effect of sleep on episodic memory. Participants encountered images of cooperative and cheating partners during exposure. Item (is this person old/new?) and source memory (did they cooperate/cheat?) were then measured, before participants chose whether to cooperate with old and new partners. Experiment 1 ruled out time-of-day influences on our measures. In Experiment 2, a ~12 hr delay separated exposure and memory/cooperation phases. The Sleep group slept overnight in between whilst the Wake group experienced a day awake. Experiment 3 replicated the paradigm and measured trust in a contextually-novel task relative to exposure, measuring the extent to which participants would accept each partner as their neighbour. In a combined analysis across Experiments 2 and 3, participant-level item and source memory correlated with the frequency of adaptive decisions. Recognition of cheating partners was enhanced in the Sleep group (item memory), but there were no group differences in recalling the past behaviour of partners (source memory). Participants were more likely to cooperate with cooperators than cheaters and more likely to accept cooperators than cheaters as their neighbours (Experiment 3). Importantly, both effects were enhanced in the Sleep group. These findings are consistent with sleep promoting socially-adaptive decision-making. Given there was no significant evidence that sleep influenced explicit memory for behaviours, sleep may facilitate decision-making by integrating new memories into generalised knowledge structures in long-term memory, supporting more flexible decision-making.

articles_hidden.title: Motor precision shapes information seeking in perceptual decisions
articles_hidden.authors: Alessandra Loretani; Claire Bédé; thibault gajdos; Andrea Desantis
articles_hidden.abstract: Adaptive behavior relies heavily on the confidence we have in our decisions. For instance, in the absence of explicit feedback, the confidence associated with a decision determines whether we seek additional evidence or are likely to change our mind. Recent studies suggest that confidence estimation also depends on motor processes involved in implementing perceptual decisions. However, whether motor-induced changes in confidence meaningfully affect behavior, such as by altering information-seeking, remains uncertain. The present study addresses this question. Participants performed a perceptual task requiring discrimination of the orientation of Gabor patches. The motor cost of the perceptual response was manipulated by varying the size of the response circles that participants had to reach to report their judgment. Consistent with previous findings showing that easier motor responses are associated with lower confidence ratings, we found that such responses were also linked to a greater tendency to seek additional evidence compared to more costly responses. Importantly, this increase in information-seeking behavior was not accompanied by any change in perceptual accuracy. These findings support the idea that the motor costs associated with perceptual decisions modulate confidence, and that such motor-induced changes in confidence play a functional role in guiding subsequent behavior.

articles_hidden.title: ADHD symptoms, rejection sensitivity and the mediating role of peer rejection: A longitudinal study
articles_hidden.authors: Nina Chmielowice-Szymanski; Antonius H. N. Cillessen; Leentje Vervoort
articles_hidden.abstract:
In addition to challenges explained by neurocognitive differences, young adults with ADHD also
experience challenges related to psychosocial processes. Heightened levels of rejection
sensitivity among young adults with ADHD symptoms may be explained by peer rejection
experiences in adolescence. In the current study, which is part of the Nijmegen Longitudinal
Study, we examined among 116 young adults whether peer rejection experiences in adolescence
(age 16) mediated the association between previous ADHD symptoms (age 12) and rejection
sensitivity (age 20). ADHD symptoms were not significantly associated with peer rejection (β =
0.21, p = .200), which were also not associated with rejection sensitivity (β = 0.05, p = .747). There
was no significant direct effect (β = -0.04, p = .817) or indirect effect (β = -0.01, BCa CI = [-0.02,
0.09]) of ADHD symptoms on rejection sensitivity. The current study provided no evidence for an
association of ADHD symptoms with rejection sensitivity, or a mediating role of peer rejection.

articles_hidden.title: Arousal by Any Other Name? Testing the Specificity of Sexual Arousal in Men’s Cue-Based Judgments of Potential Flirt Partners
articles_hidden.authors: Ingo Landwehr; Alexander F. Schmidt
articles_hidden.abstract: Inferring whether a woman is showing romantic or sexual interest can be challenging, especially when multiple cues conflict or cue integration is influenced by physiological states such as arousal. Building on research linking sexual arousal to men’s overreliance on global cues (OGC) when assessing women’s sexual interest, this preregistered study tested whether a similar cue-weighting bias would emerge under nonsexual arousal. Heterosexual men (N = 275) completed a decision task judging which of two women was more likely to be flirting with them. Stimuli from a validated image set combined global sexual (clothing) and specific affective (facial) cues in congruent versus incongruent pairings. Error rate (ER) indexed OGC, whereas reaction time (RT) captured complementary decision dynamics. Incongruent trials yielded longer RTs and higher ERs, but nonsexual arousal did not reproduce the OGC-related performance pattern previously observed under sexual arousal. Findings suggest that sexual arousal may exert distinct effects on cue weighting and conflict-related processing, highlighting the importance of specifying the conditions under which arousal alters the integration of global sexual and specific affective cues in social judgments.

articles_hidden.title: A Psychometric Analysis and Primer for Decision Making in Public Third-Party Funding Allocation
articles_hidden.authors: Rima-Maria Rahal; Daniel Leising; Finn Luebber
articles_hidden.abstract: A significant portion of research is financed by public resources, with the expectation that it will deliver societal benefits in return. But how good are current funding allocation processes at effectively identifying and supporting research ideas that will end up contributing to societal good? In this primer, we address the critical challenge of assessing the effectiveness of funding allocation procedures by treating the selection process as a diagnostic procedure and applying psychometric tools to its assessment. We highlight an apparent disconnect between the mission of funding beneficial research and prevailing practices in funding allocation, emphasizing a lack of understanding regarding how to measure and predict the quality of research proposals. We advocate for greater transparency in funding decision processes, and for empirical investigations of how funding systems may yield optimal outcomes under existing constraints and objectives.

articles_hidden.title: “If you look at my collection, you get a real flavour of who I am.”  The influence of identity on collectors’ behaviours.
articles_hidden.authors: Tom Robert White; Luke Hodson
articles_hidden.abstract: Collecting is common human behaviour, characterized by purposeful selection of items, forming interrelated sets, and valued beyond their utilitarian use. The extant literature offers insight into collector categories, motivations, and behaviours. However, a paucity of research exists on the specific decisions collectors make and how they are informed by identity. To explore this, the present study utilized semi-structured interviews with ten self-identified collectors of mass-produced products. Thematic Analysis identified an overarching theme: “Habits and Hierarchy,” encapsulating the related, but distinct themes of “Collections Dictate Behaviour” and “Better Than You,” plus further themes: “Need for Control,” with a sub-theme “As Intended?” and “Sacred From The Profane.” These themes illustrate links between specific collecting decisions our sample makes and the influence of self and social identities. The study evidences the connection between identity formation, augmentation and enhancement with decision-making. Specifically, how ‘collector’ identity competes with other self-identities, and how collectors compete amongst themselves, by illustrating how collections are reflective of, and enhance collectors’ individual identities, and how this creates a perceived hierarchy within collector communities.

articles_hidden.title: ChatGPT Dots for Educators and Students in Psychology  Education
articles_hidden.authors: Oleksii Nalyvaiko
articles_hidden.abstract:
This study examines the conditions for using persistent AI agents in higher education, with ChatGPT Dots and psychology education as its analytical focus. An exploratory documentary analysis was conducted on eight public OpenAI documentation pages: six describing Dots and two providing contextual information on ChatGPT and ChatGPT Work. Sixteen purposively selected source statements were coded and recorded in a ledger that distinguishes documented functionality from 
educational interpretation. The analysis develops the Continuing Educational Delegation (CED) 
framework, consisting of six documented conditions: bounded continuity, separation of task completion from verified achievement, distinction between access and permission, audience boundaries across communication channels, explicit control over continuing work, and recognition of capabilities shared with adjacent ChatGPT workflows. Four constructed scenarios apply the framework to seminar preparation, rubric and feedback development, fictional psychological case analysis, and student research planning. The resulting propositions specify how continuing assistance can be 
organised while preserving assessable student reasoning and educator judgment. A prospective comparative protocol defines twenty-four workflow trajectories and distinguishes artifact quality, human review effort, and student learning as separate evaluation targets. The contribution is a source grounded analytical framework and a reproducible specification for subsequent evaluation. No live Dots trials, participant observations, or measured learning effects are reported; the framework therefore requires empirical examination before claims of educational effectiveness can be made.

articles_hidden.title: Re. The influence of personality on the risk of myocardial infarction in UK Biobank cohort
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander Weiss
articles_hidden.abstract: Dahlén, Miguet, Schiöth, and Rukh1 used items from UK Biobank2 to construct “proxies” of the five domains of human personality—Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Neuroticism, Extraversion, and Openness3. However, the items used came from an existing Neuroticism scale. In my analyses, I demonstrated that the discriminant validities of these proxies are poor, and so should not be used to study personality in UK Biobank or any other dataset.

articles_hidden.title: The Cultural Logic of Honor and Antisocial Punishment in Social Dilemmas: A Multi-Lab Study Across Three World Regions
articles_hidden.authors: Shuxian Jin; Dina Rabie; Jinkwon Lee; Jinkyung Na; Rania Miniesy; Vivian L Vignoles; Ayse K. Uskul
articles_hidden.abstract: Punishment can sustain cooperation by targeting free riders (prosocial punishment), but it may also backfire by triggering retaliation; and when punishment is directed at cooperators (antisocial punishment), it can lead to a decline in cooperation. Samples exhibiting greater antisocial punishment in previous research have tended to come from societies where honor is believed to play a stronger role in shaping social behavior. Here, we tested the role of honor in antisocial punishment through a preregistered multi-lab experiment conducted in Egypt (n = 266), South Korea (n = 212), and the United Kingdom (n = 192), using public goods games with and without punishment. While the level of antisocial punishment was higher among the Egyptian sample, compared to the South Korean and British samples, individual-level honor values and norms were not associated with antisocial punishment across all three samples. Nevertheless, individuals with stronger personal honor values exhibited heightened retaliation, particularly targeting cooperators after being punished unfairly. These findings suggest that honor is not a cultural aspiration that provokes, nor a norm that prescribes, aggression toward cooperators, but rather a cultural logic that shapes when and for whom punishment becomes a tool of harmful retaliation rather than cooperation enforcement.

articles_hidden.title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Qualitative Research Training: Opportunities, Limitations and Lessons from Case Studies in Bilingual Autism Research
articles_hidden.authors: Naomi Portillo; Arisa Rincon Rodgers; Stacey L Bevan
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background—Interviews are a fundamental method of qualitative research, yet the opportunity to train interviewers may be limited by time and costs. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have created new possibilities for generating realistic interview simulations that may support training and skills development for researchers.

Purpose—To explore the feasibility of using a Large Language Model (LLM) to simulate qualitative interview responses and describe the strengths and weaknesses of AI-generated interactions as a training tool for researchers.

Methods— Using clinical case studies from caregivers of autistic children, we created a series of AI-generated interview simulations. Research assistants engaged with simulations in both English and Spanish to evaluate the model’s capacity for multilingual responses to a qualitative interview guide. We present a summary of the responses’ thematic relevance, coherence, and conversational authenticity. A focus was given to the model’s ability to maintain consistency across languages while reflecting the experiences represented in the source data.

Results—AI-generated simulations demonstrated the ability to produce coherent, contextually relevant responses in both English and Spanish, suggesting potential training opportunities in multilingual qualitative research studies. 

Conclusions / Implications for Practice—The findings indicate that AI may support researchers working with linguistically diverse populations by providing accessible opportunities to practice interviewing across languages. Additionally, our team found the simulations especially useful for familiarization with the interview format, question flow, and overall process of conducting qualitative interviews. However, simulations lacked several features characteristic of authentic human interaction, including spontaneity, silence, vocal fillers, and nuanced emotional expression. Despite these limitations, we conclude that AI-generated interview simulations have considerable potential as a supplemental tool for qualitative research training and cross-cultural research applications.

articles_hidden.title: A Risk-Formulation Framework and Candidate Screening Items for Dangerous Use of Large Language Models in Clinical Psychiatry
articles_hidden.authors: Armando N. Braz; Punit Matta; Joshuah Muthee; Eren M Veziroglu; Daniel Price
articles_hidden.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and related conversational artificial intelligence (AI) systems have moved rapidly from novelty into ordinary use across education, work, social life, and mental-health-related help seeking. Members of the public now use these systems for advice, companionship, self-disclosure, emotional support, psychoeducation, and quasi-therapeutic interactions. Existing instruments assess problematic or dependent AI use, but they do not ask whether AI has entered a pathway toward serious harm by entrenching ideation, operationalizing capability, displacing human support, or amplifying harmful conduct. To our knowledge, no brief, clinically oriented psychiatric screener has yet been developed and validated specifically for this purpose. We define dangerous AI use as generative AI use that appears to increase the likelihood, feasibility, persistence, organization, or scale of serious harm to self or others. This paper describes LLMs as interactive capability amplifiers and quasi-social systems rather than informational technologies alone, situates their risk within the technical problems of alignment and behavioral stability, and proposes a four-dimensional clinical formulation: Ideational Entrenchment, Operationalized Capability, Relational Displacement, and Broader Amplification. We then introduce two candidate instruments awaiting formal validation: the STEPS-5, a brief screen for AI involvement in acute self-harm and suicide risk, and the HEAT-4, a research-oriented framework addressing broader harmful-use amplification. These tools are intended to open clinical inquiry rather than diagnose, predict behavior, or determine disposition. Ultimately, we argue for the need to avoid both over-pathologizing ordinary AI use and ignoring when AI has become meaningfully relevant to psychiatric safety.

articles.title: Understanding climate actions: The cost-impact trade-off
articles.authors: Gian Luca Pasin; Eva Vriens
articles.abstract: Why do individuals commit to some climate actions but not others? Although concern about climate change is widespread, stated willingness to act often falls short. In a preregistered between-subjects survey experiment with UK respondents (N = 900), we randomly assigned participants to one of four climate actions that differ in personal cost and environmental impact: reducing meat consumption (high cost, high impact), reducing car use (high cost, moderate impact), reducing food waste (low cost, moderate impact), and reducing plastic waste (low cost, low impact). After receiving standardized information about their assigned action, participants reported their stated commitment to adopting it, their compensatory green beliefs, their expectations about others' commitment, and the share of others who would need to adopt the action before they would do so themselves (i.e., individual threshold for behavioural change).} We found that participants correctly perceived differences in the cost of the action, but misjudged environmental impact, substantially underestimating the impact of high-impact actions like dietary change and overestimating the impact of limiting plastic waste. \hl{Consistent with the reasoning behind the low-cost hypothesis}, low-cost actions elicited higher and more homogeneous \hl{stated} commitment, lower and more homogenous thresholds for \hl{behavioural change, and greater potential for social tipping}. On an individual level, we also found indications that actions that are perceived to be more costly are positively associated with compensatory green beliefs. Finally, individuals exhibited a systematic ``better-than-average'' bias, though this bias disappears among low-commitment individuals facing high-cost actions. \hl{Objective environmental impact added little once cost was taken into account, although actions that participants perceived as more impactful elicited higher commitment. In terms of policy, our results suggest that low-cost actions are a promising target for norm-based interventions, whereas high-cost, high-impact actions such as reducing meat consumption call for measures that lower their personal cost.

articles.title: Early climate change coverage in news media: A comparison of East and West Germany from 1950-1978
articles.authors: Viktoria Cologna; Alexander A Kaurov; Mike S. Schäfer; Naomi Oreskes
articles.abstract: Press coverage of climate change provides a historical window into how different societies perceived climate change at a given time in a given place. For historically significant emitters such as Germany, reconstructing such news coverage provides important insights into public awareness on the issue. We present the first systematic and comparative analysis of early climate change reporting in East and West Germany between 1950 and 1978. We constructed and validated a corpus of relevant articles through keyword searches, manual screening, and large language model-assisted validation, resulting in a final sample of 122 articles, which we analyzed qualitatively. Our analysis identified four roughly chronological discursive phases: 1) observed glacier melting and the greenhouse effect hypothesis; 2) a perceived end of warming due to decreasing temperatures; 3) growing scientific consensus on human-caused climate change and model uncertainties; 4) increasing attention to the risks of climate change. Human-caused climate change was first mentioned in 1957 and then discussed more extensively in the 1960s and 70s. Despite profound ideological differences, the content and development of the four discursive phases were similar in East and West Germany. However, West German coverage focused more strongly on the impacts on future generations and renewable energy, and gave space to minority skeptical voices, whereas East German coverage focused more strongly on climate modification. This analysis sheds light on the beginnings of climate change reporting in Germany and historically contextualizes awareness of the issue in one of the countries that bears legal and ethical responsibility for addressing climate change.

articles.title: Unequal Parenting across Childhood: How Class Differences in Parental Control of Screen Use Reverse with the Child's Age
articles.authors: Abel Aussant; Andreas Roaldsnes
articles.abstract: Research usually treats class differences in parenting style as constant throughout childhood. We show instead that they can reverse with the child's age. Our case is parental control of children's screen use, for which expert advice is restrictive when children are young and divided when they are adolescents. We draw on an original survey of 20,670 Norwegian households with children aged 3 to 17 to estimate class differences in time limits, control of content and the negotiation of rules at each age. We find that better-resourced parents are stricter than others with young children, but more permissive with adolescents. The composition of the resources available to the household shapes the pattern: income and education have different, complementary associations with parental control. The observed reversal across childhood suggests that the advantage of well-resourced families in child rearing lies less in a fixed repertoire of practices than in adaptability, a capacity to adjust as the appropriate practice changes with the child's age.

articles.title: Gender and long-term trends in educational attainment, income and returns to education in Norway
articles.authors: Liza Reisel; Adrian F. Rogne; Sara Seehuus
articles.abstract: This study addresses the economic returns to education among men and women in Norway, during five decades of changing and widening gender disparities in educational attainment. We ask how gender differences in educational attainment and returns have contributed to change and persistence in the gender income gap, and whether young men have started trailing behind due to women’s relative gains in higher education. Analyses based on Norwegian register data show that while rising real incomes have contributed to a narrowing relative income gap, the absolute gap has decreased more slowly. In the past decade, both real incomes and the gender income gap have stagnated. While both men and women in Norway have increased their education levels, women’s gains have been mainly in higher education, while men’s gains have disproportionately been in vocational upper secondary education. Contrary to the situation in the US and other liberal market economies, income growth among younger cohorts of men with vocational education in Norway has recently outpaced every other group, resulting in a decreasing college premium. Women’s relative gains in higher education are partly offset by their lower incomes at all education levels, and the relatively strong income growth among men with vocational degrees.

articles.title: Are EU Kidding Me? Notes from a Poorly Drafted Social Media Ban
articles.authors: Michael Veale
articles.abstract: In September 2026, the European Commission published a proposed EU KIDS Act, responding to the demand for restrictions and further design obligations applying to digital services accessible to children, including social media. This Article argues that regardless of what one believes about the merits of this policy direction, the EU KIDS Act is not the legislative text we need. The scope and drafting are little short of chaotic, full of holes, enormous ambiguities, and unintended consequences. Recitals contradict articles. The use of scope borrowed from other pieces of legislation not designed for this purpose brings services into scope that should not be subject to the relevant provisions, like book-recommendation websites, music services, or exercise trackers. The infrastructural requirement for assurance of age and parental responsibility attestation simply omits enormous issues of complex families and childhoods. Complex design obligations are written in ways that can be plausibly interpreted as implicitly prohibiting entire swathes of products, such as voice assistants. This Article outlines these issues, and many more. The Commission should withdraw this proposal and reissue a workable and realistic text.

articles.title: Safe (felt) by design: Understanding cyclists’ needs for traffic guidance at roadworks – A mixed-methods study on behaviour, perception, and infrastructure requirements
articles.authors: Frederik Hilden; Peer-Benedikt Degen; Robin von Elm; Angela Francke
articles.abstract: Introduction: Urban construction sites frequently disrupt cycling infrastructure and create safety risks for vulnerable road users. Despite regulatory frameworks for temporary traffic management, cyclists often encounter unclear or unsafe guidance around roadworks. Empirical evidence on how cyclists actually respond to such conditions remains limited. This study investigates cyclists’ behaviour, routing decisions, and safety perceptions at urban construction sites. Method: A mixed-methods design combined behavioural observations and a nationwide survey. Observational data were collected at four construction sites in Hamburg, Germany using inductive loop sensors and video recordings, capturing 146.168 bicycle passages. Behavioural interactions were coded to identify compliance, routing choices, and conflict-avoidance strategies. In addition, a web-based survey of 1,071 cyclists across Germany examined perceived safety, behavioural adaptation, and infrastructure preferences at roadworks. Results: Observational analysis identified substantial deviations from designated traffic guidance: 42% of 790 coded cyclist interactions involved non-compliant behaviour, such as riding on sidewalks or against the intended direction. Route choice was primarily influenced by motorized traffic volume and pavement quality. Cyclists frequently selected routes that maximized perceived safety and riding comfort rather than following formal guidance. Despite frequent non-compliance, cyclists often adopted cooperative strategies, including speed reduction and conflict avoidance with pedestrians. Conclusions: The findings highlight a gap between formally regulated traffic guidance and cyclists’ safety perceptions and behaviour. Temporary infrastructure that lacks clarity, comfort, or protection can lead to widespread deviations from prescribed routes. Practical applications: Temporary traffic management at construction sites should prioritize intuitive guidance, surface quality, and physical separation from motorized traffic. Incorporating cyclist needs into roadwork design can reduce conflicts and improve safety for vulnerable road users.

articles.title: Creationism as a Mediating Construct Between Religiosity, Scientific Epistemology, and Science Attitudes: A Secondary Analysis of the Science Attitudes Dataset
articles.authors: Christopher Ryan Deraney
articles.abstract:
Since publication of the original analyses in Ideological Mosaic: Examining Political and Religious
Factors in Science Attitudes (Deraney & Ault, 2025), a secondary exploratory reanalysis of the original
dataset using additional statistical procedures and a revised conceptualization of the Evolutionary
Attitudes and Literacy Survey, EALS, (Short & Hawley, 2012). The purpose of this reanalysis was not to
replace the original findings, but rather to investigate whether the EALS contained multiple theoretically
distinct constructs that were obscured by the original composite score (Deraney & Ault, 2025).
Keywords: Science Attitudes, Conservatism, Ideology, Religiosity, Scientific Epistemology, Young-
Earth Creation, and Politics.

articles.title: Extractive conditionality: Participation and datafication in the Netherlands
articles.authors: Marijke Roosen
articles.abstract: Research on welfare conditionality has shown how access to social assistance is tied to behavioural and informational obligations. It has paid less attention to what recipients’ compliance produces for welfare institutions. This article develops the concept of extractive conditionality to describe arrangements in which activities and information provided under conditions of material dependency are transformed into institutionally usable resources. Drawing on an interpretive case study of Dutch social assistance, the analysis combines autobiographical testimony with policy documents, official evaluations and investigative journalism. It identifies two dimensions of extraction. First, activation requirements mobilise recipients’ time and activity even when they do not facilitate durable labour-market exit. Second, disclosure requirements generate information that can be standardised and reused for purposes such as organisational oversight and risk classification. These processes are extractive when recipients have little control over how their compelled contributions are subsequently used. The article further develops the hypothesis that this institutional productivity may help reproduce conditional arrangements despite their limited success in reducing welfare dependency. It shows how policies may fail to achieve their stated objectives while continuing to generate organisational capacities. The concept redirects analysis from what conditionality demands towards what compliance produces, who can use these outputs and how they may contribute to the persistence of conditional welfare.

articles.title: The Digital Undertow of Penal Supervision: An Ethnography of Electronic Monitoring in Belgium
articles.authors: Marijke Roosen
articles.abstract: Electronic monitoring (EM) relies on digital systems to supervise people in the community, but these systems also organise the work of monitoring officers. This article examines how digital monitoring systems shape officers’ everyday work and decisions, and how these practices give meaning to penal supervision. It draws on 74 days of observation and 22 interviews with control-room officers in Belgium, conducted between 2014 and 2017. Using a strong sociomaterial perspective and the concept of the digital undertow, the analysis connects three aspects of supervision: the recording and potential scrutiny of officers’ activities, their assessments of monitored individuals, and their emphasis on rule-following. The findings show how telephone exchanges, software records and organisational expectations together shape what requires attention, and which responses count as responsible work. Officers interpret compliance as preparation for reintegration, while accurate and traceable actions become ways of demonstrating professional responsibility. These practices involve judgement and negotiation, even when officers describe their decisions as required by rules. The article contributes to research on digital penal work by showing how the practical organisation of information connects assessments of monitored individuals to standards of professional competence. It identifies processes through which institutional values acquire meaning in everyday supervision.

articles.title: Issue Accountability Among Public Meeting Commenters
articles.authors: Alexander Sahn; Tyler Simko
articles.abstract: Standard theories of accountability suggest politicians respond to voter preferences for fear of electoral sanction, yet many voters are ill-informed about policy actions. One solution to this tension is that a small group of highly engaged citizens, an issue public, may generate the conditions for accountability. We test this claim by tracking over 7,000 members of the public who submit comments on land use policies in San Francisco, CA. We measure commenters’ expressed preferences on proposed agenda items, survey them following the decision, and observe subsequent political activity with administrative data. We show that over three-quarters of commenters accurately recall their past positions, but most do not learn the subsequent policy action and rarely update their political attitudes. However, we find that a subset of anti-development voters are more likely to contribute to ideologically aligned candidates when they do not see their preferred policies enacted; yet pro-development commenters do not.

articles.title: Digital Doubles: How does AI-generated imagery affect human engagement with biodiversity conservation?
articles.authors: Maya Mukherjee; Diogo Veríssimo; Amy Hinsley
articles.abstract:
1.	Wildlife images created by generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools are rapidly growing in quantity and sophistication. Viewing these AI images could influence how people perceive and understand the real natural world, affecting their reactions to real wildlife imagery and potentially in direct wildlife interactions. 
2.	In this study, we look at how people donate money for conservation purposes to real and AI-generated birds, as well as whether they can accurately discriminate between images in these categories. We further investigate how participant moderating factors and perceived artificiality (i.e. how much an image looks AI-generated) affect these outcomes. 
3.	Using the contingent valuation method to assess willingness-to-donate, we found that participants award AI-generated and real bird images donation amounts that are not statistically discernible. However, greater perceived artificiality of an image was associated with higher donation amounts. No demographic factors significantly influenced donation behaviour.
4.	We also found that participants were able to correctly identify AI vs real images. A nature relatedness score measuring how connected participants were to nature being the only factor to positively predict ability to accurately choose between real and AI images. 
5.	These findings indicate the potential risk of AI-generated imagery replacing real nature imagery and experience, with artificial representations of wildlife being valued equally to real biodiversity. Conservationists must focus on promoting nature relatedness and real-life, direct nature experiences to combat AI-generated misinformation and decreased understanding of ecological realities.

articles.title: The Subnational Fertility Transition in Italy (1871-1971): A Century of Fundamental Change
articles.authors: Riccardo Omenti; Nicola Barban; Michail Raftakis
articles.abstract: The Italian fertility transition has drawn sustained interest from historical demographers, thanks to rich archival sources, especially parish records, and a well-established scholarly tradition. Yet no study has offered a comprehensive account of how the transition unfolded subnationally across the second half of the nineteenth and first half of the twentieth centuries. Drawing on extensive yet underutilised data from the Italian National Institute of Statistics (ISTAT), we present annual total fertility rate (TFR) estimates for all Italian provinces covering the historical period 1871–1971, using an established Bayesian modelling framework. Combining convergence analysis with measures of relative dispersion and variability, we examine whether provincial fertility differences widened or narrowed over the transition. We further investigate urban-rural fertility trajectories within Italy’s nine most populous provinces. The results reveal a geographically uneven transition: northern and central provinces led the fertility decline, while southern provinces lagged behind, resulting in divergence across provinces. Nonetheless, urban–rural differences narrowed substantially in northern and central provinces and remained negligible in southern provinces. These findings underscore the spatial heterogeneity of Italy’s fertility transition, displaying the co-existence of increasing provincial disparities with diminishing urban-rural differences in the areas leading the fertility decline.

articles.title: Where Silicon Samples Go Wrong: Item-Level Coefficient Distortion in LLM-Simulated Chinese Public Opinion
articles.authors: Mingkun Cui; Shenghao Xiong
articles.abstract: Do regressions fitted to survey responses simulated by large language models return the coefficients human data would? We used four 2026 models to generate responses to the full attitude-item bank of two Chinese General Social Survey waves, conditioning on 1,000 respondents’ demographic profiles per wave and requesting each person’s most likely answer. For 10 items analyzed in both waves, we compared human and simulated coefficients on the human-anchored scale, with Holm adjustment across 240 tests. The 28 supported differences concentrate in three patterns: an inflated income gradient in perceived fairness, an urban–rural gradient in premarital-sex morality where the human coefficient is near zero, and an overstated sex difference in gender-ability beliefs. Marginal fit does not locate these distortions. Standardizing each source by its own standard deviation changes 33 test decisions, showing why regression validation requires a declared outcome scale.

articles.title: The Grumpy Meme and Irritability Ecology: How Low-Intensity Negative Affect Spreads, Survives, Sediments, and Becomes a Workplace Climate
articles.authors: Koichi Hiraoka
articles.abstract:
Research on negative affect in organizations has largely focused on relatively visible phenomena such as anger, aggression, abusive supervision, workplace bullying, and incivility. Yet much of everyday organizational life unfolds between overt anger episodes, when no one is shouting but employees still monitor facial expressions, short replies, sighs, silence, or reduced responsiveness and conclude that someone appears grumpy. Such low-intensity signals may alter whether people approach, speak, seek advice, or share information. To theorize this domain, this paper distinguishes Irritability, Grumpiness, and the Grumpy Meme, and introduces Irritability Ecology as an integrative framework.
Irritability refers to a relatively low-intensity internal affective state that need not be externally expressed. Grumpiness refers to socially perceivable expressions through which others infer that a person appears to be in a bad mood. The Grumpy Meme refers to a socio-affective transmission process in which perceived grumpiness alters another person’s affect or behavior and is subsequently re-expressed in another interaction. Thus, irritability may exist without observable grumpiness, while perceived grumpiness does not necessarily demonstrate underlying irritability.
The paper argues that low-intensity negative affect may survive in workplaces because it is inexpensive to express, highly repeatable, difficult to sanction, and often protected by ambiguity regarding both the event and the actor’s intention. Repeated expressions may accumulate through Affective Sedimentation, creating background vigilance, mood-reading, and eventually a workplace climate. A two-axis model of anger and irritability is proposed, yielding four affective climate types: Calm–Stable, Quiet Tension, Eruption–Recovery, and Pervasive Anger–Irritability. The paper further introduces Affective Non-Transmission as the capacity to experience negative affect without automatically transferring it to others, and connects this capacity to post-conflict relational repair.
Irritability Ecology is therefore not a weaker version of Anger Ecology. Whereas Anger Ecology examines the visible fire of workplace affect, Irritability Ecology examines the ambient climate that persists between fires. The framework shifts attention from identifying “grumpy people” to examining how low-intensity negative affect is expressed, transmitted, sustained, sedimented, interrupted, and repaired within organizational environments.

articles.title: The sociolinguistic labor of incarcerated people
articles.authors: Gabriella Licata; Robert Tyler; Mesro Coles; Anthony Habib Watkins; Brian Asey Gonsoulin
articles.abstract: Through participatory action research, we draw on interviews with 40 incarcerated students to examine how linguistic practices are shaped by institutional power in carceral environments. We argue that the magnitude of surveillance under incarceration produces sociolinguistic labor: the effortful management of one’s communicative repertoire. Our analysis identifies a distinctive form of dual-direction sociolinguistic labor, whereby incarcerated individuals are required to extend their repertoires both toward stigmatized vernaculars to gain social capital and toward hyperstandardized registers for institutional capital. We examine this dynamic across educational, social, and procedural domains, with particular attention to boardspeak—an emotionally-constrained, bureaucratic register through which rehabilitation is performed and assessed at a Board of Parole hearing. By situating these practices within broader critical linguistic theories and perspectives, we show incarcerated people self-surveil and create, prompting varying levels of sociolinguistic labor and innovation that are mediated by race, ethnicity, ability, socioeconomic class, and in-group membership. These findings demonstrate how high-stakes, surveilled environments intensify the stakes of language use and reshape the boundaries of communicative agency.

articles.title: Exploring Nonlinear Associations Between AI Comment Volume and Retail Investor Sentiment
articles.authors: Yuze Tang
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence comment generators have proliferated in online stock forums. However, how AI comment volume associates with retail investor sentiment, and whether this association is conditional on market volatility and annual AI comment density, remain under-explored. Using weekly data from the East Money Stock Forum and the Shanghai Composite Index spanning May 2019–October 2024 in China, this paper proposed a two-detector ensemble for AI comment detection, then investigated nonlinear associations between AI comment volume and retail investor sentiment under three tiers of market volatility and six annual AI comment densities. Our generalized additive model (GAM) results show that AI comment volume exhibits a weak, net-positive nonlinear association with mean retail investor sentiment, and a very weak net-negative nonlinear association with sentiment divergence. We find no statistically significant pairwise differences in these associations across low-, medium- and high-volatility levels. For annual AI comment density, statistically significant cross-density differences are observed for sentiment standard deviation in multiple year pairwise comparisons, whereas only one comparison yields significant differences for mean sentiment. Collectively, our findings indicate that merely considering the number of AI comments provides limited information regarding the sentiment of retail investors.

articles.title: Who Manufactured Pseudo-History Theories? The Emergent Collective Creation of Historical Narratives on the Chinese Internet
articles.authors: ZY Liu; Di Yuan
articles.abstract: This paper examines the formation, expansion, and functions of pseudo-history theories (伪史论) on the Chinese internet from the perspective of cultural economics, and proposes the analytical concept of “Emergent Collective Creation.” This concept refers to the process whereby a large number of relatively independent content producers, acting on the basis of their respective local motivations and in the absence of any unified overall plan, generate a collective narrative system that exceeds the original planning and control of any single participant through imitation, competition, the recombination of arguments, and the migration of topics. The paper first investigates relevant figures who possess formal academic credentials or publishing experience and analyzes the pathways through which early pseudo-history resources entered public circulation. It then takes as examples the extension of pseudo-history theories from ancient Greece and Rome to other civilizations, historical figures, and issues concerning Chinese dynastic history, exploring how competition for traffic, content imitation, and the selective recombination of historical materials drive narrative expansion. Finally, using online controversies surrounding the film The Penghu Naval Battle as a case study, it analyzes how pseudo-history theories have been deployed by different participants in conflicts over historical identity and in online opinion confrontation, and discusses possible links between controversial historical discourses and public trust in academic authority. The paper argues that even dispersed individual actions lacking unified coordination may, through indirect interaction, produce collective narrative outcomes and enable pseudo-history theories to move from a form of content competition for traffic into ideological contention. Because this study relies primarily on publicly available online materials, publications, and media reports, and lacks internal platform data as well as continuous records at the creator level, the mechanisms identified remain exploratory explanations whose chains of transmission, causal relations, and actual effects await further verification.

articles.title: Are Women Comedians Less Funny?: Empirical Analysis of Gender Differences in 1-on-1 Competitive Comedy
articles.authors: Yuhei Yamaguchi
articles.abstract:
"Is there a difference in funniness between men and women?'" This study addresses this question. The perception that "women are less funny than men" is widespread, and some studies have indeed shown that men have a better sense of humor. In addition, in industries dominated by men, the presence of women tends to be relatively low. In the comedy industry, where men make up the overwhelming majority, women comedians are thus exposed to a double stereotype of this kind. We examined whether, under such a double stereotype, women comedians are able to be as funny as men comedians. We collected and analyzed data on a total of 3,925 matchups from a television program in which comedians compete directly over funniness in one-on-one contests. The results showed that, although a simple statistical model makes men comedians appear funnier, an analysis using a model that accounts for individual funniness revealed no significant difference in funniness between men and women.
Although concerns remain about the generalizability of the findings, the results call into question existing research on gender differences in sense of humor, as well as the associated stereotypes.

articles.title: A Sociolinguistic Inquiry into Vietnamese Swearing: Regional Variation and Cross-Cultural Parallels
articles.authors: Hàng Hỷ Vinh
articles.abstract: This exploratory, pilot-scale study investigates the Vietnamese swearing construction built from an obscene verb, a kinship term and a second-person pronoun (địt mẹ mày, đụ má mày 'fuck your mother', mả cha mi 'your father's grave') through two questions: how kin-directed swearing differs across regions and which part of the construction reveals the speaker's region (RQ1); and why Vietnamese swearing targets kin and women, viewed against the full repertoire of swearing themes in Vietnamese and neighbouring languages (RQ2). It combines eight Vietnamese dictionaries (1651–2021) and comparative dictionaries of Mường, Cham, Teochew and Cantonese with an online convenience-sample survey of 50 young speakers across four regions, a small Quốc ngữ prose corpus, and a thematic comparison with ten other language communities. For RQ1, the dictionaries show no regional boundary in the verb before 1931, whereas the survey finds a clear North/South split in both the verb and the word for "mother"; regional information is asymmetric, with Southern and Central forms acting as strong markers while standard-compatible forms (địt, mẹ) and online abbreviations (đm, vkl) spread across all regions. For RQ2, sex and kin dominate the free lists; the mother-directed sexual formula occurs in Vietnamese, Chinese, Thai, Hindi and English but is absent from Japanese, so it cannot be attributed to Confucian heritage alone. Kin-directed swearing is rated more offensive than self-directed swearing and triggers more active responses; swears that deny the hearer's descent (đồ con hoang, cả họ nhà mày) are the heaviest and the least mitigated among friends. Young respondents name affection for kin, not family face, as the main reason; we read this as a contemporary synchronic reinterpretation of templates whose diachronic origin lies in honour-based lineage norms. Taken together, the target of kin-directed swearing is the hearer's legitimate standing within the lineage. Results describe young, internet-using speakers and should be read as hypothesis-generating.

articles.title: Who Does Prevention Reach? Psychosocial Risk Assessment under Brazil’s Regulatory Standard 1 (NR-1)
articles.authors: Iara Teixeira
articles.abstract: Employers who assess psychosocial hazards can report an improved workplace average while some workers become more exposed. Brazil's Regulatory Standard 1 has required employers to manage work-related psychosocial risk factors since May 2026, and employers are now producing their first inventories. The standard already requires them to identify exposed groups, involve workers, and monitor preventive measures. International guidance supports subgroup analysis but says less about how to verify whom a preventive measure reached. Drawing on regulatory documents and research on organizational inequality and workplace interventions, this policy analysis proposes a record that links exposure evidence to the working condition an employer decides to change, the workers each measure reaches, and the distribution of subsequent change. The record also addresses uncertainty, measurement comparability, confidentiality, and workforce turnover. Regulators and employers in countries that mandate psychosocial risk assessment can judge prevention by the overall reduction in exposure and by its distribution.

articles.title: Impact of Social Media Platforms on Youth: An Anthropological Study
articles.authors: Sivakumar A
articles.abstract:
Social media has become a ubiquitous sociocultural phenomenon, transforming how young people communicate, socialize, and construct identities. This anthropological study examines social media use among young people aged 18–25 in urban and semi-urban areas of Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu, South India. It explores usage patterns, self-identity expression, maintenance of social relationships, digital literacy, and the influence of gender, education, and socioeconomic background on digital participation. It also considers how young people perceive social media’s everyday effects on their social and cultural lives.

A mixed-methods design was adopted. Quantitative data were collected through a questionnaire administered to 60 youth respondents, while semi-structured interviews were conducted with 10 participants. The questionnaire demonstrated high overall reliability (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.91), and its individual scales showed acceptable to high reliability. Content validity was reviewed by experts, while exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses were used to assess construct validity. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests of independence; qualitative data were analyzed thematically using NVivo.

Findings indicate that social media is embedded in young people’s everyday lives: 73.3% reported using platforms more than once daily. WhatsApp (93.3%), Instagram (88.3%), and YouTube (81.7%) were the most widely used platforms. Entertainment (90.0%) and maintaining contact with friends (85.0%) were the leading purposes, followed by information seeking (63.3%) and identity expression (35.0%). Digital literacy levels were low for 23.3% of respondents, medium for 48.3%, and high for 28.3%. Differences were particularly evident in advanced skills, including evaluating information and managing privacy.

Hypothesis testing found significant associations between digital literacy and frequency of use (p = 0.048; Cramér’s V = 0.324), digital literacy and platform diversity (p = 0.047; Cramér’s V = 0.283), gender and identity expression (p = 0.037; Cramér’s V = 0.331), and gender and platform choice (p = 0.041; Cramér’s V = 0.326). Other hypothesized relationships were not statistically significant. The qualitative analysis identified five themes: curated identity performance, digital kinship and connectivity, stratified digital competencies, gendered digital surveillance, and ambivalent impression perceptions.

The study contributes to digital anthropology by illustrating how global platforms are locally adopted in South Indian contexts, how social relationships are sustained in digital spaces, and how digital literacy may function as cultural capital. It offers recommendations for educators, parents, policymakers, platform designers, and young people to promote more equitable and beneficial digital participation.

articles.title: A preference for long-distance friendships, even in the absence of those friendships, can foster collective action
articles.authors: Kristopher M Smith; Anne Pisor; Bertha Aron; Kasambo Bernard; Paschal Fimbo; Rose Kimesera; Monique Borgerhoff Mulder
articles.abstract: Long-distance friendships can build interdependence and trust, which can foster collective action across distance around shared goals. However, social norms, resource availability, and limited time can prevent the formation of long-distance friendships. Here, we examine whether simply having a preference to form long-distance friendships – independent of having those friendships themselves – is associated with participation in collective action across distance. We call this preference long-distance orientation (LDO). We developed an initial measure of LDO through ethnographic research in Tanzanian fishing communities and refinement in two online US samples (n = 200, n = 300) before deploying it in a larger study of coastal Tanzanian communities. In Tanzania (n = 777), we examined associations among LDO, long-distance friendships, long-distance trust, and participation in fisheries management, where management requires collective action across communities. People with greater LDO had greater participation independently of long-distance friendships and trust, while also having greater long-distance friendships and trust. Long-distance friendships and trust were independently associated with greater participation in fisheries management. These findings suggest multiple, potentially overlapping pathways linking long-distance sociality to collective action: (1) preferences for forming relationships, (2) realized relationships, and (3) trust in people living elsewhere. LDO therefore shows promise as a construct for understanding variation in long-distance sociality and cooperation, but further measurement refinement and cross-cultural research are needed to establish its nature and scope.

articles.title: Instrument Revision and False Change in Repeated Surveys: A Typology and Diagnostic Protocol for Secondary Users
articles.authors: Iara Teixeira
articles.abstract: Repeated surveys revise their instruments between rounds and document each revision item by item. Such documentation records what changed but not what the change does to a trend, so secondary users can mistake an instrument effect for change in the population. This article proposes a typology that classifies revisions by their consequence for the information in the released data (removal, redistribution, stimulus change, and misidentification), links each type to its identification status and remedy, and puts it into practice through a five-step diagnostic protocol: comparing source instruments, screening against a reference distribution of unmodified trend items, classifying the revision, choosing an estimand, and auditing metadata. Applied to the 2024 European Working Conditions Survey, the protocol shows that a filter and a self-labeling question placed before the discrimination battery leave the 2015 to 2024 contrast identified only as a lower bound; six of seven grounds fell below every unmodified reference item, and the observed decline would be real only if the new instrument retained more than 60 percent of reports. A new cyberbullying item redistributed reports from the adjacent bullying item, and the data bound the comparable change between odds ratios of 0.75 and 0.98. Changes in item order and response coding left a pace-of-work battery unresolved, while a minor stem change produced no detectable break. The metadata audit found nine variables labeled with the stem of a different question, in both data editions, and a harmonized trend variable that omits one of the two items its label combines. Comparability should be established from the source instruments and the released data before substantive analysis begins.

articles.title: Visual Resistance Assemblages: Recurring Multimodal Configurations in Kenya’s Gen Z Finance Bill Protests
articles.authors: Castro Chebukosi
articles.abstract: Social-media protest communication is increasingly multimodal, combining language, imagery, typography, sound, performance and platform-specific features. While existing research has demonstrated how such resources produce meaning within individual artefacts and genres, comparatively less attention has been given to how functionally related multimodal configurations recur across heterogeneous artefacts within the same protest corpus. This study addresses this corpus-level problem through a qualitative multimodal analysis of 72 protest artefacts published or circulated on X during Kenya’s June–July 2024 Finance Bill protests, analysed through multimodal social semiotics and cross-artefact comparison. The analysis identifies five recurring configurations: Constitutional Legitimation, Distributed Agency, Comparative Fiscal Information Design, Visual Witnessing and Collective Identity, and Satirical Recontextualization. These configurations are not treated as mutually exclusive artefact categories; rather, they represent recurring relationships among heterogeneous semiotic resources that retain comparable communicative functions despite variation in genre and surface realisation. The study proposes the concept of Visual Resistance Assemblages (VRA) as a descriptive analytical unit for identifying such corpus-level recurrence. The findings demonstrate how constitutional discourse, distributed participation, comparative fiscal reasoning, collective representation and satirical recontextualisation were organised through heterogeneous multimodal resources. VRA complements existing multimodal, assemblage-oriented and digital activism approaches by shifting attention from multimodality within individual artefacts to recurring multimodal organisation across protest corpora.

articles.title: The Emotional Meaning and Sociocultural Implications of 'Eojunggan-hada' in Korean Society: An Exploratory Study
articles.authors: Heeju Lee
articles.abstract: This study explores how the Korean expression 'eojunggan-hada' (being in-between) extends beyond simple linguistic ambiguity to reflect issues of personal identity and social belonging. Unlike previous Korean linguistics research that focused on linguistic ambiguity and mitigation expressions, this study defines 'eojunggan-hada' as a way of being positioned at the boundaries of identity and belonging, analyzing its sociocultural implications. A survey of 111 respondents revealed that participants frequently experience being in-between in daily life (mean 3.44), perceiving it more as a product of social structural conditions (mean 3.46) rather than personal character traits (mean 3.22). Notably, daily experience of in-betweenness showed a strong positive correlation with attributing it to one's personality (r = .64, p < .001), suggesting that the more frequently people feel in-between, the more they blame their own character for it. Qualitative analysis of open-ended responses confirmed that being in-between functions simultaneously as discomfort and survival strategy. This study conceptualizes 'eojunggan-hada' as a boundary emotion formed within Korea's unique collectivist culture and relational pressures, proposing that it represents not individual indecisiveness but rather a way of existence created by social structures.

articles.title: Manufactured Desire： How Social Media and Influencer Agencies Sexualise and Monetise Pregnant Influencers
articles.authors: Yuting Qin
articles.abstract: This article examines how pregnant influencers on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, are sexualised and monetised through the interlocking practices of the platform, influencer agencies and influencers themselves. Taking the 2024 controversy around the appearance influencer YīLìXiǎoShāZi and the # 孕妇摇 (Pregnancy Swing Dance) challenge as its point of departure, the study combines visual analysis of top-ranked Douyin posts, in-depth interviews with an influencer, an influencer agency employee and a platform employee, and sentiment analysis of 4,874 user comments. This article interprets platform monetisation structures and influencer agency production routines as organising influencers’ embodied labour into standardised production roles and measurable commercial attributes. It proposes the “factory of desire” as a framework for understanding how platforms, influencer agencies and influencers mutually enable and constrain the commodification of pregnant bodies. Interviewees described unwritten rules through which sexualised content can remain visible under mainland China's restrictions on pornography: perceived emphasis on skin exposure in automated moderation, a grey zone known as 擦边 (cābiān, "skirting the boundary"), and appeals framed around "pregnancy beauty". The analysis suggests that these commercial and regulatory conditions can encourage pregnant influencers to reproduce porn chic conventions, while constraining their subsequent commercial options. Within the sampled comments on videos criticising the sexualisation of pregnancy, disgust had the highest average model score; these findings describe this selected discussion rather than public opinion as a whole.

articles.title: Generalised Conversational Implicature in Kenyan Generation Z Digital Protest Discourse: Q-, I-, and M-Heuristics in the 2024 Finance Bill Protests on X
articles.authors: Castro Chebukosi; Bernard Kodak; Jane Ombati
articles.abstract: The June–July 2024 Finance Bill protests in Kenya produced a distinctive corpus of digitally mediated political communication in which Gen Z-associated protesters on X (formerly Twitter) relied on omission, shared background knowledge and stylistic markedness to construct political meaning beyond the literal content of their posts. This study examines how such strategies generated Generalised Conversational Implicature (GCI), applying Levinson’s (2000) Q-, I-, and M-heuristic framework to a purposively sampled corpus of 72 protest artefacts retrieved from X in June 2026. Using thematic and pragmatic coding, the analysis shows that condensed slogans, mobilisation language and constitutional citation generated Q-heuristic implicatures through informational economy; shared political, cultural and generational knowledge generated I-heuristic implicatures; and marked linguistic, visual and performative choices generated M-heuristic implicatures, extending Levinson’s lexical account of markedness into a multimodal register. The three heuristics frequently layered within single artefacts, and thematic coding further revealed six protest-specific inferential patterns beyond Levinson’s original typology: anti-co-optation, constitutional-sovereignty, trauma-memory, care-based, data-activism and digital-network patterns. The study demonstrates how GCI analysis can be extended to fast-paced, multimodal, digitally networked political communication when its categories are made explicit and their limits are clearly bounded.

articles.title: Watchdog Capture and the Social Licensing of Child Harm: A Case Study of Common Sense Media and OpenAI
articles.authors: Travis Gilly
articles.abstract:
This paper examines a structural failure mode in the validation chain that legitimizes consumer artificial
intelligence products marketed to or used by minors: a child safety advocacy organization that arrives at
each crisis after journalists and litigants have already exposed it, or plays the harm down when it arrives
first, and that enters endorsement, development, and funding relationships with the firm whose product
produced the harm. It documents a twenty-three year response pattern at Common Sense Media (CSM),
a United States based organization that reports reaching more than 150 million users and 1.4 million
educators worldwide each year, across three crisis cycles: YouTube Kids during the Elsagate incidents
of 2017, video game loot boxes between 2017 and 2019, and generative artificial intelligence chatbots
between 2023 and 2026. The paper situates the pattern within Carpenter and Moss’s (2014) account of
corrosive capture, regulatory intermediary theory, and the social license literature. It argues that CSM’s
September 2025 endorsement of OpenAI’s parental controls as “a good starting point,” controls that
contemporaneous reporting described as developed by OpenAI with CSM, and CSM’s January 2026
ballot measure merger with OpenAI, which dropped provisions from CSM’s original ballot initiative that
had tracked its vetoed bill, together constitute a transfer of social license rather than a substantive safety
remedy. It then examines the October 2026 risk assessment in which CSM’s Youth AI Safety Institute,
funded in part by the OpenAI Foundation, rated ChatGPT for Teens an Unacceptable Risk on the strength
of a parental notification mechanism that CSM had helped develop and had endorsed at launch. CSM’s
own October 2025 review had already tested that mechanism, recorded parental alerts arriving more than
twenty-four hours after a tester discussed suicide, and recorded the account bypass, yet described the
product as meaningful progress and kept it rated for teens thirteen and up for a further 349 days. Archived
copies of CSM’s ChatGPT rating page show that the product carried a thirteen and up label from October
2023 and a Moderate risk rating from August 2024 through at least September 2025, so that the rating
available to parents on the day a sixteen year old user died after extended use of ChatGPT was Moderate.
The October 2026 findings were authored for the public by the former newspaper columnist who had
documented the bypass three days after launch, without reference to that earlier reporting. The paper
proposes public record indicators for detecting watchdog capture in other consumer safety intermediaries.

articles.title: Rails, Risks, and Resilience: A Dynamic Spatial Equilibrium Analysis with Catastrophic Natural Disaster Risk
articles.authors: Daisuke Adachi
articles.abstract: We develop a dynamic stochastic spatial model in which catastrophic disasters temporarily reduce regional productivity and disrupt the transportation network, applied to Japan's Tokai Trough Earthquake (TTE) risk and the Chuo Shinkansen (CS) maglev train project. Productivity-recovery and network-disruption are estimated on the 2011 Tohoku Earthquake, and the model qualitatively reproduces the observed slow population decline and wage overshoot in the affected regions. The population-weighted welfare cost of TTE risk is 4.96\% of permanent consumption, of which 97\% flows through the migration option-value channel, representing a spatial-spillover mechanism where even far-epicenter zones lose welfare because their fallback destinations also become riskier. As the CS plays a role as insurance against transport-network disruption, it delivers welfare gains of 0.83\% under TTE risk versus 0.63\% in the risk-free benchmark, resulting in a 0.19 percentage-point redundancy premium. Overall, our framework extends dynamic spatial analysis beyond perfect-foresight counterfactuals to reveal spatial welfare spillovers and a redundancy value of infrastructure under catastrophic risk.

articles.title: Partial Exit and Bargaining Power: How Exit Menus Shape Institutional Design
articles.authors: Chendi Wang
articles.abstract: A government can often refuse a collective undertaking in more than one way. It may leave the organization, stay out of one initiative, withhold a contribution or block one legal route. I extend exit, voice and loyalty to such exit menus. The refusal a government would actually choose fixes both its own fallback and the others' cost of disagreement. A narrower exit can therefore activate leverage or displace a threat that had secured accommodation. Others who still want the government inside can pay it, restrict common uses or change the scale of provision, and relative marginal costs shape which margin adjusts. Accommodation need not benefit its recipient. When what refusal yields depends on the capacity on offer, an improved alternative can lead the others to build less and leave a retained government worse off despite larger payments. Euro-area rescue finance documents decision-specific refusal rules, rejected protections and reciprocal conditions.

articles.title: Silicon Ethics: Comparing the Dynamics of Human and LLM Responses to Ethical Dilemmas
articles.authors: W. Russell Neuman
articles.abstract: A key element in alignment research is commonly captured by the phrase “alignment with human values.” Human ethical judgment, however, is plural, unstable, affectively charged, socially embedded, and often justified after the fact. This article proposes a systematic comparative methodology emphasizing the potential complementarity of how human and silicon ethics may differ.   Drawing on literature of moral psychology, it identifies five dynamics of human ethical judgment systematically comparing them with their functional analogues in generative models. The goal is not to anthropomorphize LLMs or treat human judgment as a gold standard, but to compare the latent structures of the dynamics in vivo and in silico. The article argues that such comparison can extend alignment research beyond mimetic reproduction of human preferences toward compensatory intelligence: AI systems that help humans notice neglected consequences, test consistency, consider alternative moral frames, and deliberate more responsibly about their own commitments.

articles.title: El mundo según Polymarket: control del futuro en mercados de eventos
articles.authors: Aldo Mascareño; Fabian Belmar; Juan Rozas
articles.abstract: Los mercados de eventos o mercados de predicción como Polymarket han irrumpido en la escena global bajo la estructura de contratos derivativos de mercados financieros digitales; más allá del dinero, han expandido la lógica financiera hacia eventos principalmente geopolíticos sobre cuya realización cualquier ciudadano puede adquirir acciones y algún nivel de supervisión. Por medio de una amplia investigación bibliográfica y de fuentes primarias, en este artículo argumentamos que la frontera de aceptabilidad de las apuestas se ha desplazado en décadas recientes desde el casino online a apuestas deportivas y eventos geopolíticos socialmente generalizadas. Este desplazamiento cumple la función específica de aportar a los participantes un control de incertidumbre mediante la reducción de un futuro indeterminado a un presente observable a través de las trayectorias de las apuestas y su dinámica en vivo. El futuro se convierte en un presente proyectable de corto plazo. Los análisis muestran que este control de futuro resulta particularmente atractivo para nuevas comunidades especulativas compuestas mayoritariamente por jóvenes. Ellas combinan sociabilidad online y offline, expresan opiniones sobre el mundo a través de sus apuestas y movilizan acciones simbólicas y materiales en plataformas algorítmicas. Los riesgos asociados son múltiples; van desde el clásico insider trading hasta el insider agency, esto es, actores que apuestan sobre eventos en los que ellos mismos intervienen. El artículo concluye que el escenario general es el de una frontera aún difusa entre ilegalidad y operación regular. En ello, la legislación chilena sobre casas de apuestas deportivas, una vez que sea aprobada por el Congreso, quedará obsoleta en relación con la frontera que ya han movido los mercados de eventos.

articles.title: Similar disruptions, different reactions? Refugee crises and the politicization of immigration in Sweden and Switzerland
articles.authors: Marco Bitschnau; Didier Ruedin; Anders Hellström; Marie Sundström
articles.abstract: We investigate how major refugee crises affected the immigration debate in Sweden and Switzerland, two countries that have long been among the most popular European destinations for immigrants in general and refugees in particular. Analysing claims from newspapers during two crises, the Balkans refugee crisis of the 1990s and the European refugee crisis of 2015–16 (N=3,593), we find (1) fairly diverse patterns of politicization, with slightly greater polarization in Switzerland but higher salience peaks in Sweden; (2) no significant differences in how actors position themselves in relation to the status quo; and (3) substantial differences in how they use certain frames. We conclude that despite their proximity to immigration matters, refugee crises do not always lead to more politicized debates. There may be some crisis impact—but certainly no reason for crisis determinism. Instead, factors such as the domestic context and the relative shock value of each crisis appear to be relevant and should be given more consideration.

articles.title: Group Affect and the Electoral Protection of Transgender Rights
articles.authors: Sophie Mainz; Michal Grahn
articles.abstract: When does positive affect for a minority group translate into electoral protection for its rights? We examine this question for trans rights, which are being rolled back in many democracies. We ran a pre-registered experiment with 1,500 British adults in May 2025, weeks after the UK Supreme Court restricted the legal definition of `woman' to biological sex. Respondents chose between candidates from their preferred party who either endorsed or opposed the Supreme Court ruling, alongside other traits. We find a preference for candidates who endorse trans rights retrenchment that transcends much of the left-right divide. Crucially, although warm feelings toward trans people are twice as common as cold ones, cold affect translates more readily and more strongly into candidate choice. This asymmetry produces an overall electoral advantage for candidates endorsing trans rights retrenchment, with only those holding the warmest feelings toward trans people preferring candidates who oppose the ruling.

articles.title: Solidarity at War: The Quest for the Decolonial Subject in Russian Feminism
articles.authors: Leandra Bias
articles.abstract:
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine a new debate in transnational feminism
and feminist security studies has framed decolonisation as a precondition for solidarity.
This discussion has primarily focused on relations between Western and Ukrainian and
