Central and Eastern European feminists, leaving Russian feminism largely unexamined.
This article thus asks whether and to what extent these decolonial debates have
travelled to Russia by analysing the Feminist Anti-War Resistance (FAR). Drawing on a
content analysis of FAR’s Telegram channel and its self-published newspaper the article
shows that while FAR has an awareness of decolonial critiques, the engagement remains
limited in breadth and direction. References to decolonisation and imperialism are
marginal, concentrated in the early months of the full-scale invasion, and inwardlooking,
focusing on internal hierarchies within the Russian Federation while eclipsing
Ukraine. The article concludes with an assessment of the implications for future crossborder
solidarity between Russian and Ukrainian feminists.

articles.title: Digital capacity in Brazilian municipalities: fiscal autonomy, bureaucratic structure and heterogeneity
articles.authors: Yago Paiva; Lizandro Lui
articles.abstract: Over the past decades, digital transformation has become a central aspect of state modernization. In this article, we treat this process as a form of state capacity building — specifically, of the digital capacity of the state. Our aim is to assess whether, at the municipal level, fiscal capacity and bureaucratic quality account for higher levels of digital capacity. To this end, we adapt to the municipal context a concept originally formulated for national states and construct the Municipal Digital Capacity Index (ICDM), a novel and comprehensive measure built from the seven waves of the Brazilian Survey of Basic Municipal Information (MUNIC) that include an information and communication technology module between 2004 and 2024, covering virtually all Brazilian municipalities in each wave. Using the ICDM as the dependent variable, we estimate panel models designed to recover between-municipality effects. Fiscal autonomy is the strongest determinant of digital capacity, with a magnitude far exceeding that of bureaucratic attributes, whose effects are positive but modest. None of these effects, however, operates uniformly: own-source revenue yields more in low-income municipalities, staff qualification pays off only where there is organizational structure to absorb it, and the share of politically appointed staff, whose average effect is null, is positive in poorer municipalities and negative in wealthier ones.

articles.title: Following the Feedback: Audience Engagement and Politicians’ Issue Attention on Social Media
articles.authors: August Lohse; Tobias Priesholm Gårdhus; Snorre Ralund; Hjalmar Bang Carlsen
articles.abstract: Political representatives increasingly communicate in social media environments where every message generates immediate and quantified audience feedback. Although likes are not a representative measure of public opinion, they provide information about which issues attract attention from politicians' online audiences. We examine whether politicians devote more attention to issues that generate high engagement. Our analysis draws on 128,204 Facebook posts published by 123 Facebook-active Danish Members of Parliament between 2011 and 2018. We find that issues receiving relatively more audience feedback are consistently more likely to appear in politicians' subsequent posts. This pattern is present across political topics and different forms of engagement, but weakens during election campaigns, when heightened electoral incentives and institutional constraints coincide. The findings show that quantified platform feedback is systematically linked to the allocation of political attention, but that this alignment varies with the context in which politicians communicate.

articles.title: Unmade Ground: Displacement, Dispossession, and the Erosion of Spatial Memory Among Kurdish Forced Migrants
articles.authors: Ramazan BOZTEPE
articles.abstract: Forced displacement does not merely relocate people; it dismantles the material infrastructure through which place becomes memory. Drawing on 80 semi-structured interviews conducted across three settings of the Kurdish experience of internal displacement and diaspora resettlement in Turkey (Bölge, n=25; Central Anatolia, n=25) and Western Europe (Diaspora, n=30), this article examines how the destruction, abandonment, and transformation of inhabited space unmakes collective and intergenerational memory. Transcripts were coded thematically against an eleven-category framework, independently verified through a two-coder reliability process (Cohen's κ=0.838 overall; κ=0.667 for the spatial-memory category, which was coded positive in 45 of the 80 interviews). Using Cernea's (1997) Impoverishment Risks and Reconstruction model alongside Malkki's (1992) critique of sedentarist assumptions about place, the analysis identifies four interlinked processes: urban redevelopment, rural demographic hollowing, diaspora gentrification, and the institutional foreclosure of access to common and sacred land. Participants describe memory as materially anchored — carried in streets, soil, and threshold spaces — such that narrative transmission alone cannot repair its loss. The article argues that spatial memory loss constitutes a distinct impoverishment risk inadequately addressed by existing frameworks, extends Cernea's model by specifying the memorial — and not only economic — stakes of lost access to common property, and proposes the concept of inherited spatial memory: attachment to places the second generation has never physically inhabited.

articles.title: A Representation-Theoretic Method for Analyzing Order Dependence in Decomposition Analysis: An Application to Fertility Change in Korea
articles.authors: Changin Jeon
articles.abstract: Decomposition analysis is widely used to attribute changes in an aggregate outcome to changes in its underlying components. When several factors change simultaneously, however, sequential replacement generally yields different contributions depending on the order in which factors are replaced. The Shapley value resolves this problem by averaging marginal contributions over all possible orders, but the variation across those orders is itself potentially informative. This study proposes a decomposition method that analyzes this order dependence rather than averaging it away. For each factor, its contribution over all decomposition paths is treated as a function on the symmetric group. Harsanyi dividends are used to express path dependence in terms of interaction components, and irreducible representations of the symmetric group are then used to decompose the variance of path-specific contributions into interpretable spectral components. This framework distinguishes three properties of a decomposition result: average contribution, order instability, and the interaction complexity underlying that instability. For a decomposition with six factors, the method generates 64 counterfactual states and 720 replacement paths. Synthetic experiments confirm the predicted relationship between interaction order and admissible representation components and verify the numerical decomposition of order variance to machine precision. The empirical application examines fertility change among Korean women aged 20–49 using population size, age structure, marital composition, parity composition among married women, nonmarital fertility, and parity-specific marital fertility. Between 2000 and 2024, marital composition and parity-specific marital fertility contributed strongly to the decline in births, while changes in parity composition substantially offset that decline. The results also show that path-specific contributions can vary substantially around their Shapley means: for marital composition, parity composition and parity-specific marital fertility, the path standard deviation amounts to roughly 31–42% of the total change between 2000 and 2024. Cross-period differences in spectral structure, however, are strongly shaped by the magnitude of change over each interval. The proposed method extends decomposition analysis from the allocation of average contributions to the analysis of the full distribution and structure of path-specific contributions. It therefore provides an additional diagnostic layer for studying interaction, robustness, and structural dependence in multi-factor decomposition.

articles.title: “My (22m) Girlfriend (23f) Comes Home and Does Nothing”– Gendered Perceptions of Paid and Unpaid Work in Reddit Relationship Discussions over Time
articles.authors: Birgit Zeyer-Gliozzo; Johanna Hölzl; Gundula Zoch; Philipp Doebler
articles.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic reignited longstanding debates around gender inequalities in paid and unpaid work. While survey research has advanced our understanding of these disparities, it typically relies on predefined categories and is susceptible to social desirability and recall bias. Online postings, by contrast, capture intimate experiences in real time but rarely include demographic attributes. We leverage a unique dataset of discussions in Reddit relationship communities that combines rich descriptions of conflicts around (un)paid work with demographic information to examine: Which topics do men and women discuss in relationship conflicts around paid and unpaid work? We use Large Language Models (LLMs) and systematically vary GPT-family models and prompting strategies to classify manifest (demographic information) and latent variables (whether posts discuss romantic relationships, paid, and unpaid work) in Reddit posts. Using classifications from the best-performing approach, we apply Structural Topic Models to explore which topics partners discuss and how discussions evolve over time. We find temporary pandemic shifts in topics, and women more often discuss mental health in paid work-related conflicts, while men more frequently emphasize career objectives. In conflicts related to unpaid work, men more frequently express concerns about sexual intimacy. Our analysis offers new insights into topics driving relationship conflicts around (un)paid work. We also contribute to the growing literature on LLMs’ capabilities and limitations in classifying social-science constructs. By combining demographic information with sensitive narratives, our dataset captures forms of relational conflict rarely accessible in survey or social-media research, opening promising avenues for future research.

articles.title: Given and Chosen Ties: Status, Personal Networks, and Political Behaviour in Britain
articles.authors: Giacomo Melli
articles.abstract: Political participation in Britain is stratified not only by where people stand but by who stands with them. Bringing social network analysis to the study of social stratification, this article draws on ego-networks from the British Household Panel Survey, which link respondents to their closest friends and to partners and relatives who are themselves panel members. It examines how the status of these networks relates to turnout, political interest, and party choice across four general elections, and whether given ties, such as parents and siblings, differ from chosen ties, such as partners and friends. Status homophily is strongest among friends. The status of partners, friends, and the family of origin is associated with each outcome. The family of origin is as closely associated as chosen ties, and more closely with interest, whereas adult children stand largely apart. Status also reaches further than behaviour: two steps from ego, alters' status is still associated with ego's turnout, while their turnout is not. These associations reflect stable differences between people, pointing to durable status milieux. Between 1992 and 2005, these milieux came to separate voters from abstainers more, and Labour from Conservative voters less.

articles.title: In Silico Advertising Tests
articles.authors: Marta Trales; Guillaume Hochard; Christophe Benavent
articles.abstract:
This research examines whether large language model agents can produce analytically useful evidence for advertising testing when treated as synthetic respondents rather than as substitutes for human consumers. We report an in-silico comparative post-test of two television advertisements in the French telecommunications market, conducted on a panel of 800 profile-conditioned consumer agents. The study evaluates the synthetic corpus through internal validity criteria: whether the questionnaire covers the main dimensions of advertising response, whether evaluative dimensions form coherent relations, whether the two stimuli are discriminated across preference labels, scores, lexical patterns and semantic embeddings, and whether responses vary intelligibly across social profiles.
The results indicate that the synthetic panel produces structured and interpretable evidence. The contribution is not that the analysis discovers a contrast invisible in the advertisements themselves: Bouygues and Orange are clearly built around different persuasive registers. Rather, the contribution is methodological. The synthetic-interview pipeline consistently recovers and differentiates these registers across preference labels, scores, lexical patterns and semantic comparisons. Bouygues is associated mainly with creative, humorous and memorable qualities,
while Orange is associated with reliability, informativeness, purchase orientation and overall preference. This structure is visible quantitatively in the main six dimensional coding scheme. Among all 800 synthetic agents, Bouygues leads on creativity (83.6% versus 14.8% for Orange), whereas Orange leads on informationseeking or consideration (76.8% versus 14.8% for Bouygues) and overall preference (54.8% versus 20.6% for Bouygues), with the remaining responses classified as mixed or neutral. The analysis remains deliberately limited to synthetic respondents.
Claims about similarity to human preferences or market behaviour would require external comparison with representative human data or market-level indicators.

articles.title: Why We Cling to Flawed Influencers: Psychological Mechanisms Behind Loyalty to Deceptive Social Media Figures
articles.authors: Asma Alolyan
articles.abstract:
Abstract  
Existing studies on loyalty to social media influencers have mainly focused on cognitive  dissonance, parasocial bonding, halo effect, social identity, and just world belief, each in  isolation. This paper advances another argument: that these five mechanisms occur not  independently but in a predictable sequence, each reducing psychological resistance to the next,  producing loyalties more resistant than any single mechanism alone. We call this the  compounding loyalty model. Cognitive dissonance is the initial motivation causing a follower to  realise something is wrong; parasocial bonding makes rationalisation a requirement, not an  option; the halo effect provides a surface level base for maintaining trust despite misbehaviours;  social identity makes loyalty costly to lose; and just world belief provides a final, motivated  argument that deception did not happen at all. We draw this model from cases including James  Charles (2021) and Ramon Abbas, convicted of fraud in 2022. Media literacy, ethical marketing  and platform policy are discussed. 

Keywords: Influencers, social media, Cognitive dissonance, Para-social relationships, Halo  effect, social identity theory, just world hypothesis, Compounding loyalty model.

articles_hidden.title: Chapter 2: Surprise, Revisited: An EU Performance Evaluation of the Arab Uprisings
articles_hidden.authors: Nikki Ikani
articles_hidden.abstract:
Most actors and commentators across the West were caught by surprise when anti-government protests started in Tunisia and then spread across the Middle East and North Africa in the winter of 2010-2011. The events became known as the Arab Spring, the Arab revolutions or, as will be used in this volume, the ‘Arab uprisings’. 

This sense of surprise when the uprisings started applies to the institutions of the European Union  and its major allies in the region – the United States, France and the UK, with their dense network of contacts, embassies and intelligence operatives.  Nor, as will be discussed below, did any of the big NGOs or mainstream media working and reporting on the Middle East and North Africa emit clear warnings on the prospect of such an event. Even once the protests started in Tunisia in the third week of December 2010, the rapidly growing discontent in both Tunisia and Egypt initially went largely unreported in Western media as well as in reporting from the big NGOs, some of whom were at the time largely focusing on the impasse in Iraq and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. This volume, amongst others, asks to what extent and when ‘being surprised’ is to be expected, and when it indicates failures in intelligence collection, analysis, communication, or receptivity. In this chapter it will be argued that only after investigating in detail which characteristics of the Arab uprisings were particularly surprising to the European institutions and to what extent, and whether these degrees of surprise were spread evenly across analysists and decision-makers, it is possible to properly explain why the Arab uprisings were so surprising. In keeping with the aims of this volume, this subsequently serves to identify to what extent the surprising nature of the Arab uprisings, and any potential errors made in anticipating this event by the European Union, were excusable given the complexity and diagnostic difficulty of the Arab Uprisings, or whether they point to broader structural problems and shortcomings in the European intelligence-policy nexus.

articles_hidden.title: Lessons learnt? The EU and the Arab uprisings
articles_hidden.authors: Nikki Ikani
articles_hidden.abstract: A reboot of the Arab Uprisings has become more likely in the wake of the COVID-19 Pandemic. In order to assess whether the European institutions are currently better able to anticipate an event such as the Arab Uprisings, this paper contends one must first investigate in depth what made the Arab Uprisings so surprising, and to whom. Hereto, this paper unpacks this surprising nature of the Uprisings and the performance of the EEAS, INTCEN and DG NEAR, challenging some of the extant explanations in this literature. To this aim and following previous research, it dissects surprise into three elements. By unpacking who was surprised (the spread of the surprise), on what (the scope of the surprise) and to what degree (the dissonance of the surprise), it complements the extant literature which prioritizes the explanation of their ‘surprisingness’ over an in-depth investigation of the characteristics which made the Arab Uprisings so surprising. It subsequently probes which factors negatively affected the EU’s performance, preparing the field for the learning of specific lessons.

articles_hidden.title: Born to Govern or to Extract? Party types across administrative levels in Colombia
articles_hidden.authors: Juan Sebastián Lara-Rodríguez
articles_hidden.abstract:
Political parties and corruption research relies predominantly on political spectrum, overlooking the organisational attributes that shape whether parties constrain or facilitate corrupt behaviour. This paper proposes a typological framework that classifies parties by their organisational origins — traditional, personalistic, ethnic, rebelorigin, and neo-Pentecostal — and examines how these are related to corruption across mayoral, gubernatorial, and presidential administrative levels. Drawing on prosecutorial records from Colombia’s Attorney General covering 2011–2020, I construct a composite corruption indicator for 1,122 municipalities across three local and two presidential
elections. The empirical strategy combines municipality and two-way fixed effects, spatial econometric models, and a regression discontinuity design exploiting close elections. The results show that rebel-origin parties and citizen-signature movements consistently
reduce corruption, whilst traditional and personalistic types remain statistically indistinguishable; ethnic parties appear insignificant in the main classification, but the sensitivity analysis reveals that once parapolitically captured parties are reassigned, genuine indigenous parties significantly reduce rent-seeking. This relationship varies across governmental tiers: party structure binds at the municipal level, church-based accountability operates at the gubernatorial level, and armed-group networks override party type at the presidential level. Voter turnout is positively associated with municipal corruption, consistent with clientelistic mobilisation. These findings demonstrate that how parties are built matters for understanding corruption in multi-party democracies.

articles_hidden.title: Leaves instead of ballots: The Colombian formal and informal governance of coca
articles_hidden.authors: Juan Sebastián Lara-Rodríguez
articles_hidden.abstract:
Colombia produces more coca than ever, yet scholarship remains anchored in security frameworks that overlook how institutional configurations shape this illegal crop. This article treats coca cultivation as a governance outcome, arguing that the interaction
between formal institutions — political parties and electoral processes — and informal entities — criminal and rebel armed groups — determines where coca takes root. Drawing on a municipality-level panel covering the national territory from 2011 to 2023, and
employing fixed effects, spatial Durbin models, and a difference-in-differences leveraging the 2016 peace settlement, the analysis reveals that no party or coalition bears a significant association with coca once municipal heterogeneity is absorbed. What persistently predicts cultivation is electoral fraud risk and armed group presence, specially the ELN guerrilla. The latest peace accord caused coca expansion rather than contraction. These findings suggest that phasing out coca demands strengthening democracy and extending the rule of law to plantation clusters.

articles_hidden.title: How Do Unconditional Cash Transfers Break the Poverty Trap? Identifying Pathways of Behavioral, Economic, and Psychosocial Transformations through Lived Experiences in Rural Uganda
articles_hidden.authors: Lukas Neuwirth; Khamisi Musanje; Karen Schelleman-Offermans; Mathias Kayanga; Martin Mabunda Baluku
articles_hidden.abstract: This longitudinal mixed-methods study (n=32) investigates the mechanisms through which Unconditional Cash Transfers (UCTs) alleviate extreme poverty in rural Uganda. Drawing on in-depth interviews conducted at three timepoints (baseline, n = 32; one month after, n = 32; one year after, n = 11), alongside economic data and standardized psychological measures, we explored changes in lived experiences, examined individual differences and reconstructed personal trajectories following a combined UCT and behavioral micro-intervention.  Findings reveal that, for all participants, UCTs initiated a similar three-stage pathway of change. First, they alleviated material scarcity, leading to a state of basic sufficiency that reduced stress, restored cognitive bandwidth, and fostered future orientation. Second, they served as start-up capital for future-oriented investments and microenterprise development. Finally, as participants engaged in their investments, they initiated an upward spiral of self-reinforcing processes that facilitated poverty graduation. Nonetheless, UCTs demonstrated varying effects. For some, they served as economic relief, while for others, they initiated a cycle of multidimensional transformation. These individual differences were explained by the varying degrees to which participants progressed along this pathway and how strongly underlying processes were activated. Eight psychosocial processes emerged as key drivers of transformation; (1) removing scarcity; (2) goal setting and action planning, (3) experiencing positive emotions; (4) improving self-concepts; (5) developing psychological capital; (6) improving social capital; (7) psychological needs fulfillment and (8) behavioral activation. Our results suggest that UCTs must be understood as interventions that directly engage the psychological, social and behavioral dimensions of poverty. However, future research is needed to replicate and expand our findings.

articles_hidden.title: What do culture vouchers really buy? Evidence from France's ‘pass Culture’ policy uses
articles_hidden.authors: Abel Aussant
articles_hidden.abstract: Over the last decade, states throughout Europe have begun implementing universal culture vouchers for young adults to boost cultural participation. Little is known about the effects of these large-scale subsidies, specifically whether they are an effective means of widening participation. This article addresses this question by looking at the French ‘pass Culture’, a €300 stipend for cultural consumption offered to all 18-year-olds since 2021. This study examines whether the intensity of voucher use is associated with higher cultural participation, and whether this association varies across cultural practices. The empirical investigation relies on the statistical analysis of a large-scale survey (N = 5,010) of young people aged 18 to 21 that documents both cultural participation and ‘pass Culture’ use. While the voucher is not associated with participation in institutional highbrow cultural activities like museum visits, theater, or opera attendance, it is positively correlated with engagement in commercial popular culture consumption, including cinema and comic book reading. This is consistent with the view that financial barriers are not the primary obstacle to consumption in cultural capital-intensive activities. However, financial constraints do appear to be associated with non-participation in popular cultural life. The article then discusses the theoretical implications of these findings for our understanding of the relationship between cultural consumption, cultural policies, and social inequalities.

articles_hidden.title: How is Social Status Distributed? A Conjoint Experiment on Social Status Judgements in Great Britain
articles_hidden.authors: Jonathan Mellon; Jack Bailey; Geoffrey Evans
articles_hidden.abstract: Social status is a core aspect of societal inequalities, yet its determinants and distribution remain understudied. We investigate the factors that shape social status judgments in Great Britain using a conjoint survey experiment with 7,680 respondents making 30,720 status assessments. Drawing on the extant literature, we test economic (occupation, income, wealth, education), cultural (leisure activities and supermarket choice), and ascribed (gender, class background, and ethnicity) factors as determinants of social status. Income has a substantial positive effect on status judgments, as do pro-social occupations (teaching and healthcare). Cultural capital, measured through leisure activities and supermarket preferences, plays a major role in status assessments. We also find that housing wealth, private schooling, higher education, and being White British all increase perceived status. We also contribute to understanding what factors distribute the most status by combining our experimental estimates with data on the prevalence of status predictors in the British population. We find that economic factors, particularly income and wealth distribute the most status. Cultural factors distribute less status, with ascribed characteristics like ethnicity and gender distributing the least status across the whole population, despite sizeable individual-level status penalties for ethnic minorities. Finally, we show that while women, ethnic minorities, and people from working class backgrounds have lower status descriptively in the population, the causes of this lower status differ with ethnic minorities and those from working class backgrounds suffering direct ascribed penalties, whereas women’s lower status derives almost entirely from their worse economic situation (particularly lower income). Our findings support multiple sociological theories of status, demonstrating the importance of occupation, economic resources, cultural capital, and racial hierarchies in status judgments. However, economic factors dominate the distribution of status across society.

articles_hidden.title: Embattled Identities: Masculinities and Organizational Behavior in the Iranian Sphere of Influence
articles_hidden.authors: Vanessa Zorrilla-Muñoz; Manuel Cuerno; Ines Juaristi
articles_hidden.abstract: Most research on masculinities in armed conflict and tension focuses on violence and militarization, overlooking how care (Communion) and dominance interact within masculine identities under chronic insecurity. Using data from the Towards Gender Harmony (TGH) project, this study compares gender self-constructions and care stereotypes between Western liberal democracies and societies under Iranian geopolitical influence or chronic conflict, focusing on the integration versus separation of care and dominance in masculine identities. Gender self-concepts (Communion, Dominance, Agency, Weakness, and Precarious Manhood Beliefs, PMB) were analyzed via t-tests and k-means clustering (k = 4); care stereotypes were examined using Bipolar Class Analysis (BCA) to identify latent cognitive structures (construals) regarding the compatibility of communion and agency traits. The Iran & Conflict group scored higher on Communion, Dominance, Agency, and PMB, and lower on Weakness, and showed a distinctive Provider-Protector cluster profile (high Communion, Dominance, and Agency) absent in the Western sample; PMB behaved as an underlying structural condition rather than a profile-specific trait. Male-only analyses replicated and often intensified these differences, except for Weakness, suggesting that difference was driven by the female subsample. BCA also revealed greater heterogeneity in caregiving stereotypes within the Iran & Conflict group. These results show that caregiving and dominance can integrate into a coherent model of protective, provider masculinity under chronic insecurity, challenging simplistic associations between masculinity and violence and highlighting configurations that legitimize male authority through protection and provision. The study contributes to theorizing masculinities and informs interventions on gender norms in conflict-affected regions.

articles_hidden.title: Wealth, inequality and deforestation: a scale-dependent relationship
articles_hidden.authors: Elodie Adam; Leland Werden; Melissa Chapman
articles_hidden.abstract: Understanding how wealth and economic inequality shape global land-use change is both a long-standing and urgent challenge. While existing empirical evidence largely relies on either national-scale metrics of wealth and inequality or small-scale case studies, few analyses combine global scope with local-scale data. Here we do so, linking local wealth and local inequality to satellite-derived deforestation and its proximate drivers for 27,657 household survey clusters across 52 countries. We find that local wealth, rather than inequality, is the stronger predictor of forest loss, but the direction of this effect is not uniform: depending on the country, a one-standard-deviation increase in local wealth is associated with anywhere from a 19% decrease to a 36% increase in the expected deforestation rate, with no discernible effect in most countries. The share of tree cover loss due to permanent agriculture tends to be higher in wealthier clusters, while the share due to shifting cultivation tends to be higher in areas with lower wealth. We further identify clusters with high wealth, low inequality, and low deforestation, to understand the environmental and socioeconomic drivers of these "triple-win" clusters. Triple-win areas tend to cluster spatially, suggesting that district-level analysis is key to identifying policy levers and institutional structures that can reconcile human development with environmental protection.

articles_hidden.title: The Impact of Maternal Preconception Health on Long-Term Child Health and Developmental Outcomes: A Scoping Review
articles_hidden.authors: Catherine Stewart; Katie Harron; Jennifer Hall
articles_hidden.abstract:
The preconception period is a critical window during which maternal health and behaviours can influence pregnancy and offspring outcomes. However, preconception care remains limited, and existing research has largely focused on short-term pregnancy or neonatal outcomes. This scoping review aimed to synthesise evidence on the associations between maternal preconception health and long-term health, developmental, and educational outcomes in children.

Primary studies were eligible if they examined the independent effect of maternal preconception health on child health and developmental outcomes assessed after age 1 year and up to 18 years. Five databases (MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science) were searched. Data were extracted using a standardised form and summarised descriptively. Studies were mapped by type of preconception exposure and child outcome.

From 9,539 records identified, 186 studies met the inclusion criteria. Preconception BMI was the most frequently studied exposure (n=130) while neuro/cognitive development (n=83) was the most common outcome. Higher preconception BMI was consistently associated with adverse long-term outcomes, including higher offspring BMI and poorer cognitive, behavioural, and developmental outcomes. Pre-existing maternal physical and mental health conditions were also linked to poorer child health and developmental outcomes. Evidence for preconception smoking, alcohol, and substance use was limited but suggested potential harms, while diet quality and supplementation were generally associated with beneficial outcomes.

These findings highlight the preconception period as a key opportunity for intervention to support positive outcomes for children and underscore the need for higher-quality, long-term research to inform policy and practice.

articles_hidden.title: Who stops answering? Breakoff, smartphone use and educational bias in a web survey
articles_hidden.authors: Alžbeta Ľudmová; Martin Kreidl; Barbora Hubatková; Martin Lakomý
articles_hidden.abstract:
Survey data collection has been moving towards the online self-administered mode (CAWI), which is usually seen as an effective answer to falling response rates and rising fieldwork costs. This mode, however, comes with drawbacks of its own, especially when respondents use a smartphone to fill out the survey. Related major challenge is a higher tendency of these respondents to break off, i.e. to end the interview before completion. Breakoff matters most when it occurs non-randomly and compounds existing biases, such as those based on age or education. To find out whether it does, we used questionnaire data and paradata from the CAWI component of the first wave of the second cycle of the Czech Generations and Gender Survey (2020–2022; N = 5,468, 244 breakoffs). Treating each of 118 unfiltered questionnaire items as one unit of analytical time, we analysed progression through the questionnaire using Cox regression supplemented by Kaplan–Meier survival curves. Younger respondents broke off somewhat more often than older ones, though the difference was not statistically robust. The education gradient was both steeper and more persistent: 7% of the least educated broke off as compared with 3% of the most educated, and device only partly explained this gap, leaving education and device to operate as largely independent processes. The gap was, however, concentrated on small screens - among smartphone users, breakoff rose from 4% among the most educated to over 11% among the least educated, while on larger devices it stayed flat at 3–4%. Breakoff thus adds to, rather than merely reflects, the educational bias of self-completion samples. 

Keywords: breakoff; web surveys; smartphone; device effects; survival analysis; paradata; representativity; Generations and Gender Survey

articles_hidden.title: Under what conditions does complexity become unmanageable? A capacity threshold for megaprojects
articles_hidden.authors: Matthias Huemmer
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose. Project complexity research describes complexity in rich dimensional detail but rarely states the condition under which it stops being manageable. This paper states one and derives what remains possible past it.
Design/methodology/approach. Conceptual theory elaboration from the delivering organization’s standpoint, building on requisite variety, organizational information processing and bounded rationality, illustrated with a worked calculation and a documented revision series from a public inquiry.
Findings. Complexity becomes unmanageable from within at a point of no return: when the capacity demanded of a governance level exceeds the information-processing capacity available to it, set by its binding constraint, to the degree that the level can no longer remove its overload with its own means. Past it the feasible response set collapses to three moves, deceleration, external capacity and requirement reduction, because every other method consumes the missing capacity. In megaprojects the threshold falls early, because both sides of the balance are fixed before work begins. The Elbphilharmonie's public record shows the predicted signature: revisions moved both ways before contract award and one way after it.
Research limitations/implications. The threshold is stated as a testable claim, not a measured constant. Five propositions with falsification conditions follow.
Originality/value. Not a new inventory of complexity but a threshold within the inherited mechanism, and the identification of the translation of requirements into demanded capacity as the operation where complexity becomes subjective and manageable.

articles_hidden.title: Overcoming inertia: Addressing barriers to managing coastal legacy waste in a changing climate
articles_hidden.authors: Isabel Cotton; James J. Porter; James S. Robinson; Rhys H.S. Kelly; Ute Kelly; Megan Clinch; Rhys E. M. Jones; Deborah P. Dixon; Patrick Diamond; Suzy O’Hara
articles_hidden.abstract: Climate change will increase the number of legacy waste sites (older waste sites without pollution control mechanisms) that are at risk of coastal flooding and erosion in the UK and worldwide. Whilst the need to adapt to coastal change is well documented, the combined risks of coastal change and legacy waste has received less attention. Through interviews and workshops with policy stakeholders, this paper explores current perspectives on the barriers to managing coastal legacy waste in England and Scotland. Both the interviews and workshops reveal a high awareness of the potential risks from coastal legacy waste. However, limited sources of funding, alongside knowledge gaps on the nature of pollutant risk, many competing priorities at a local authority level, and a lack of clarity on roles and responsibilities, is creating an inertia that frustrates the proactive management of the issue. Using Moser and Ekstrom’s (2010) adaptation planning cycle as an analytical framework, findings reveal that managing legacy waste is unable to progress beyond the first stage of adaptation planning due to these systemic barriers. Overall, findings indicate the urgent need for a long-term strategy designed at a national level that provides sufficient resources and capacity-building for proactive local governance.

articles_hidden.title: Social complexity is not correlated with wartime trophy-taking in a cross-cultural sample
articles_hidden.authors: Kiran Basava
articles_hidden.abstract: The taking of body parts from enemies during war has been widely recorded across cultures through human history. Qualitative research on trophy-taking suggests it was prevalent among small-scale societies to demonstrate warriors’ military skill and increase status, as well as chiefdoms and early states to display leaders’ monopolization of violence and intimidate external populations. Two sets of analyses were conducted to quantitatively test relationships between trophy-taking practices and social complexity in historical societies. For the first, a dataset was built using ethnographic, historical, and archaeological sources for 110 societies to test whether trophy-taking was more likely at intermediate levels of social complexity. For the second set of analyses, data on headhunting practices were analyzed using a dataset of Austronesian-language speaking societies and the Austronesian language phylogeny. The results for both the global and Austronesian analyses did not support a consistent relationship between trophy-taking practices and social complexity. This work assembles a novel dataset of trophy-taking practices for a global sample of societies, and adds to efforts to study patterns of violence and human social complexity with quantitative methods and comparative historical data.

articles_hidden.title: Heterogeneous Effects of Local Government Financing Channels on Industrial Structure: Evidence from Provincial-Level Panel Data in China
articles_hidden.authors: Liangkun Shi; Huanqi Wu; Hanfei Yang
articles_hidden.abstract: Local government financing channels provide an essential perspective for understanding the investment decisions of local governments and their economic effects. In China, broadly defined local government debt includes two categories: statutory debt and the debt incurred by local government financial vehicles (LGFVs). This paper uses provincial-level panel data from 2016 to 2025, constructs a data-driven industrial structure index, and estimates a two-way fixed-effects model controlling for the overall debt scale. The empirical evidence suggests that the different financial channels on industrial structure are associated with different and opposing changes in industrial structure. When the debt composition shifts toward LGFV debts, the share of relatively high-productivity efficiency industries increases, particularly that of the tertiary sector. In contrast, when the debt composition shifts toward statutory debt, the share of relatively low-production efficiency industries increases, particularly that of the secondary sector. Therefore, the composition of local government debt, rather than its scale alone, is relevant to changes in regional industrial structure.

articles_hidden.title: Archaeologies of Indigenous Foodways and Collective Capacities
articles_hidden.authors: Molly Carney
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent archaeological scholarship has embraced food security and food sovereignty frameworks to connect past foodways to present-day crises. However, these studies require critical examination of the colonial origins and ideological foundations of these frameworks, which emerged from industrialized western economic paradigms that do not align with Indigenous worldviews. Drawing on food studies scholarship, I argue that archaeologists must move beyond the uncritical adoption of food security and sovereignty frameworks to embrace culturally grounded paradigms developed by and for descendant communities. This paper advocates for reframing North American archaeological investigations of foodways through Indigenous philosopher Kyle Powys Whyte’s concept of collective capacities: webs of relationships among humans, non-human beings, and landscapes organized together to support responses to change and continuance. As a linking tool, collective capacities help archaeologists carry out the material and analytical work that Indigenous Food Sovereignty movements call for. An archaeology of collective capacities shifts our focus to understanding how food systems functioned as relational infrastructures of care, responsibility, and reciprocity that sustained communities across millennia. In this contribution I outline an archaeological framework identifying key material signatures of collective capacities. Applying this framework to the Pend Oreille Valley in northeastern Washington State, I demonstrate how paleoethnobotanical and archaeological data from the last 1,500 years reveal Indigenous food systems were sustained through active management, coordinated labor, and intergenerational knowledge transmission across climatic and sociopolitical changes. I also consider how contemporary practices of reciprocity and relationality mirror the archaeological record of stability and stewardship. By centering culture-specific terminology and philosophies, an archaeology of collective capacities offers a methodological and theoretical approach that supports, rather than imposes frameworks upon, past societies while documenting the enduring systems that enabled communities to thrive across deep time.

articles_hidden.title: Competency Restoration Timeliness in Washington Under Trueblood 2018-2026
articles_hidden.authors: Sudhanshu Rai
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective. A federal court found Washington State's competency-restoration system unconstitutional in 2015 because defendants who had been found incompetent to stand trial were made to wait months in jail for a psychiatric bed. The State did not appeal that part of the injunction, and the Ninth Circuit left it undisturbed in 2016. The system did not turn around until after years of escalating enforcement culminating in a contempt finding and a $100 million fine. We ask whether that timing reflects sustained federal-court enforcement, and what drove it. Methods. We built an open monthly panel of Washington's Trueblood court-monitor data (January 2018-May 2026; 1,033 rows) and analyzed statewide inpatient restoration timeliness as an interrupted time series against a 7-day admission standard, alongside a jail-based-evaluation comparator on a looser clock. Results. The system was non-compliant for six years (annual median waits 28.0-63.5 days; compliance rarely above 30%, and 6% in March 2023 when the median wait peaked at 97 days). It then improved sharply, to a median of 5.0 days and 90.4% average compliance, a level that has held over 26 months of continued oversight. The gain concentrated in bed-dependent services: restoration admission and inpatient evaluation both moved sharply, while the bed-independent comparator's median wait moved +0.0 days on the raw median split and a small but statistically significant −1.3 days on the regression estimator. Coding by Washington's Department of Social and Health Services (DSHS) attributes an average 90.8% of restoration delays to bed availability, though almost all of that coding predates the turnaround. All facilities improved; demand rose, not fell, and the completion metric counts hospital admission, case dismissal, and jail release identically (Limitations). Conclusions. The improvement coincided with sustained Trueblood enforcement; this single-jurisdiction design supports association, not causation. The open, re-executable panel offers an independent compliance monitor complementary to the state's own.

articles_hidden.title: Spiritual Healing Methods in Los Angeles: the Cultural Heritage and Western Representation of Alternative Medicines
articles_hidden.authors: Scott Altsuler; Eric Heller
articles_hidden.abstract: Throughout the United States of America, complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) has become increasingly popular over the past fifty years. These include any practices that stem from tradition and spirituality rather than practices that are derived from empirical evidence. With many popular spiritual healing practices originating from specific traditions across the world and across a wide range of time, there is much to explore about the mechanisms through which culturally specific spiritual healing practices adapt to Western consumerist culture. In the current study, we examine the cultural origins and development of CAM, mostly the use and popularization of Reiki, Yoga, and ayahuasca. We interviewed six spiritual health practitioners in the greater Los Angeles area to understand the modern CAM practitioner’s perspective on how spiritual healing methods have taken hold in Western culture, how they align with the original practice’s tradition, and how they have adapted to modern consumer culture. This study explores how Los Angeles’ cultural emphasis on individuality and marketability has cultivated an environment for its population to disseminate and recontextualize traditional spiritual healing methods to fit contemporary mental health demands.

articles_hidden.title: The LINGACON Multilingualism Assessment Standard (L-MAS): Definitions, Thresholds, and a Review of Survey Practice
articles_hidden.authors: Areg Hovhannisyan
articles_hidden.abstract: How many languages does a person speak? The question bears on human linguistic capacity, global connectivity, and language education policy, yet we found no standardized protocol for measuring it. In the course of constructing a global estimate of ALPS (Average Language a Person Speaks) for the 237 jurisdictions in the LINGACON scope (Hovhannisyan, 2026a), we found that existing data sources use at least six distinct and mutually incompatible methods for assessing multilingualism, from self-reported repertoires and census repertoire items to home-language questions, expert aggregation, first-language distributions, and inference from education statistics. These methods measure different constructs at different thresholds, and their results cannot be compared directly. For entire regions, among them the Arab states, Latin America, and most of Asia, we found no standardized, comparable repertoire data. We present a taxonomy of current measurement approaches, document their biases and incompatibilities, describe three under-documented sources of error and non-comparability (the diaspora residual, the linguistic concealment effect, and the dubbing–subtitling asymmetry), and propose a standard: the LINGACON Multilingualism Assessment Standard (L-MAS), a five-level measurement framework that ranges from a single survey question (Level 1, minimal marginal cost) through a national audit with tested proficiency (Level 4) to a longitudinal tracker of change over time (Level 5). If Level 1 were adopted by the five major cross-national survey programs, some 100–110 countries, holding about three-quarters of the world’s population, would have comparable multilingualism data within one round of each program, provided the Asian Barometer continues to field in China and India. The full L-MAS specification is freely available at l-mas.com.

articles_hidden.title: Is there a niche for the NAP in mature climate policy frameworks? An analysis of flood risk management in England and its alignment with adaptation policies
articles_hidden.authors: Andrew Russell; Aakash Dipak Patel; Isabel Cotton
articles_hidden.abstract:
The National Adaptation Programme (NAP) in England is a wide-ranging, statutory, 5-yearly plan that, within the Climate Change Act 2008, has a requirement to develop adaptation objectives to manage climate risks. Since NAP1 in 2013, it has been repeatedly assessed as inadequate by many stakeholders. Here, we investigate how and why it has failed, and assess whether there is a niche for a NAP in a well-developed environmental risk management policy space.

We conducted a survey (n=112) that collected quantitative and rich qualitative responses, alongside 4 interviews, with flood risk management (FRM) professionals from England to examine how well the NAP has integrated into this sector, and which policy gaps the NAP could fill. The results indicate that the NAP is much less important to FRM professionals than other relevant strategies and policies, and that its goal or ambition was articulated poorly compared to other policies or plans; the NAP ranked second-bottom for both criteria out of 12 relevant strategies and policies presented. The factors seen as inhibiting adaptation integration were: fragmented governance; avoiding big decisions; and funding alignment with protection rather than resilience measures. Arbitrary targets linked to infrastructure (eg. number of properties better protected) were seen as a barrier to working towards a resilient society. There was significant support for using progress measures more relevant to communities, that cut across policy silos and that apply a wider, resilience-focused interpretation of risk management (eg. saving lives, reforming funding approaches, greater social equity, ensuring insurance availability).

articles_hidden.title: Assessing the Trust Crisis in European Security: A New Approach to Measuring Unthinking Trust
articles_hidden.authors: Tobias Wille; Anton Peez
articles_hidden.abstract: Trust between the United States and its European allies appears to be in crisis, but our knowledge of the exact extent and consequences of this crisis is limited. To address this knowledge gap, we propose a novel approach for measuring deep, unthinking trust in public opinion. We conceptualize unthinking trust as the unquestioned expectation that others will reciprocate cooperation. We qualitatively capture this expectation through open-ended responses in a survey, which we then systematically code, creating a quantitative measure of unthinking trust. We apply our approach to study how recent breaches of trust affect unthinking trust among the German public in two key NATO allies, the UK and the US. Our findings show that a vignette reminding German respondents of Brexit and its aftermath significantly reduces unthinking trust in the UK. A comparable vignette reminding respondents of recent US behavior toward its European allies does not measurably affect unthinking trust in the US, presumably due to salience effects. Furthermore, we find that the Brexit treatment significantly affects respondents’ policy preferences, making them more wary of multilateral security cooperation and, surprisingly, of a national strengthening of defense. A mediation analysis shows that the mechanism of unthinking trust contributes to these effects.

articles_hidden.title: Participatory Narrative Inquiry as an Aligned Approach for Understanding and Addressing Queer Impostor Phenomenon with Bisexual+ Femmes
articles_hidden.authors: Devin Madden; Timnit Berhane; Christine Marie “Lovely” Luis Torres Nunez; Alana López; Daniel Eisen; Jean M. Breny; Talina Corvus
articles_hidden.abstract: Queer impostor syndrome, as it is colloquially called, is a clear nod to the well-researched concept of impostor phenomenon (IP). Bi+ people experience a disproportionate burden of mental distress and are at the forefront of community dialogues about feelings of queer impostorism, but those discussions are lacking from scientific literature. There is a need for more research with bi+ people for bi+ people, and participatory methods are critical for ensuring responsiveness to this marginalized populations’ needs. This equity-driven study leveraged participatory narrative inquiry to elevate the voices of bisexual+ femmes who self-identify with experiences of queer impostorism as it relates to their sexual identity. Twelve bi+ femmes from New York City shared and analyzed their stories and the stories of their research cohort to characterize QIP for bi+ femmes. This paper details the participatory narrative inquiry process, a community-engaged research approach that asks participants to analyze their own stories and data to yield richer, more resonant results and strategies to bring research-to-action. This manuscript offers researchers insight, through the case study of this research project, into a less traditionally considered qualitative method that allows for meaningful engagement across the research lifespan and may be particularly well-suited for bisexuality research.

articles_hidden.title: Evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) for Coding Open-Ended Survey Responses: A Total Survey Error Framework
articles_hidden.authors: Laone Maphane; Gabriele Durrant
articles_hidden.abstract:
Open-ended questions are commonly used in survey research to supplement closed-ended questions by capturing respondents’ views, reasons, and priorities in their own words. However, coding these responses for analysis remains time-consuming and difficult to standardise. Recent advances in automated coding, especially through large language models (LLMs), have renewed interest in using open-ended responses at scale, but their evaluation is often difficult and framed mainly in terms of classification accuracy and agreement with human coding. This paper develops a Total Survey Error framework for evaluating automated coding of open-ended survey responses as part of survey measurement and data production. Model outputs are assessed using existing human-coded data as a high-quality operational benchmark, with the evaluation examining six complementary dimensions, such as processing agreement, measurement validity, prevalence distortion, coding density, response-form sensitivity, and operational reliability. The framework is applied to data using open-ended survey responses from the National Centre for Social Research (NatCen). The paper aims to inform how automated coding systems, including LLMs, can be assessed in practice, and what issues survey researchers should consider when evaluating their suitability for open-ended survey coding, and how improved coding may enable wider use of open-ended questions in large-scale quantitative surveys.
Keywords: automated coding; large language models; measurement validity; open-ended survey responses; survey data quality; Total Survey Error

articles_hidden.title: Passive Behavioral Tracing: A Non-Interventional Fairness Protocol for Cooperative AI
articles_hidden.authors: kazutaka hayashi
articles_hidden.abstract: Emerging AI governance regimes, including the EU AI Act's post-market monitoring obligation and the NIST AI RMF's measure function, require ongoing fairness monitoring but leave open which statistics should satisfy it. Interventional audits (A/B tests, counterfactual procedures, adversarial probing) manipulate the system, and often the people, under audit, and are episodic where monitoring is continuous. This article argues that a useful part of that monitoring can be done passively, and proposes Passive Behavioral Tracing (PBT), a protocol that audits fairness in AI-mediated cooperative systems using only behavioral traces the system already records. PBT formalizes four constructs computable from ordinary logs (consistency of treatment, parity across naturally occurring groups, proportionality to contribution, and drift over time) and combines them into two indicators, PBT-Ethics and PBT-Coop. A Monte Carlo study with released code shows that the constructs form two families: reciprocity and parity register unfair treatment whether it has always existed or began recently, while consistency and drift respond to change, and only drift locates when the change happened. This distinction carries regulatory weight: unfairness present since deployment implicates a system's design, while unfairness with an onset points to a dateable change, and the two call for remedies that a single score cannot separate. The study also shows the protocol's limits: mild, sustained unfairness against a small group is often missed. All results come from a stylized synthetic model; PBT is a specification validated in principle and complementary to interventional audits, not a finding about any operating system.

articles_hidden.title: An Empirical Study on How Private College Counseling Perpetuates Structural Disadvantage A Mixed-Methods Study Combining Survey, Interview, and Social Media Content Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Alayna ellahi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Equitable access to higher education is widely regarded as a cornerstone of social mobility, yet the rapid growth of an independent educational consulting (IEC) industry has introduced a market-driven layer of college admissions guidance available only to families who can pay for it. This study investigates whether private college counseling functions as a neutral support service or as a mechanism of structural disadvantage that converts economic capital into institutional advantage, drawing on Pierre Bourdieu's theory of cultural and social capital. Using a triangulated, mixed-methods design, the study combines a 20-respondent Likert-scale survey of students and parents, semi-structured interviews with six purposively sampled respondent groups (student and parent users and non-users, school-based counselors, and private consultants), and an original content analysis of eight social media acceptance posts from a private counseling agency, coded against a seven-theme promotional codebook. Findings converge across all three methods: 82% of survey respondents reported that private counselors reveal "unspoken" admissions criteria unavailable to public-school peers; 65% identified fee-based, unadvertised opportunity-brokering as a distinguishing service; and interviews revealed overwhelming cross-group consensus — among both users and non-users of private counseling — that the practice constitutes an unfair structural advantage rather than a neutral commercial service. The content analysis found that aspirational imagery and institutional-legitimacy signaling appeared in 100% of coded posts, empirically confirming the marketing mechanisms respondents described. The study concludes that, absent structural reform — expanded public counseling capacity

articles_hidden.title: Enhancing Dementia Awareness and Specialized Nurse Training in the Gulf: A Policy Roadmap for Oman, Qatar, UAE, and Saudi Arabia
articles_hidden.authors: Sukant Khurana; Sanampreet Kaur; Mohammad Saddam Khan; Gaurav Deepak Patel; Prajwal Anand; K. Vijaya Lakshmi; Ahmad; Brooks Robinson
articles_hidden.abstract: The countries of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) are projected to see more than a threefold increase in dementia by 2050, due to a rapidly aging population. However, health care systems across Oman, Qatar, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia are still skewed towards acute rather than chronic care.  Nurses are the primary dementia caregivers, but  they often are not specialists. This situation is exacerbated by non-standardized curricula, heavy reliance on expatriate workforce, linguistic and cultural barriers, high workforce turnover, limited career incentives, and low public and institutional awareness, which delays diagnoses.This study synthesizes available regional and international evidence on dementia related nurse training and workforce preparedness in the GCC and develops evidence-informed policy recommendations for strengthening dementia education and workforce capacity. We propose several regional recommendations including accredited certification, compulsory continuing professional development, multidisciplinary care teams, and awareness-raising initiatives. Coordinated investment in specialized nurse training and workforce policy is important to prepare GCC healthcare systems for the region’s growing dementia burden.

articles_hidden.title: Urban Human-Canine Conflict Mitigation: A 2023 Pilot Study on Stray Dog Population Management in Chembur, Mumbai
articles_hidden.authors: Ojus Wankhede
articles_hidden.abstract: This study investigates the urban stray dog population in Mumbai, Maharashtra, and proposes actionable policy recommendations to mitigate human-canine conflicts. A mixed-methods retrospective pilot study was utilised, incorporating a March 2023 community survey (n=91) in the Chembur area, alongside site visits to local Non-Governmental Organisations and semi-structured interviews with Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) officials. The survey revealed that 61.53% of respondents supported the relocation of stray dogs, whereas only 21.97% supported neutering. The findings indicate a pressing need for enhanced infrastructural capacity within the Animal Birth Control (ABC) programme. Core policy recommendations include the systematic expansion of sterilisation drives, the integration of private veterinary practitioners into mass vaccination campaigns, and the strict enforcement of the Animal Birth Control Rules, 2023.

articles_hidden.title: When Execution Is Cheap: Specification, Evaluation, and Rent Capture in AI-Enabled Work
articles_hidden.authors: Babu George
articles_hidden.abstract: As artificial intelligence lowers the cost of executing well-specified tasks, economic value may shift toward defining desired outcomes and evaluating machine-generated outputs. This paper examines the conditions under which that shift creates economic rents and identifies who may capture them. It separates defining success into four activities: eliciting intent, selecting among admissible specifications, ratifying a choice, and validating outputs. Two models clarify the underlying mechanisms. The first shows that gains from cheaper execution approach a ceiling determined by evaluation cost, which makes evaluator attention more consequential as generation becomes inexpensive. The second shows that generating more candidates increases the marginal value of proxy fidelity, linking abundant output to specification overfitting and Goodhart-type failures. These mechanisms indicate where value may concentrate without determining who receives the returns. Rent requires inelastic supply, exclusion from the created surplus, and the absence of cheaper substitutes. These conditions are most likely when specifications scale across many executions, ratification carries liability, trust institutions certify judgment, organizational systems control codified knowledge, or concentrated model providers set influential defaults. The analysis further distinguishes machine-checkable evaluation against a stated specification from a principal’s assessment of fit to purpose. The former is increasingly commoditized; the latter remains tied to authority, attention, and accountability. The paper develops six testable predictions and a factorial experiment examining evaluation costs, specification fidelity, authority drift, and psychological ownership. Cheap execution relocates bottlenecks, while institutions and market structure determine whether specification, evaluation, default setting, or scarce execution inputs generate rents and who captures them.

articles_hidden.title: The prestige precedes the prize: Top-journal papers and new federal grants
articles_hidden.authors: Haining Wang
articles_hidden.abstract: Evaluators and scientists treat a top-journal paper as a step toward the next grant. We asked whether it is one. We linked 2.19 million last-authored papers by 1.07 million US scientists, 2014–2021, to new lead-investigator awards from the National Institutes of Health and the National Science Foundation, defining top journals as the 5% most cited in their topic and year. The design rests on timing and on holding the scientist fixed: if a top-journal paper brings grants, the advantage should open after the paper. Top-journal papers were followed by a new award twice as often as other papers (55.3 against 26.3 per 1,000), yet the difference was as large two years before publication. For the same scientist, award rates after a top-journal paper and another paper differed by −0.3 per 1,000 (95% confidence interval −8.0 to 7.4), an upper limit at 25% of the difference between scientists. Researchers' small lead over matched researchers was similar before and after their first top-journal paper (3.1 and 3.3 per 1,000). Within three years, journal prestige worked mainly as a record of accumulated advantage, and the funding gap should not be read as the return on one more top-journal paper.

articles_hidden.title: The Intersection of Fascia, Fascism, and Language: Reframing Neurodivergence as an Adaptive Response to Environmental Stress
articles_hidden.authors: Isha Sarah Snow
articles_hidden.abstract: This theoretical paper argues that global autism prevalence data are better read as a map of social ecology than as a map of biology. Diagnostic prevalence reflects the interaction of neurodevelopmental variation, distress, recognition and diagnostic access, and I argue that identified rates rise where relational buffering weakens, institutional demands intensify, and diagnostic systems are primed to read difference as dysfunction. The argument integrates three domains that are rarely analyzed together. First, fascia is treated as a body-wide communication network that densifies under chronic stress, and I propose, as a hypothesis, that the cell danger response (Naviaux, 2014, 2025) may link sustained social threat to physiological rigidity. Second, language is treated as regulatory infrastructure: drawing on Jackson et al. (2019) and Fricker’s (2007) concept of hermeneutical injustice, a dominant diagnostic language shapes how bodily states are interpreted, governed, and pathologized. Third, fascism, which shares its etymological root with fascia in the Roman fasces, is used as a conceptual analogy for systems in which control replaces communication and feedback is suppressed. Apparent anomalies in prevalence across India, Spain, Japan, Australia, and the Nordic countries are examined, and a testable prediction is stated for each. The paper distinguishes established findings from its own hypotheses throughout. The paper concludes that the aim is less distress, not less autism, which shifts intervention upstream toward environments that restore co-regulation and tolerate difference.

articles_hidden.title: GLCI (Global Linguistic Connectivity Index): How Connected Is the World?
articles_hidden.authors: Areg Hovhannisyan
articles_hidden.abstract:
Eight billion people speak more than seven thousand languages. If two of them meet by chance, how 
likely is it that the one listening understands the one speaking, without a translator? We estimate 
about one chance in nine. Greenberg (1956) defined this probability for a single population as an 
index of communication; we compute it for the world. The data come from an audit of individual 
language repertoire compiled from hundreds of census, survey and reference sources, mapped onto 
a common conversational threshold (level A2 of the Common European Framework of Reference for 
Languages, CEFR) and a common individuation standard (ISO 639-3, the language codes of the 
International Organization for Standardization). That audit, reported with ALPS (Average Language a 
Person Speaks) in Hovhannisyan (2026a), covers 237 jurisdictions and 8.16 billion residents; 
connectivity is computed for the 216 with language-level data, which hold 8.09 billion, while the 
other 21, with 69 million residents, have a national ALPS value but no language rows. The audit is 
extended with a directional table of intelligibility between related languages, which covers 591 
language pairs, most of them assessed and few measured. The resulting index, the Global Linguistic 
Connectivity Index (GLCI), is the probability that a randomly drawn listener comprehends a randomly 
drawn speaker. 
GLCI is 0.1129 (95% interval 0.1083–0.1176); the interval covers only row-level, sampling-type 
uncertainty in the input shares, and single modelling choices move GLCI between 0.096 and 0.134 
(§6.1). Within a single jurisdiction the probability is 0.6284 (0.5907–0.6660), a pair-weighted figure 
dominated by India and China; across two jurisdictions it is 0.0747 (0.0711–0.0788), and because 
91% of pairs span two jurisdictions, the lower value governs. Connectivity is concentrated: nearly a 
third of cross-jurisdiction pair mass lies below 0.01, and the median pair sits at 0.022. It also rests on 
one language. English carries 39.2% of global connectivity and 61.9% of the connectivity between 
countries. 
In a simple model relating repertoire to connectivity, which languages are learned matters far more 
than how many. At a mean repertoire of four languages per person, GLCI is 98%, 58% or 15% 
depending on the allocation rule, that is, chiefly on which languages are learned and also on where. 
Compared with a dataset that other researchers built from Ethnologue, the LINGACON estimates 
agree closely on first languages (r = 0.951). On the full layer, leaving out the intelligibility term that 
the other dataset lacks, they are 1.45 times higher, and the difference lies mainly in the coverage of 
acquired languages.

articles_hidden.title: The ALPS Index: A Global Estimate of the Average Number of Languages a Person Speaks
articles_hidden.authors: Areg Hovhannisyan
articles_hidden.abstract:
How many languages does the average person speak? The question has an established qualitative answer, that "probably more than half of the world's population is bilingual" (Grosjean, 2012), but no quantitative one at global scale.

We audited individual language repertoire in 237 jurisdictions with 8.16 billion residents. Survey, census and reference sources were mapped onto a common conversational threshold (CEFR level A2) and a common individuation standard (ISO 639-3), graded on a seven-band evidentiary scale, and treated for twelve documented biases of census and survey instruments. The resulting index, ALPS (Average Language a Person Speaks), is the population mean of individual repertoire size.

The global population-weighted value is 1.568 languages per person. Its grade band, 1.42 to 1.70, reflects the evidentiary grade of the sources, not sampling error. The alternative specifications we could compute place the figure between 1.53 and 1.60; an adjustment for the ages of survey respondents lowers it by at least 0.041; the value documented by official and survey instruments alone is 1.48. As a mean, the figure limits the share of people who speak two or more languages to no more than 57% (42%–70% across the band).

The unweighted mean across jurisdictions (1.87) is well above the weighted mean: individual multilingualism is concentrated in smaller populations. Group-level linguistic diversity and individual repertoire are only moderately associated (r = 0.43). A direct arithmetic test locates incomplete domestic bridging: in ten jurisdictions holding 38.9% of the audited population, mean repertoire is below the level that complete bridging through the largest first language would require; in three of them (India, Ethiopia and Côte d'Ivoire, 19.8%) the shortfall exceeds the jurisdiction's band.

The audit synthesises existing sources and involves no new fieldwork. Its central limitation is that source quality is distributed inversely to linguistic diversity. For each specification choice whose effect can be computed, we report the value the alternative would produce; the choices whose effect cannot be computed are named.

articles_hidden.title: Une approche dynamique de la réception des pré-annonces pharmaceutiques dans les réseaux sociaux - Le cas des vaccins contre la Covid-19 sur twitter
articles_hidden.authors: Olivier Caron; Christophe Benavent
articles_hidden.abstract:
à 90 %. Cette préannonce est à la fois une information et un signal stratégique porté par une entreprise intéressée au succès de son produit. Que deviennent alors le message et son émetteur
dans la conversation publique ? Les travaux sur la transmission sociale établissent qu’un message se transforme à mesure qu’il circule et s’assimile aux préoccupations du milieu qui le reçoit.
À partir de ce cadre, de l’amplification sociale du risque et du Persuasion Knowledge Model, nous étudions les préannonces d’efficacité de Pfizer/BioNTech, Moderna et AstraZeneca sur
le Twitter francophone, comparées à des événements où les mêmes entreprises font l’actualité sans être à l’origine de la nouvelle. Deux temporalités apparaissent. Le contenu du débat se
transforme presque immédiatement, puis se réinscrit dans des préoccupations préexistantes, comme l’obligation vaccinale ou l’actualité politique. Le jugement de l’entreprise apparaît plus
tard : les utilisateurs passent surtout du relais du message à l’évaluation de son émetteur, sans hausse nette de la négativité des jugements déjà exprimés. Cette bascule est absente lorsque
l’entreprise est seulement l’objet de l’information. Une préannonce met en circulation deux objets : un message et celui qui le porte.

articles_hidden.title: Unmade Ground: Displacement, Dispossession, and the Erosion of Spatial Memory Among Kurdish Forced Migrants
articles_hidden.authors: Ramazan BOZTEPE
articles_hidden.abstract: Forced displacement does not merely relocate people; it dismantles the material infrastructure through which place becomes memory. Drawing on 80 semi-structured interviews with Kurdish participants in their region of origin (n=25), Central Anatolia (n=25) and Western Europe (n=30), this article examines how the destruction, abandonment and transformation of inhabited space unmakes collective and intergenerational memory. Using Cernea's (1997) Impoverishment Risks and Reconstruction model alongside Malkki's (1992) critique of sedentarist assumptions about place, the analysis identifies four interlinked processes: urban redevelopment, rural demographic hollowing, diaspora gentrification, and the institutional foreclosure of access to common and sacred land. Participants describe memory as materially anchored, carried in streets, soil and threshold spaces, so that narrative transmission alone cannot repair its loss. The article argues that spatial memory loss is a distinct impoverishment risk inadequately addressed by existing frameworks, extends Cernea's model by specifying the memorial stakes of lost access to common property, and proposes the concept of inherited spatial memory: attachment to places the second generation has never physically inhabited.

articles_hidden.title: The geopolitics of academic publishing: the case of Kazakhstan
articles_hidden.authors: Eva Hartmann; Aikerim Bektemirova
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Publications in Scopus- and Web of Science-indexed journals have become the global benchmark of academic excellence. This article examines how Kazakhstan has placed this new ‘gold standard’ at the centre of its academic publishing policy, which has become a key part of its university reform agenda since 2010. Using a Gramscian lens on power and knowledge, we show how the government employs this policy to position itself between the West and Russia in a shifting geopolitical context. The adoption of this benchmark not only changes how Kazakhstan's academic community relates to the broader academic world. It also significantly reshapes the hierarchy within Kazakhstan’s academic community. We argue that this has profound implications for the societal role of universities and academic research and their ability to address local challenges. Our study makes both empirical and theoretical contributions to the growing literature on the geopolitics of knowledge, highlighting the interplay among local, national, and global dynamics.

articles_hidden.title: Who protects Science Diplomacy from being weaponised?  The role of domestic policies
articles_hidden.authors: Eva Hartmann
articles_hidden.abstract:
Many researchers have voiced concerns about the weaponisation of policy-relevant international research collaborations. But why does this pose a problem?
